en: The Sutra of the Precious Rain Spoken by the Buddha, Volume One: The Bestowal of the Prophecy of Non-retrogression upon Bodhisattvas, translated by the Tripitaka Master Dharmaruci of India during the Tang Dynasty.
Thus have I heard: At one time, the Bhagavat was dwelling on the summit of Mount Gayā in the city of Gayā.
He was accompanied by a great assembly of seventy-two thousand bhikṣus, all of whom were arhats whose outflows were exhausted, who were free from further afflictions, and had attained true mastery;
their minds were well-liberated and their wisdom was well-liberated;
they were like well-trained wise horses and also like great elephants.
Having done what was to be done and accomplished what was to be accomplished;
having laid down the heavy burden and attained one’s own benefit;
having exhausted all fetters of existence and clearly realized the True Dharma.
Having attained mastery of mind, they reach the supreme further shore;
having penetrated the dharma-realm, they become crown princes of the Dharma;
regarding all gain and offerings, their minds are free from attachment.
They have successfully attained the going forth and perfected the full precepts;
their understanding is complete, and they dwell upon the path to Nirvana—
with the sole exception of one person, namely the Elder Ānanda, who still remains on the stage of a learner (*śaikṣa*).

There were eighty-four thousand bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, all of whom were in their final birth before buddhahood (*ekajātipratibaddha*). They were able to enter into the presence of omniscience (*sarvajñatā*), followed it with reverence, and had attained the *dhāraṇī* gate of non-attachment. Abiding in the Śūraṅgama Samādhi, they sported with supernatural powers (*abhijñā*) and realized effortlessness (*anābhoga*). Free from all hindrances, they gave rise to great compassion that pervaded all worlds throughout the ten directions. They skillfully gathered in boundless Buddha-fields, practiced within emptiness (*śūnyatā*), and dwelt in signlessness (*animitta*). Their minds were like space, like a profound ocean, and like Mount Sumeru, unmoved by the eight winds; they were also like lotuses, unstained by attachment, like bright and pure jewels, and like refined gold. For the sake of benefiting all sentient beings, they gave rise to boundless wisdom and entered the realm of the Buddhas.
Their names were: Bodhisattva Ratnāgni, Bodhisattva Ratnapāṇi, Bodhisattva Ratnamudrāhasta,
Bodhisattva Ratnacūḍa, Bodhisattva Ratnaśikhin, Bodhisattva Ratnakūṭa, Bodhisattva Ratnagotra, and Bodhisattva Ratnaśekhara.
...Bodhisattva Ratnaketu, Bodhisattva Vajragarbha, Bodhisattva Ratnagarbha, Bodhisattva Ratnākara,
Bodhisattva Guṇākara, Bodhisattva Vimala, Bodhisattva Tathāgatagarbha, Bodhisattva Jñānagarbha, Bodhisattva Sūryagarbha,
Bodhisattva Samādhigarbha, Bodhisattva Padmagarbha, and Bodhisattva Vimukti...
The Bodhisattva Moon-Liberated, the Bodhisattva Universal Moon, the Bodhisattva Pure Moon, the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara,
the Bodhisattva Mahāsthāmaprāpta, the Bodhisattva Samantabhadra, the Bodhisattva Universal Eye, the Bodhisattva Lotus-Eye,
the Bodhisattva Universal Dignified Conduct, the Bodhisattva Upright and Majestic, and the Bodhisattva Universal Wisdom-Practice.
Dharmamati Bodhisattva, Vijayamati Bodhisattva, Uttaramati Bodhisattva, Vajramati Bodhisattva,
Siṃhavikrīḍita Bodhisattva, Mahāghoṣarāja Bodhisattva, Siṃhanāda Bodhisattva, Gambhīraghoṣa Bodhisattva, Asaṅga Bodhisattva, and Sarvamalāpagata Bodhisattva.
...the Bodhisattva Candraprabha, the Bodhisattva Sūryaprabha, the Bodhisattva Jñānaprabha,
the Bodhisattva Jñānaguṇa, the Bodhisattva Bhadraguṇa, the Bodhisattva Candraguṇa, the Bodhisattva Padmaguṇa, the Bodhisattva Ratnaguṇa,
and the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta, and so forth.
Furthermore, there were sixteen great virtuous men, with the Bodhisattva Bhadrapāla as their leader;
furthermore, there were the bodhisattvas of the Bhadrakalpa, with the Bodhisattva Maitreya as their leader;
furthermore, there were the gods of the Caturmahārājakāyika realm, with the Four Great Heavenly Kings as their leaders.
Furthermore, there was the assembly of the Trāyastriṃśa devas, with Śakra Devendra as their leader;
furthermore, there was the assembly of the Yāma devas, with Suyāma Devendra as their leader;
furthermore, there was the assembly of the Tuṣita devas, with Santuṣita Devendra as their leader.
Furthermore, there was a host of Nirmāṇarati devas, with the King of the Nirmāṇarati devas as their leader;
furthermore, there was a host of Paranirmita-vaśavartin devas, with the King of the Paranirmita-vaśavartin devas as their leader;
furthermore, there was a host of the Māra of the white portion, with the Māra Śreṣṭhin as their leader.
Furthermore, there was a host of Brahmā kings, with Mahābrahmā as their leader;
furthermore, there was a host of Śuddhāvāsa devas, with Maheśvara Deva-king as their leader;
furthermore, there were immeasurable hundreds of thousands of asura hosts, with Vemacitrin Asura-king, Śambara Asura-king, Bali Asura-king, Rāhu Asura-king, and others as their leaders.
Furthermore, there were immeasurable hundreds of thousands of hosts of nāga kings, headed by the nāga kings Anavatapta, Manasvin, Sāgara, and Vāsuki;
there were also immeasurable hundreds of thousands of nāga princes, headed by Ojasa;

and there were immeasurable hundreds of thousands of nāga queens, along with countless others—devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras, mahoragas, humans, and non-humans—all of whom had gathered for this assembly.

At that time, the summit of Mount Gayā, extending for four yojanas, was filled without a single speck of dust remaining empty, both on the ground and in the air; and in order to make offerings to the Buddha, the World-Honored One, they prepared lion thrones.

That lion throne was one yojana in height, adorned with immeasurable hundreds of thousands of exquisite silken fabrics, jeweled bells, jeweled nets, and jeweled canopies; furthermore, hundreds of thousands of silk ribbons hung down from it.

That lion throne and its surrounding area were all composed of vajra, firm and indestructible; they were as level as the palm of a hand, swept clean, strewn with various celestial flowers, and most delightful.

Upon that ground, immeasurable hundreds and thousands of golden lotuses with a thousand petals grew forth; their stalks were of lapis lazuli and their calyxes of sapphire, their fragrance being so exquisite as to delight the hearts of all.
On the four sides of that seat grew four jewel-trees, half a *yojana* in height, their branches and foliage casting shade for three *krośas*.

At that time, the Tathāgata sat upon the lion throne amidst the great assembly, turning the sublime wheel of Dharma with pure wisdom. He subdued the hosts of Māra and his enemies; unstained by worldly dharmas, he was free from all alarm or fear. He was like a lion king, like a pure pool, and like the great ocean; like Mount Sumeru, like the radiance of the sun, and like the coolness of the moon; like a great dragon king raining down the rain of Dharma everywhere, and like Brahmā, the lord of gods, who transcends all the multitudes of beings.

Surrounded before and behind by an immeasurable and boundless assembly of disciples, as well as hundreds of thousands of Śakras, Brahmās, and the World-Protecting Four Heavenly Kings, the entire multitude gazed upon his venerable countenance, their eyes never for a moment turning away.
At that time, the World-Honored One emitted a great radiance from the crown of his head, which eclipsed the entire assembly.

This emitted light was named "Universal Radiance" (*Puyao*); it had immeasurable rays of light as its retinue, pervading all worlds throughout the ten directions. Returning to the Buddha’s presence, it circled him three times to the right and entered through the opening of his face; yet, there was no change in the appearance of the Buddha’s face.
Just as the moonlight pervades the void without any difference in appearance, so too is it with this radiance entering the Buddha’s face; there is likewise no difference in appearance.
Furthermore, just as when water, ghee, oil, or the like are poured into a heap of sand, the sand and such do not undergo any change in appearance;
so too it is with light entering the facial aperture.

At that time, there was a devaputra from the eastern quarter named Candraprabha, who mounted a five-colored cloud and came to where the Buddha was. He circumambulated the Buddha three times to the right, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and withdrew to sit to one side.
The Buddha told the deva:
"Your radiance is truly rare! O Devaputra!"

In the past, before immeasurable Buddhas, you have already venerated and made offerings with various kinds of fragrant flowers, precious jewels, articles for adorning the body, clothing, bedding, food and drink, and medicinal decoctions, thereby planting all manner of roots of goodness.
"O Devaputra!
It is because you have planted immeasurable roots of goodness in the past that you now obtain such radiant illumination.
O Devaputra!"

For this reason, after my parinirvāṇa, during the final period—the fourth five-hundred-year era when the Dharma is about to perish—you shall be in the country of Mahācīna in the northeast of this Jambudvīpa; established in the stage of *avaivartika*, you are in truth a bodhisattva, and thus you shall manifest in a female body as a sovereign ruler.
Having ruled according to the True Dharma for many years, he nurtured sentient beings as if they were his own infants, causing them to cultivate the ten wholesome actions;
he was able to extensively uphold my Dharma and establish stupas and monasteries,
and furthermore, he provided offerings of clothing, food and drink, bedding, and medicinal decoctions to the śramaṇas.
Having constantly practiced the pure conduct (brahmacarya) at all times, he was named the Devaputra Candraprabha.
However, the bodies of all women have five obstructions. What are these five?
First, one cannot become a Wheel-Turning Sage King; second, Śakra; third, Mahābrahmā.
Fourth, the avaivartika bodhisattva;
fifth, the Tathāgata. O Devaputra!
"However, among the five stages, you shall attain two positions, namely, the stage of non-retrogression (*avaivartika*) and the position of a universal monarch (*cakravartin*).
O Son of Heaven!
This is the first auspicious sign."
At that time, after you have received the royal throne, a mountain shall emerge within that kingdom and five-colored clouds shall appear.
At that very moment, a mountain shall likewise appear to the north of this Mount Gayā.
"Son of Heaven!

You shall further experience immeasurable hundreds of thousands of diverse auspicious omens; I shall now describe them briefly. That land will be peaceful, secure, abundant, and prosperous, with a flourishing population that is most delightful. You should maintain right mindfulness and bestow fearlessness upon all."
"Son of Heaven!

At that time, you shall dwell for an immeasurable lifespan; subsequently, you shall proceed to the Tuṣita Heaven palace to make offerings to and serve Maitreya Bodhisattva. Until the time when Maitreya attains Buddhahood, he shall further bestow upon you the prophecy of Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."

At that time, having heard the prophecy from the Buddha, the World-Honored One, the Devaputra Candraprabha was filled with exultation and joy; his body and mind were serene. Rising from his seat, he circumambulated the Buddha seven times, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and immediately cast off his precious robes and bodily ornaments to offer them to the Buddha.
He spoke these words:
“World-Honored One!

Having now personally heard such a discourse on the causes and conditions from beginning to end in the presence of the Buddha, and having received the prediction of Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, I have attained great and wholesome benefit!”
Having spoken these words, he circumambulated the Buddha three times and withdrew to sit at one side.

At that time, to the east, beyond worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, there was a world named Padma. Its Buddha was named Padmanetra Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Perfect in Knowledge and Conduct, Sugata, Knower of the World, Unsurpassed Worthy One, Tamer of Men, Teacher of Gods and Humans, Buddha, Bhagavān. He was revealing the True Dharma for the sake of all bodhisattvas, and what he proclaimed was exclusively the Single Vehicle (Ekayāna).
In that buddha-field, there are no names for śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas; all sentient beings are avaivartika, having dedicated themselves toward anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Furthermore, the bodhisattvas in that world all take the joy of meditative concentration as their sustenance, having no need for solid food or the like.

The light of that Buddha is pure and pervasive, requiring neither the light of the sun, moon, nor the stars. The ground is level as the palm of a hand, devoid of grasses, trees, walls, bricks, rubble, mountains, or rivers, and is thus pure and magnificently adorned.
At that time, when the light emitted by Śākyamuni Buddha had pervaded the entire land, the great assembly rejoiced all the more.
Among them was a bodhisattva named Sarvanīvaraṇaviṣkambhin. For what reason did this bodhisattva receive this name?

“If any sentient beings hear his name, they will immediately be able to sever all hindrances and fetters; thus he is named ‘The One Who Stills All Obscurations. At that time, the Bodhisattva Śamathakleśa, riding upon the Buddha’s light, went to that Buddha’s abode. Descending from the lotus flower, he bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, joined his palms in reverence, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
‘World-Honored One!’”
"From where do such various pure radiances come, which gladden both body and mind?
At that time, the Tathāgata Padmanetra addressed the Bodhisattva Vigatāvaraṇa, saying:
"O son of good family!"

To the west, beyond as many world-systems as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River from this buddha-field, there is a buddha-land named Sahā. Within it dwells a Buddha named Śākyamuni Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Perfect in Knowledge and Conduct, Sugata, Knower of the World, Unsurpassed Worthy One, Tamer of Men, Teacher of Gods and Humans, Buddha, Bhagavān.
If sentient beings hear the name of that Buddha, they shall attain non-retrogression from *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*; such various kinds of pure radiance manifest from that Tathāgata!
"Any sentient beings who encounter this light will find their bodies and minds filled with joy.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Zhigai addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!..."
“By what causes and conditions does one, upon hearing the name of that Buddha, immediately attain non-retrogression from *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*?
The Buddha told the Bodhisattva Vigata-āvaraṇa: “Good son!
When that Tathāgata was formerly practicing the bodhisattva path, he made this vow:
"Once I have attained buddhahood, may all sentient beings who hear my name attain non-retrogression from *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*!"
The Bodhisattva Zhigai addressed his Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
If this is so, do all sentient beings in that world who merely hear the name of the Buddha become non-retrogressive regarding bodhi?”
The Buddha said, "No.
The Bodhisattva Zhigai (Cessation-of-Coverings) then spoke:
“World-Honored One!
Since those sentient beings have already heard the name of that Buddha, how is it that among them there are some who regress and others who do not?
The Buddha said:
“Good son! Merely by causing them to hear the name of the Tathāgata, one creates for them the causes and conditions for non-retrogression; for this reason, they are also called *avaivartika*.”
"Good son! It is like planting a seed that has not yet decayed, which later encounters the conjunction of water and soil.
What do you think? Would such a seed be said to have 'arisen'?"
The Bodhisattva Nivaranaviskambhin addressed his Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Such seeds are not subject to destruction; if they encounter the necessary causes and conditions, they will certainly sprout.”
The Buddha said, "Good son! It is so, it is so!"
By hearing the names of those Buddhas, those sentient beings will certainly become *avaivartika* and receive the prediction (*vyākaraṇa*) of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Nivāraṇaviṣkambhin addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

I now wish to go to the Sahā world to pay homage to the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Śākyamuni, to serve and make offerings to him, and to honor and praise him. I pray that you will grant me your permission!”
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Bodhisattva Vidyutpradīpa, saying: "Good son!
If you wish to go there, now is precisely the right time."
Those bodhisattvas again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
We, too, wish to go to the Sahā world to pay homage, visit, revere, and make offerings to Śākyamuni Buddha!”
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed those bodhisattvas, saying:
"Sons of good family!
If you wish to go, now is precisely the right time."
You should not give rise to thoughts of contempt or negligence toward that land. Why is this? Because the sentient beings in that land abound in greed, anger, and delusion;

they do not respect śramaṇas or brahmins, commit unrighteous acts, and are coarse, cruel, and fierce. They are hypocritical, treacherous, arrogant, and full of self-conceit; they are attached to worldly things, stingy, envious, and lazy; they violate the prohibitions and precepts, practice all manner of unwholesome deeds, and are bound by immeasurable afflictions. Yet, that Tathāgata is able to teach and transform sentient beings within such a degenerate age.
Those bodhisattvas addressed their Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Śākyamuni Tathāgata is truly rare and extraordinary; he is able to perform what is difficult to do!”
The Buddha told the bodhisattvas:
"So it is, so it is! It is just as you have said!"

In this degenerate age, if any sentient beings can give rise to pure faith for even the duration of a finger-snap, or uphold the prohibitive precepts, or abandon stinginess and greed, or give rise to great compassion and resolve their minds upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, they shall surpass those who practice for hundreds of thousands of kalpas in pure lands.

At that time, the Bodhisattva Nivāraṇaviṣkambhin and the other bodhisattvas, having received the Buddha’s instruction, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and set out from their original dwelling, intending to travel to the Sahā world.

Desiring to make offerings to Śākyamuni Buddha, they immediately manifested various supernatural transformations, displaying jewel trees, flower trees, fruit trees, and kalpavṛkṣa trees, all adorned with pure gold, lapis lazuli, and crystal; these were lofty, vast, and exquisite, with branches spreading in lush profusion.
Furthermore, they manifested various garments, ornaments for the body, wonderful fragrances, and precious canopies, as well as the music of the devas, descending like clouds.
Manifesting such immeasurable transformations, he addressed the assembly of bodhisattvas, saying:
"O virtuous ones! That Sahā world is filled with manifold sufferings and afflictions; each of you should manifest spiritual miracles to cause those sentient beings to attain supreme bliss!"
At that time, all the bodhisattvas replied, "So be it!

Then, from the bodies of the Bodhisattva Vighuṣṭaśabda and the other bodhisattvas, various kinds of pure radiance issued forth. This light pervaded the trichiliocosm; all those in the realms of hell, the animal kingdom, and the world of Yama who were touched by this light were freed from suffering and attained peace and happiness. They turned toward one another with hearts of loving-kindness, abandoning greed and hatred, and regarded each other as they would their own parents.
Furthermore, within the darkness of the world where the light of the sun and moon cannot reach, all became brilliantly illuminated so that beings could see one another.

This majestic radiance shone forth, filling the entire world; it pervaded everything from the Iron Ring Mountains, the Great Iron Ring Mountains, Mount Mucilinda, Mount Mahāmucilinda, and other dark mountains, up to the Brahma-world and down to the Avīci Hell, leaving no place untouched.
Wherever his majestic light reaches, all sentient beings who seek food obtain food; those who seek clothing obtain clothing;
those who seek vehicles obtain vehicles; those who seek wealth obtain wealth;
the blind regain their sight, and the deaf regain their hearing.
The insane shall attain right mindfulness; those who suffer shall obtain happiness;
and those who are pregnant shall naturally find peace.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Zhigai (Vighuṣṭa), together with the other bodhisattvas, having arrived at the Sahā world, proceeded to Mount Gayā.
By the majestic spiritual power of the bodhisattvas, the trichiliocosm was completely covered with jeweled nets, appearing in magnificent array.

Throughout the void, great clouds spread everywhere, raining down exquisite celestial lotuses, various flowers, and wonderful fruits; or they rained down celestial flower garlands, fine incense, powdered incense, kāṣāya robes, garments, pearl canopies, banners, and streamers.
When these various kinds of offerings were manifested, all sentient beings in the Sahā world attained the most supreme and immeasurable happiness.
At that time, by the power of the Bodhisattva’s majestic spiritual authority, all stumps, trees, and groves on the summit of Mount Gayā and throughout all directions ceased to appear.

Furthermore, it revealed all the jewel trees, flower trees, fruit trees, sandalwood, aloeswood, and kalpavṛkṣa trees, their branches, leaves, flowers, and fruits adorned in successive order, most lovely and delightful; while celestial music played in the midst of the void, making offerings and offering praise.

At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Vidyutpradīpa rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, joined his palms toward the Buddha in reverent salutation, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
"I wish to ask the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha a few questions; I only pray that you will grant me your permission.
The Buddha said to the Bodhisattva Nivaraṇaviṣkambhin, "Good son!..."
"In accordance with your questions, I shall explain them for you; all Tathāgatas grant their approval.
Now, you should properly restrain your own mind!
Having heard the Buddha’s permission, Ceasing-Obstruction Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
How does a bodhisattva attain the perfection of giving?
How does he attain the perfection of pure ethical discipline?”
How is the perfection of patience established?
How is the perfection of diligence established?
How is the perfection of meditative concentration established?
What is the perfection of wisdom?
What is the perfection of skillful means?
What is the perfection of great vows?
"How is the perfection of supreme power attained?
How is the perfection of wisdom attained,
World-Honored One?"
How do the bodhisattvas become equal to earth?
How do they become equal to water?
How do they become equal to fire?
How is one equal to the wind?
How is one equal to space?
How does one become like the moon?
How does one become like the sun?
How is one like a lion?
How is one well-tamed?
What is the nature of quiescence?
What is it like a lotus flower?
What is the vast mind?
What is the pure mind? What is the mind free from hesitation?
How does one attain wisdom like the ocean?
How does one attain skill in subtle wisdom?
How does one achieve eloquence that accords with reason?
How does one attain the eloquence of liberation?
How does one attain pure eloquence?
How can one cause all sentient beings to be joyful and satisfied?
How does one speak so that others believe and accept it?
What is meant by one who is able to preach the Dharma?
How does one attain practice in accordance with the Dharma?
And how does one attain skillfulness regarding all phenomena?
How does one attain skillfulness regarding the dharma-realm?
How does one practice emptiness?
How does one practice signlessness?
How does one practice wishlessness?
How does one attain the intrinsic nature of loving-kindness?
How does one attain the intrinsic nature of compassion?
How does one attain the practice of joy?
How does one attain the practice of equanimity?
How can one attain the playful exercise of supernormal powers?
How can one attain freedom from the eight states of no leisure?
How can one abide in the bodhicitta without regressing?
And how can one attain the supernormal knowledge of recollecting past lives?
How does one come to draw near to spiritual friends?
How does one come to distance oneself from evil associates?
And how does one realize the Dharma-body of the Tathāgata?
How does one cultivate and attain a vajra-body?
How does one become a great caravan leader?
How does one attain skillfulness regarding the path?
How does one preach without error?
How does one constantly attain all states of meditative equipoise (*samāhita*)?
How does a bodhisattva accept rag-robes (*pāṃśukūla*)?
How does one come to make use of the three robes?
How does one come to not follow after others?
How does one always practice begging for food?
How does one attain sitting in a single session?
How does one attain eating a single meal?
How does one attain the state of an araṇya-dweller?
How does one dwell under a tree?
How does one dwell in the open air?
How does one dwell among the tombs?
How does one attain the practice of constant sitting?
How does one sit according to whatever seat is spread out?
And how is one a practitioner of yoga?
How can one uphold the Sūtra Piṭaka? How can one uphold the Vinaya Piṭaka?
And how does one attain the perfection of rules of conduct, spheres of activity, and majestic decorum?
How can one become free from stinginess and envy?
How can one attain a mind of equanimity toward all sentient beings?
How can one skillfully make offerings to the Tathāgata?
How does one subdue the pride of self?
How does one possess abundant pure faith?
How does one attain skillfulness regarding the conventional world?
How does one attain skillfulness regarding the ultimate truth?
How does one deeply enter into skillfulness regarding dependent origination?
And how does one achieve self-knowledge?
How can one know the world?
How can one be born in a pure buddha-field?
How can one dwell in the womb without being defiled by dust and impurity?
How does one delight in leaving the household life?
How does one obtain a pure livelihood?
How does one become free from weariness?
How does one respectfully follow and obey the Tathāgata’s instructions, never transgressing them?
How does one maintain a harmonious countenance with a smile, forever free from frowning?
How does one become fully endowed with extensive learning and dhāraṇī?
How does one skillfully embrace the true Dharma?
How does one become a prince of the Dharma?
And how does one come to be followed by Śakra, Brahmā, and the World-Protectors?
How does one understand the intentions and latent dispositions of others?
What constitutes skillfulness in maturing sentient beings?
And how does one attain a state of dwelling in accordance [with reality]?
How does one dwell in common peace and security?
How does one attain skillfulness in the matters of gathering [disciples]?
How does one achieve the perfection of the primary and secondary marks of physical excellence?
How does one obtain the basis for what is to be done?
How does one become like the king of medicinal trees?
How does one diligently cultivate the karma of merit?
"How does one cultivate and realize skillfulness in transformations?
How does one swiftly realize unsurpassed bodhi?
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Bodhisattva Nivaranaviskambhin, saying:
“Excellent, excellent, noble son! For the sake of benefiting immeasurable sentient beings,
for the sake of bringing peace and happiness to immeasurable sentient beings, and out of compassion for the entire world, you have asked about such a meaning!”
"Listen attentively, listen attentively, and reflect upon it well!
I shall speak for your sake.
At that time, having heard these words, the Bodhisattva Vighuṣṭaśabda addressed the Buddha, saying:
“Certainly, World-Honored One!
We wish and desire to hear it.
The Buddha said:
“Good son! There are ten dharmas which, if bodhisattva-mahāsattvas can accomplish, they will attain the perfection of giving (*dānapāramitā*). What are these ten?
First, the accomplishment of the gift of Dharma;
second, the accomplishment of the gift of fearlessness;
third, the accomplishment of the gift of material wealth.
Fourth, they achieve giving without expectation;
fifth, they achieve giving with compassion;
sixth, they achieve giving without contempt.
Seventh, they achieve the gift of reverence;
eighth, they achieve the gift of worship;
ninth, they achieve the gift of non-reliance.
Tenth, they achieve pure giving.
"Good son, how does a bodhisattva achieve the gift of Dharma?
What is called embracing the true Dharma means to receive, uphold, read, and recite it without seeking anything for oneself.

It is not for the sake of gain, offerings, or honor; nor is it for the sake of fame or to surpass others. Rather, it is solely for the purpose of causing the sins of all sentient beings suffering from affliction to be extinguished, that one expounds the sublime Dharma without any expectation of reward.

Just as he expounds the sublime Dharma to kings, princes, and even the sons of caṇḍālas with a mind that is without duality, how much more so would his mind not be unequal when expounding the Dharma to the entire great assembly!
Although they practice giving, they do not rely on it to give rise to conceit in their minds.
Good son! This is called a bodhisattva’s accomplishment of the gift of Dharma.
“Good son! How does a bodhisattva accomplish the gift of fearlessness?
It is said that a bodhisattva personally relinquishes punishment and all weapons, and also teaches others to train in relinquishing punishment and all weapons.”
Furthermore, one observes all sentient beings with the thought that they are like one's parents, like one's children, or like one's kinsmen.
For what reason does a bodhisattva form such thoughts?
As the Buddha has said:
"There is not a single sentient being who has not previously been my parent, child, or relative!
Even toward minute insects, one should cut flesh from one's own body to give as a gift; how much more so toward vast sentient beings—how could one cause them to be terrified?"
"This is called a bodhisattva’s accomplishment of the gift of fearlessness.
Good son, how does a bodhisattva accomplish the gift of material wealth?"

That is to say, when a bodhisattva perceives that all sentient beings are committing extremely evil deeds, he employs the means of giving material wealth to attract them, causing them to abandon their misdeeds and establish them in states of virtue.
Again, he gave rise to this reflection:
"The Buddha has said:
'Generosity is the bodhi of a bodhisattva.'"
"By means of giving, one attains the severance of three kinds of unwholesome dharmas, namely: stinginess, envy, and evil thoughts.
Therefore, I should emulate the Tathāgata and constantly practice giving according to whatever wealth I possess.
"Even though they give, they do not give rise to a mind of pride.
This is called a bodhisattva’s accomplishment of the gift of material wealth. "Good son!"
How does a bodhisattva accomplish the giving that is free from expectation?
It means that when practicing generosity, one never does so for the sake of oneself, nor for the sake of wealth and possessions, nor for the sake of one's retinue, nor for the sake of gain and honor.

However, when Bodhisattvas practice giving, their minds are pure; by virtue of this cause and condition, they practice giving while remaining far removed from all expectations and the desire for recompense.
This is called the bodhisattva’s accomplishment of giving without expectation. "Good son,
how does a bodhisattva accomplish the giving of compassion?"

When a bodhisattva sees sentient beings undergoing suffering and affliction—starving, thirsty, destitute, naked, clad in tattered rags, solitary, without protection, without refuge, devoid of meritorious deeds, and wandering aimlessly—the bodhisattva reflects upon this and gives rise to a heart of compassion, thinking:

"For the sake of benefiting those sentient beings, I have resolved to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. Yet these sentient beings undergo suffering and affliction; they have no destination, no protector, and no place of refuge, as they wander through birth and death."
"When shall I become a refuge, a protector, and a place of reliance for all sentient beings?
Driven by such compassion that envelops his mind, the bodhisattva, at all times and at all seasons, gives whatever objects he possesses to those sentient beings.
Although he possesses roots of goodness that benefit sentient beings, he never relies upon them to give rise to arrogance.
This is called a bodhisattva’s accomplishment of compassionate giving. "Good son!..."
How does a bodhisattva accomplish the practice of giving without contempt?
It means that when giving, one never discards or treats the recipient with disdain;
one is never possessed of anger, resentment, or a sense of bargaining.
He does not rely on wealth and status to become arrogant and haughty;
he does not seek extensive learning for the sake of fame, nor does he indulge in pride or negligence.
When giving, he does so with joy and reverence, honoring and praising the recipient, and bestows the gift with his own hands.
This is called the bodhisattva’s accomplishment of the gift of non-contempt. "Good son,
how does a bodhisattva accomplish the gift of reverence?"

That is to say, when a bodhisattva sees an ācārya, an upādhyāya, or any venerable one who practices the holy life, they pay homage with reverence, prostrate themselves, and inquire after their well-being; whatever roots of goodness are thus performed, they dedicate them, wishing: "May I likewise perform these deeds and may they be accomplished."
This is called the bodhisattva’s accomplishment of respectful giving. "Good son,
how does a bodhisattva accomplish the giving of offerings?
Regarding what is called a bodhisattva’s offering to the Triple Gem:
how does one make offerings to the Buddha?

This refers to [offering] flowers, incense, scattered perfumes, burning incense, or the smearing and sweeping of the ground within a stūpa of the Tathāgata; furthermore, if a stūpa is damaged, one should repair it. This is called a bodhisattva’s excellent offering to the Buddha.
What is the dharma of making offerings?

It refers to when bodhisattvas hear the true Dharma, and whether they transcribe it, receive and uphold it, read and recite it, master it, contemplate it, or cultivate it—contemplating it without inversion and cultivating it without inversion—this is called the bodhisattva’s skillful offering of the Dharma.
What is meant by making offerings to the Saṃgha?

It refers to providing robes, food and drink, bedding, and medicinal decoctions, down to even water vessels; when all such requisites are fully supplied, this is called a Bodhisattva’s skillful offering to the Saṃgha.
When one makes offerings to the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha in this manner, it is called the bodhisattva’s accomplishment of the gift of offering. "Good son,
how does a bodhisattva accomplish the gift that is without dependence?"

When a bodhisattva practices giving, they never seek the fruit of the position of a celestial king or rebirth among other devas, nor do they seek the status of a human king or minor rulers; this is called a bodhisattva’s accomplishment of non-reliant giving.
“Good son! How does a bodhisattva accomplish pure giving?

It means that when a bodhisattva practices giving, they observe that the gift, the giver, and the recipient are all not truly existent; being free from all obstacles, attachments, and faults, this is called a bodhisattva accomplishing pure giving.”
“Good son! If one can accomplish these ten kinds of dharmas, this is called a bodhisattva accomplishing the perfection of giving (dānapāramitā).
Furthermore, good son!”
When a bodhisattva accomplishes ten dharmas, they are able to fulfill the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīlapāramitā*). What are these ten?
First, guarding the discipline of the *prātimokṣa* vows;
Second, guarding the bodhisattva’s code of pure ethical discipline;
third, remaining far removed from all feverish afflictions;
fourth, remaining far removed from improper reflection.
Fifth, fear regarding the various karmic actions one has performed;
sixth, fear regarding the transgressions one has committed;
seventh, fear upon seeing the possessions of others.
Eighth, firmness in one's commitment;
ninth, attaining pure ethical discipline (*śīla*) without dependence on anything external;
tenth, the threefold purity of ethical discipline.
“Good son! How does a bodhisattva guard the prātimokṣa restraint?
It means that a bodhisattva skillfully studies the sūtras and vinaya teachings spoken by the Tathāgata, and skillfully undertakes the training rules.”

When Bodhisattvas practice and train in the precepts, they do so because they do not cling to their lineage, do not adhere to divergent views, do not become attached to their retinues, and do not perceive the faults of individuals, thereby giving rise to a mind of reverence. These training rules practiced by Bodhisattvas are called the Bodhisattva’s observance of the Prātimokṣa discipline.
"How does one guard the bodhisattva's code of pure ethical discipline?
It is as follows: a bodhisattva reflects thus:
'If I were to study only the Prātimokṣa, I would never attain unexcelled, complete, and perfect enlightenment.'"
Therefore, the bodhisattva thinks: "I should train myself in the bodhisattva training rules and the bodhisattva vows as taught by the Tathāgatas in the sūtras!"
"What are the training precepts (*śikṣāpada*) of a bodhisattva?
What is the bodhisattva’s code of discipline (*vinaya-śīla*)?

It means that bodhisattvas do not dwell in improper places, speak in accordance with the proper time, and know the right moment and the right occasion. If a bodhisattva does not act in this way, it will cause sentient beings to lack reverence and faith."
Because this bodhisattva accords with all sentient beings, he leads them to enlightenment;

and for the sake of swiftly perfecting the provisions for his own enlightenment, he accomplishes the dharmas of conduct and deportment—possessing a gentle voice, concise eloquence, and freedom from attachment, constantly cultivating tranquility, and maintaining a serene and joyful countenance.

These bodhisattvas, having accomplished the points of training within the sūtras spoken by the Tathāgata and having cultivated the morality of restraint, are said to be guarding the pure ethical discipline of a bodhisattva.
"How does a bodhisattva remain far removed from all entanglements, obscurations, and burning afflictions?

It is because a bodhisattva is not scorched by the poisonous fires of greed, hatred, and delusion, nor are they scorched by the burning affliction of lacking the necessary conditions and requisites; for bodhisattvas cultivate the methods that can eliminate greed and remain far removed from the conditions that give rise to greed."
What is the antidote for the removal of desire?
What is the condition that gives rise to craving?
It is said that the cultivation of the contemplation of impurity is the antidote for the removal of desire, while the exquisite forms of the world are the conditions that give rise to craving.
How does one practice the contemplation of the impurity of phenomena?

It refers to the bodhisattvas observing their own bodies as consisting of hair, body hair, nails, teeth, skin, blood vessels, muscles, bones, marrow, spleen, kidneys, heart, lungs, liver, gallbladder, intestines, stomach, the two receptacles of raw and cooked food, fat, grease, brain, membranes, nasal mucus, saliva, spittle, tears, pus, sweat, adipose tissue, phlegm, sores, and filth, along with excrement and urine—overflowing with various kinds of foul-smelling and impure substances.

Observing the nature of impurity in this way, one develops a profound sense of weary detachment and does not give rise to desire. Even those who are stubborn, dull-witted, deluded, deranged, or too young to understand do not give rise to desire upon seeing such things; how much less so, then, for the wise!
By means of this, the bodhisattva cultivates the contemplation of impurity.
How does he distance himself from the conditions that give rise to craving?

When a bodhisattva sees the beautiful and exquisite features of the world, or lovely forms and images, and consequently gives rise to defiled attachment, finding delight in body and mind, he reflects to himself:
"As the World-Honored One has said:
'The realm of desire is like an illusion or a dream; once awakened, it is no more.
How could a wise person give rise to a mind of craving toward such illusory and dreamlike objects?"
This is called a bodhisattva’s cultivation of the antidote for the very nature of desire and its arising conditions.
How does a bodhisattva cultivate the antidote for hatred?
How does he distance himself from the conditions that give rise to hatred?
It is said that a bodhisattva extensively cultivates loving-kindness (*maitrī*) toward all sentient beings; by reason of this, they counteract and eliminate hatred (*vyāpāda*).

When hatred arises and there is attachment to causes and conditions, those bodhisattvas suppress and extinguish the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) of hatred through this means. This is called a bodhisattva’s cultivation for the counteraction of hatred and the arising of the conditions for hatred.
How does a bodhisattva cultivate the antidote to delusion?
How does he distance himself from the conditions that give rise to delusion?

By observing in this way, the bodhisattva becomes free from delusion; because he is free from delusion, he is without feverish afflictions and remains detached from desires and material requisites. This is called the bodhisattva’s cultivation of the antidote to delusion and the distancing of conditions that give rise to delusion.
"How does a bodhisattva become far removed from improper reflection?
It means that when a bodhisattva sits alone in a secluded place, they never reflect thus:
'I dwell in a secluded place, living without distraction; I am following the Vinaya-dharma of the Tathāgata.'"
"The other śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas all dwell in confusion and are attached to many things; they do not accord with the Tathāgata’s Vinaya-dharma.
This is called the bodhisattva’s avoidance of improper reflection.
"What is meant by a bodhisattva’s dread of performing unwholesome deeds?

It means that bodhisattvas give rise to right reflection and cultivate all wholesome dharmas, for the Tathāgata has taught that bhikṣus and others should reverently guard the pure precepts, single-mindedly practice the work of meditative concentration, and study and learn in prajñā."
Why is this? Because by performing meritorious deeds with a mind of reverence, one can attract the retribution of being handsome and lovely, as well as superior retributions.
When a bodhisattva thus distances himself from all unwholesome karma, this is called a bodhisattva who is able to fear the karmic actions he performs.
"What is meant by a bodhisattva’s dread of transgressions?

It means that when a bodhisattva perceives even a transgression as small as a mote of dust, they give rise to profound fear; they harbor great trepidation even toward minor offenses, let alone feeling any sense of rejoicing toward numerous transgressions!"
Why is this? Because it is known that the Tathāgata has said:
"Bhikṣus, you should know!"
Taking a large dose of poison can cause death, and taking even a small dose of poison can also cause death.
Bhikṣus, you should know this:
if one commits many offenses, one will be reborn in the evil realms; if one commits even a few offenses, one will likewise be reborn in the evil realms.
When a bodhisattva engages in such correct reflection, they feel alarm and dread regarding transgressions; this is called a bodhisattva’s alarm and dread of transgression.
What is a bodhisattva’s dread of seeing the property of others?

This means that this bodhisattva is mutually trusted in heart by the brahmins, kṣatriyas, and others of the cities and villages; those brahmins, kṣatriyas, and others may entrust to the bodhisattva gold, silver, mani-jewels, pearls, conch shells, coral, jade, lapis lazuli, and various articles for the maintenance of life.

When a bodhisattva receives [an offering], he does so alone and without a second; though he may have no sense of personal dread or hesitation, the bodhisattva never entertains an evil thought toward the recipient nor does he hastily consume it.

Furthermore, when a bodhisattva oversees communal affairs—whether it be property belonging to a stūpa, property belonging to the Saṃgha from the four quarters, or property belonging to the general community (saṃghika)—he likewise does not consume any of those goods for himself.
Why is this? Because the World-Honored One has said:
"If others have not given food, drink, articles of livelihood, or any other things, one must not use them."

"Once the Bodhisattva has formed such a reflection, he would rather cut his own flesh and eat it than ever encroach upon the property of others; this is called the Bodhisattva’s dread of seeing the possessions of others."
"What is meant by a bodhisattva’s firm resolve?

It means that even if an evil Māra or the hosts of Māra-devas should come to disturb the bodhisattva with various exquisite desires in order to incite greed and attachment, the bodhisattva’s mind remains free from delusion or clinging toward them and does not regress; this is called a bodhisattva’s firm resolve."
"How does a bodhisattva remain unattached in mind toward pure ethical discipline (*śīla*)?
It means that while bodhisattvas well protect their prohibitive precepts, they never give rise to the thought:
'By means of this ethical discipline, may I be born in the heavens or in the families of kings and the like.'"
This is called the bodhisattva’s state of non-attachment in the mind toward pure ethical discipline (*śīla*).
What is the bodhisattva’s purity of the three spheres of ethical discipline?
It means that all bodhisattvas attain complete purity in body, speech, and mind.
How does the body attain purity?
It means that one becomes forever free from all unwholesome conduct of the body.
What constitutes unwholesome conduct of the body?
Because they constantly distance themselves from killing, taking what is not given, and sexual misconduct, this is called the purification of the body.
What is the purification of speech for a bodhisattva?
It means that one attains permanent separation from all verbal misconduct.
What constitutes verbal misconduct?
It refers to speech that is false, divisive, harsh, or frivolous; because one constantly distances oneself from these, it is called the purification of speech.
How does a bodhisattva attain purity of mind?
It means that all unwholesome conduct of the mind is forever abandoned.
What constitutes unwholesome conduct of the mind?
This means that because one has completely distanced oneself from lustful attachment, malice, and false views, this is called the purity of the mind.
This is called the Bodhisattva’s purity of the three wheels of ethical discipline.
“Good son! When a bodhisattva mahāsattva accomplishes these ten kinds of dharmas, they attain the perfection of śīla.
*The Sūtra of the Precious Rain Spoken by the Buddha*, Scroll One.
The Sutra of the Precious Rain Spoken by the Buddha, Volume Two,
translated by the Tang Dynasty Indian Tripiṭaka Master Dharmaruci.
"Furthermore, son of good family, when Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas accomplish ten kinds of dharmas, they attain patience (kṣānti)."
Perfection. What are the ten?
First, the perfection of internal patience;
Second, the perfection of external patience;
third, the perfection of patience regarding the Dharma;
fourth, the perfection of patience in accordance with the Buddha's teachings.
Fifth, the perfection of patience that is without limits;
sixth, the perfection of non-conceptual patience;
seventh, the perfection of patience that does not depend on external circumstances.
Eighth, the perfection of patience free from malice;
ninth, the perfection of compassionate patience;
tenth, the perfection of patient endurance through vows.
“What is the bodhisattva’s perfection of internal patience?

Son of good family, it refers to when a bodhisattva is able to dwell peacefully in all internal sorrow, lamentation, suffering, and affliction, with a mind free from oppression; this is called the bodhisattva’s perfection of internal patience.”
"What is the perfection of a bodhisattva’s external patience?

Son of good family, it means that when a bodhisattva hears others using coarse language, reviling, or slandering their parents, relatives, ācāryas, or upādhyāyas, or hearing them denigrating the Buddha, Dharma, and Saṅgha jewels—having heard this, the bodhisattva does not give rise to anger or resentment, nor does he retaliate with slander; furthermore, he is not pursued by the latent tendencies of hatred, but endures those afflictions and abides in peace. This is called the perfection of a bodhisattva’s external patience."
“What is the perfection of the bodhisattva’s patience regarding the Dharma?

It means that when bodhisattvas hear all the profound and subtle meanings of the Dharma within the sūtras spoken by the Buddha—namely, that they neither come nor go, that their intrinsic nature is quiescent, that they are free from conceptual grasping, and that they are by nature in nirvāṇa—they are not startled and not terrified, but reflect thus:
‘If I do not understand these profound and wondrous dharmas, I shall ultimately never attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi!’”

"By means of these causes and conditions, one gathers all dharmas, contemplates and practices them, and gives rise to faith and understanding in the mind; this is called the Bodhisattva’s perfection of dharma-patience (dharmanidhyāna-kṣānti).
What is the Bodhisattva’s perfection of patience in accordance with the Buddha's teachings (buddhānuśāsana-kṣānti)?"
That is to say, if a bodhisattva gives rise to anger and intends to cause harm, the bodhisattva should reflect in this way:
"From what does this anger arise?"
From what does it cease?
By whom is it originated?
How is it originated, such that it possesses an object of perception?
The Bodhisattva reflects in this way:
"That cause by which [suffering] could arise is utterly unfindable;
that cause by which it could cease is likewise unfindable."
"Since that which can give rise [to anger] does not exist, that which is given rise to does not exist;
even the objects of perception are all unattainable.

By means of this, the bodhisattva dwells in patient endurance, and since there is no basis for the arising of anger, this is called the bodhisattva’s fulfillment of patience in accordance with the Buddha's teaching.
"What is the bodhisattva’s perfection of patience that is without limitation?
It means that bodhisattvas do not practice patience during the day but not at night,
nor do they practice patience at night but not during the day."
One is patient toward one's own country but not toward other countries;
one is patient toward other countries but not toward one's own country.
One is patient toward those who have renown but not toward those without renown.
It is not that one endures toward those who lack renown but does not endure toward those who possess renown.
Because of this, a bodhisattva is able to endure at all times and in all lands, whether renown is present or absent; this is called the bodhisattva’s perfection of patience without limitation.
"What is the perfection of non-conceptual patience of a bodhisattva?

It means that bodhisattvas do not practice patience only toward parents, wives, children, and relatives, while being unable to endure others; rather, bodhisattvas are able to practice patience even toward those as lowly as caṇḍālas. This is called the perfection of non-conceptual patience of a bodhisattva."
“What is the perfection of the bodhisattva’s patience that does not depend on external circumstances?

It means that when bodhisattvas practice patience, they do not do so for the sake of wealth and possessions, nor out of fear, nor to perform a favor, nor to conform to worldly conventions or out of a sense of shame; rather, such bodhisattvas possess a natural and constant patience. This is called the perfection of the bodhisattva’s patience that does not depend on external circumstances.”
“How does a bodhisattva attain the perfection of patience free from anger?
It means that even if a bodhisattva has not encountered the conditions for anger, nor has encountered the anger of others, their mind remains constantly composed and patient.”

If a Bodhisattva encounters adverse conditions or the anger of others—whether being slighted, struck with fists, beaten with hands, harmed by knives or clubs, or reviled with harsh words—he reflects thus:

"The karma for being slighted and reviled was created by me; I must now receive its fruit. It is certainly not created by my parents or relatives; therefore, I shall joyfully endure it. Furthermore, this is not experienced by the internal or external earth element; the same applies to the water, fire, and wind elements."

"Because the Bodhisattva observes without error in this way, when encountering the conditions for either anger or non-anger, he is able to endure both; this is called the Bodhisattva’s attainment of the perfection of patience free from malice."
“What is the perfection of a bodhisattva’s compassionate patience?

It means that when a bodhisattva acts as a sovereign—whether as a king or a minor ruler—possessing great wealth and abundant resources, over all those sentient beings who are impoverished and suffering; and when those impoverished and suffering beings revile, rebuke, or harass him, he never harbors resentment or a mind of malice, nor does he exalt himself by manifesting his lordly power. Rather, he gives rise only to this thought:
‘These sentient beings are those whom I have taken under my care; I should nourish and protect them!’”
Because of this, the bodhisattva does not give rise to malice.
For these reasons, they arouse a mind of great compassion and abide in patient endurance; this is called the bodhisattva’s perfection of compassionate patience.
“What is the perfection of the bodhisattva’s vow-endurance?
It is when a bodhisattva reflects thus:

‘I have made a lion’s roar before all those Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas, vowing to cultivate awakening; once I have attained perfect awakening, I shall rescue and deliver all sentient beings from the ocean of saṃsāra and the mire of afflictions.’”

Because a bodhisattva does not give rise to anger or affliction on this account, I should therefore practice with diligent effort for the sake of their deliverance and maturation; desiring to discipline and bring happiness to sentient beings, if I myself give rise to anger or cause them harm, I am then lacking in forbearance.
"How can one give rise to compassionate patience (kṣānti) in order to rescue and deliver sentient beings? "Good son!
It is like a skilled physician who is well-versed in acupuncture; seeing a sentient being suffering from cataracts in the eyes, he reflects thus:"
"I ought to take pity on him and remove his cataracts so that he may be free from the obstruction of darkness.
Having thus reflected, the skilled physician then suffered from blurred vision himself.
"Good son! What do you think?
Is this physician capable of curing the cataracts of those sentient beings' eyes and removing the obscuration of darkness?
Cessation-of-Obscurations Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying:
"No, World-Honored One!
The Buddha said to the Bodhisattva Vimalacchanna: "Good son!
The Bodhisattva is also like this! He reflects:

"I should not now use the needle of prajñā to cut away the cataracts of the world; since my own mind is obscured by the darkness of ignorance, how could I extinguish the delusions of ignorance in others?"

"By reason of these causes and conditions, he never inflicts harm; he cultivates patience and dwells in tranquility. This is called a bodhisattva attaining the perfection of the patience of the vow. Good son!"
When a bodhisattva accomplishes these ten kinds of dharmas, they attain the perfection of patience.
"Furthermore, son of good family,
when a bodhisattva accomplishes ten kinds of dharmas, they attain the perfection of diligence."
What are the ten? First, adamantine diligence;
second, the diligence of attaining the unattainable.
Third, diligence that is free from the two extremes;
fourth, vast diligence; fifth, blazing diligence;
Sixth, his nature is ever-diligent;
seventh, his diligence is pure;
eighth, his diligence is unshared.
Ninth, diligence that does not disparage others;
tenth, diligence that is free from arrogance. "Good son!
What is vajra-like diligence?
It refers to the diligence initiated by bodhisattvas, who dwell diligently within the realm of sentient beings, causing those who have not attained nirvāṇa to realize nirvāṇa,
and causing those who have not attained liberation to attain liberation.
To those who are not yet liberated, may they attain liberation;
to those who are not yet at peace, may they attain peace;
to those who have not yet attained manifest perfect enlightenment, may they attain manifest perfect enlightenment.
The Bodhisattva dwells thus, diligently practicing.
At that time, a celestial Māra, seeking a vulnerability to cause destruction, approaches the Bodhisattva and speaks these words:
"O Son of Good Family!..."
Do not exert yourself with such arduous diligence. Why is this?

Although I have previously initiated such diligence and dwelt in the cultivation of the realms of all sentient beings, those who had not yet attained nirvāṇa were led to realize it; [yet even so, the realms of sentient beings remain inexhaustible].
May those who have not yet crossed over all cross over;
may those who have not yet attained liberation attain liberation;
may those who have not yet found peace find peace.
To cause those who have not yet attained manifest perfect enlightenment to attain it—such diligence deceives and deludes the foolish; it is entirely false and not the true Dharma.

"Good son! Among those who thus diligently cultivate and give rise to vigor, I have never seen a single sentient being who has been able to manifest equal and perfect awakening in *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*."
"Good son! I know immeasurable koṭis of sentient beings who are all capable of realizing the nirvāṇa of the two vehicles. Good son!"
"You and your followers are striving diligently for illusory dharmas; quickly abandon this mind and be free from all suffering and affliction!
At that time, the Bodhisattva thought to himself:
"This is certainly Māra who seeks to vex and destroy me!"
Having realized this, the Bodhisattva knew it was the Mara’s speech and addressed him, saying:
"Your evil thoughts seek to destroy me; you need only worry about yourself, and do not worry about my affairs."
The Blessed One has already said: "Māra Pāpīyān!
All in the world follow their respective karma; whether individually or collectively, they experience rebirth in various places."
“Māra! You too now follow after karma; you experience your place of birth both individually and collectively.
You should proceed according to your karma in this way; do not disturb me, for it is without benefit and will cause you to suffer for a long night!”
At that time, Māra, his intellect and wisdom being narrow and inferior, felt shame within himself; he immediately abandoned his evil intent and vanished from sight.
It is for this reason, O Bodhisattva!

When all the Māra kings and their demonic hosts come to harass and disturb you, seeking your weaknesses and attempting to destroy you, the Bodhisattva’s mind is ultimately unmoved; remaining undaunted, courageous, firm, and non-retrogressive—this is called the Bodhisattva’s adamantine diligence (*vajra-vīrya*).
“Good son! What is the bodhisattva’s unexcelled diligence?

It refers to when bodhisattvas initiate such various forms of diligence that even other bodhisattvas who have long accumulated pure karma and abide in true nature can never equal this bodhisattva who initiates such various forms of diligence—not by a numerical fraction, nor by a *kāla* fraction, nor even by calculation, analogy, or the *upaniṣad* fraction; how much less so for all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas!”

In this regard, the power of diligence through which a bodhisattva generates the resolve for awakening is able to encompass all Buddha-dharmas and further enables them to abandon all sinful karma and unwholesome dharmas; this is called the bodhisattva’s attainment of unsurpassed diligence.
"What is the bodhisattva’s diligence that avoids the two extremes?
It means that bodhisattvas constantly arouse diligence that neither increases nor decreases. Why is this?"

Because of excessive arrogance born from superior birth and because of excessive indolence born from inferior birth, one's diligence neither increases nor decreases; this is called the bodhisattva’s diligence that avoids the two extremes.
"What is the vast diligence of a bodhisattva?
It refers to the diligence initiated by bodhisattvas, thinking:
'May I thus attain the wondrous form and majestic dignity of a Tathāgata!'"
"The Buddhas possess the mark of the invisible crown of the head, the halo, and the secondary signs, all perfectly and subtly complete!
Furthermore, he arouses such diligence:
"May I attain the immeasurable and unimpeded great wisdom of the Buddhas, as well as their great majesty, power, and the nature of ultimate reality!"
"This is called the vast diligence of a bodhisattva. Good son,
what is the blazing diligence of a bodhisattva?"

This means that when bodhisattvas exert diligence, they forever leave behind all defilements and faults; like mani jewels and purple gold, which are free from all dust and impurities and possess a brilliant, magnificent, and radiant luster.
When a bodhisattva’s diligence is thus blazing, they are forever free from all dust, defilements, and afflictions.
What are called the dusts of diligence?
What are called the afflictions of diligence?

What are called laziness, indolence, lack of moderation in food and drink, not knowing one's own measure, improper mental attention, and the arising of evil thoughts—these are termed the defilements of diligence and are also called its faults.
The bodhisattva’s diligence is forever able to relinquish [all attachments]; therefore, this diligence is pure and stainless, bright white and blazing, free from further afflictions.
This is called the bodhisattva’s blazing diligence.
"What is meant by a bodhisattva’s constant diligence?

It refers to when bodhisattvas are able to constantly initiate various forms of diligence within all modes of conduct; their nature is perpetually vigorous and courageous, without any time of rest or cessation, and they never experience weariness or exhaustion, whether in body or mind. This is called a bodhisattva’s constant diligence."
“What is the pure diligence of a bodhisattva?

It means that bodhisattvas initiate such constant diligence that all transgressions, unwholesome dharmas, and unbeneficial matters that obstruct the path—even the most subtle and minute unwholesomeness or a single moment of an evil thought—are not initiated, let alone vast unwholesome dharmas!”

Therefore, the bodhisattva completely eliminates all [obstacles], accords with the principle of nirvāṇa, accumulates the provisions for the noble path, and proceeds toward the factors of enlightenment.
By cultivating such wholesome dharmas, the bodhisattva causes them to increase and expand, thereby perfecting awakening.
This is called the pure diligence of a bodhisattva.
What is the uncommon diligence of a bodhisattva?
It refers to when bodhisattvas reflect as follows:
"Suppose that the worlds of the ten directions, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, were entirely filled with masses of fire like those in the Avīci Hell.
Beyond those worlds, there is a sentient being who undergoes various sufferings and afflictions, having no refuge, no reliance, and no protector."

When a bodhisattva feels compassion for even a single sentient being, they do not shrink from the toil of crossing a mass of fierce flames to go there and teach them; how much less would they fail to rescue and deliver many sentient beings!
Such is the bodhisattva’s great compassion and diligence, which cannot be matched by outsiders or those of the two vehicles; this is called the bodhisattva’s uncommon diligence.
What is the bodhisattva’s diligence that does not disparage others?
That is to say, bodhisattvas never give rise to the thought:
"Because my diligence is feeble, inferior, and indolent, it will be difficult for me to attain awakening through its cultivation."
Furthermore, they do not entertain such thoughts as:

"I am also unable to shoulder such ascetic practices accumulated over immeasurable kalpas and ten million kalpas, and only after striving with the urgency of one whose hair is on fire can I realize Bodhi."
He does not give rise to such a discouraged mind.
For this reason, the Bodhisattva generates this thought:

"All the Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas of the past; the Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas of the present; and the Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas of the future—all those Tathāgatas attained manifest perfect enlightenment through diligent cultivation over immeasurable eons. It was because these Buddhas cultivated diligence for no small period of time that they were able to attain such manifest perfect enlightenment."

I am also like this; it is logically necessary that I cultivate various practices over many kalpas so that I may attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, for the Tathāgatas of the three periods of time have likewise attained Buddhahood through identical diligence.
Furthermore, I would rather diligently practice for the sake of all sentient beings and remain in hell than, for my own sake, practice with diligence and realize nirvana.
This is called the bodhisattva’s diligence that does not involve contempt.
What is the bodhisattva’s diligence that is free from arrogance?
It means that when this bodhisattva arouses diligence, he never relishes it to the point of becoming self-conceited or looking down upon others.
"What wise person would practice diligence merely in hope of another's favor?
This is called the bodhisattva’s diligence that is free from arrogance. Good son!..."
Because Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are able to accomplish these ten kinds of dharmas, they attain the perfection of diligence.
"Furthermore, son of good family,
when Bodhisattvas accomplish ten kinds of dharmas, they attain the perfection of meditative concentration (dhyāna).
What are the ten? First, the accumulation of merit;
second, the ability to feel great weary detachment.
Third, diligently cultivating vigor;
fourth, being fully endowed with extensive learning;
fifth, attaining non-perverted diligence in receiving and internalizing [the teachings].
Sixth, practicing in accordance with the Dharma;
seventh, attaining the nature of sharp faculties;
eighth, attaining skillfulness of mind.
Ninth, they attain skillfulness in śamatha and vipaśyanā;
tenth, they attain non-attachment.
"How does a bodhisattva accumulate merit?"

This refers to those bodhisattvas who delight in the Mahāyāna and are further able to accumulate all roots of goodness; in whatever place they are born, they gather virtuous spiritual friends and are able to practice various sublime conducts.
Furthermore, they constantly aspire to be born into the families of great brahmins, kṣatriyas, or great householders, so that in every place of birth they may always attain right faith.
By these causes and conditions, they increase immeasurable and vast roots of goodness, in order to never be separated from spiritual friends.
Spiritual friends are, namely, all Buddhas and all Bodhisattvas.

Because these Bodhisattvas have habitually cultivated roots of goodness, which have increased and flourished, they observe that the world is oppressed by suffering and affliction, a collection of manifold diseases, shrouded in ignorance and darkness, and lacking any stable abiding.
Why is this? It is because of the causal conditions of desire.
"How is it that a bodhisattva is able to cultivate great weary detachment?"

This means that by virtue of the aforementioned causes and conditions, a bodhisattva reflects: "I should not now engage in sensual desire within this world, for such desire arises solely from the conceptual constructions of deluded sentiment."

The Buddhas have extensively expounded upon all the various faults and afflictions of sensual desire: namely, that desire is like a sharp stake, like a barb, like a sword, and like a keen blade; furthermore, it is like a venomous snake, like a mass of foam on water, and like putrid, foul-smelling, and loathsome meat.

"By means of this, the bodhisattva gives rise to a mind of weary detachment, shaves off his hair and beard, dons the dharma robes, and with right faith leaves the home life to enter the homeless state.
How does a bodhisattva diligently cultivate vigor?"

This means that once this bodhisattva has gone forth, they exert great diligence so as to attain what has not yet been attained, understand what has not yet been understood, and realize what has not yet been realized.
"How does a bodhisattva fulfill extensive learning?"

This means that, due to the aforementioned causes and conditions, this bodhisattva has extensively heard and received [the teachings], and is thus well able to proclaim the profound and subtle principles of both conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya) and ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya).
"How does a bodhisattva attain non-erroneous diligent cultivation and reception?
It means that this bodhisattva internalizes the principles of the truths within the mind and diligently cultivates non-erroneous skillfulness."
"What is the bodhisattva’s practice of the Dharma in accordance with the Dharma?

It means that once this bodhisattva has attained skillfulness, they practice the Dharma in accordance with the Dharma—namely, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right intention, right effort, right mindfulness, right concentration, and right view. These constitute the bodhisattva’s cultivation of the factors of the path."
"How does a bodhisattva attain sharp faculties?
It means that once this bodhisattva has practiced the factors of the path, they possess sharp faculties and clear awakening, enabling them to understand correctly.
By means of this, the bodhisattva dwells in tranquility, remaining far removed from attachment and all worldly clamor, and taking no pleasure in much speech."
Furthermore, they are able to abandon thoughts of desire, thoughts of ill will, thoughts of harm, and thoughts of immortality, and remain detached from kin, reputation, and gain.
"How does a bodhisattva attain skillfulness in the mind?"

It means that by virtue of these preceding causes and conditions, this bodhisattva attains skillfulness regarding the mind and maintains constant tranquility of body; he observes his own mind with respect to what is wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate, reflecting to himself:
"In what nature does my mind currently abide?"
If one abides in supreme goodness and purity, the mind gives rise to faith, inclination, and joy.
What is meant by "supreme goodness"?
It refers to the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (bodhipākṣika-dharmas).
If one dwells in unwholesome states, one should cultivate weary detachment and arouse diligence; thus, one will be able to forever sever all unwholesome dharmas.
What are called these unwholesome dharmas?
They are greed, hatred, and delusion.
Greed is of three kinds: superior, middling, and inferior.
What is superior greed?

This means that this greed pervades both body and mind, conforms to what is inferior, and the mind is constantly stained by attachment, such that at all times there is no sense of shame (*hrī*) or dread of blame (*apatrāpya*).
What is meant by "lack of shame"?

This means that one who is possessed by covetousness constantly engages in contemplation and seeks out objects of desire; the mind gives rise to affection and esteem, becoming immersed in and praising them—this is called lack of shame (*āhrīkya*).
What is lack of dread (*anapatrāpya*)?

That is to say, one who is possessed by desire, for the sake of that desire as a causal condition, engages in disputes with parents and other venerable ones, treats them with contempt and deceit, and causes them harm; thus valuing that craving above all else is called "lack of shame."
This means that because of these causes and conditions, one who possesses lustful desire is born in an evil realm; therefore, it is called "predominant lustful desire.
What is "middling lustful desire"?

It refers to one who, having engaged in lustful desire, immediately gives rise to weariness and detachment, develops a mind of remorse and regret, and no longer complies with it; this is called middling lustful desire.
What is inferior greed?

It refers to when one who possesses desire gives rise to that desire; whether by touching the body, merely conversing together, or upon seeing [the object], the lustful mind immediately subsides—this is called inferior greed.
Whatever requisites for sustaining life one possesses, if the mind clings to them, this is collectively termed greed (*lobha*).
What is called hatred (*dveṣa*)?
It should be known that this hatred is also of three kinds: superior, middling, and inferior.
What is superior hatred?
It refers to one who, being full of malice, gives rise to various forms of hatred and commits any one of the five deeds of immediate retribution (*ānantarya-karman*), or slanders the True Dharma.

The offense of one who slanders the True Dharma exceeds those five deeds of immediate retribution; it cannot be reached by any fraction, nor by any *kalā* part, nor even by any calculation of analogy or *upaniṣad* part. By reason of these causes and conditions, such a person is born in the hells (*naraka*).

If born among humans, one will have a dark and withered appearance and eyes that are constantly red; being violent and evil by nature, one will constantly inflict harm, and due to these causes and conditions, one will be reborn in the hells.
This is called superior anger.
What is middling anger?
It refers to one who, having committed a sinful deed out of anger, is able to quickly repent and immediately give rise to the resolve to eliminate it; this is called middling anger.
What is inferior anger?

It refers to one who, being prone to anger, utters harsh and evil words due to the arousal of anger, and through belittling, taunting, and disparaging, accumulates unwholesome karma; yet, within a single kṣaṇa, a lava, or a muhūrta, they are able to repent and reform, cultivating the practice of its removal—this is called inferior anger.
It should be understood that this delusion is also of three kinds: namely, superior, middling, and inferior.
What is superior delusion?
It refers to one who, being foolish and ignorant, constantly dwells in greed and hatred and never feels remorse; this is called superior delusion.
What is middling delusion?

It refers to one who, being deluded, commits a minor unwholesome act and is immediately able to disclose and repent it before fellow practitioners of the holy life (*brahmacārin*), because they do not perceive that the evil karma would entail a heavy retribution; this is called middling delusion.
What is inferior delusion?

It refers to one who, being foolish, slightly violates those precepts established by the Buddha that are not of the nature of natural offenses (*prakṛti-sāvadya*), and is able to abandon them after committing only one, two, or three instances; this is called inferior delusion.
The bodhisattva is able to restrain those states of greed, hatred, and delusion through skillfulness of mind.
Having attained such skillfulness, they never again take delight in or become attached to them.

Why is this? Because they have attained skillfulness regarding the mind; if it abides in the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*), they immediately apply diligent observation, giving rise only to right mindfulness.
What is meant by "indeterminate"?
It refers to when, upon the arising of the mind, the mind is neither within nor without;
it does not abide in the wholesome, nor does it abide in the unwholesome;

it does not abide in vipaśyanā, nor does it abide in śamatha. Instead, the mind becomes inferior and gives rise to sleep, causing the mind to become dull and obscure, just as when a man who has been in a very deep sleep first awakens, his faculties and consciousness are昏昧 (hūn-mèi—obscure and dim), and he cannot perceive clearly.
It is likewise when he dwells in a neutral state of mind;
because a neutral mind is not lucid, the Bodhisattva maintains mental vigor and sharpness, abiding securely in joy.
This is called the bodhisattva’s skillfulness regarding the mind.
How does a bodhisattva attain skillfulness regarding śamatha and vipaśyanā?
It is when this bodhisattva, having already attained skillfulness regarding the mind, observes all phenomena as being like illusions and like dreams, and contemplates all phenomena thus:
"This is a wholesome dharma; this is not a wholesome dharma;
this is a dharma of renunciation; this is not a dharma of renunciation.

This means that all bodhisattvas contemplate all dharmas as being dependent upon the mind, with the mind as their intrinsic nature and the mind as their leader. Because they are able to grasp the mind, skillfully subdue the mind, and thoroughly understand the mind, they are thus able to encompass all these dharmas.

Having become well-disciplined and possessing thorough understanding, one is thereby able to cultivate the dharma of śamatha—thus binding the mind, thus calming the mind, and thus establishing the mind in abiding.
By diligently cultivating such śamatha, one is able to abide in one-pointedness of mind.
Once the bodhisattva abides in one-pointedness of mind, they enter meditative concentration and observe, thereby attaining the joy and bliss born of seclusion.

Having attained joy in the mind, one becomes detached from the evil and unwholesome states of the desire realm, as well as from applied and sustained thought; this is called practicing and abiding in the first dhyāna.
