Furthermore, having abandoned applied and sustained thought, and without relishing the joy and bliss, one contemplates impermanence and emerges from the first dhyāna to abide in internal purity, attaining the joy and bliss born of concentration; this is called the bodhisattva entering the second dhyāna.

Next, having become weary of and detached from joy, and having contemplated suffering, one dwells in equanimity, mindfulness, clear comprehension, and bliss, with the mind settled in right meditative absorption.
The Buddha said:
"Accomplishing the dwelling in equanimity, mindfulness, and bliss, one enters the third dhyāna and abides therein through practice."
Having cultivated the understanding of emptiness, he enters the fourth dhyāna and thereby relinquishes the grasping at a self.

Because he has relinquished the grasping at a self, suffering and pleasure are also severed; because sorrow and joy have ceased, he dwells in neither-suffering-nor-pleasure with equanimity and pure mindfulness. This is called the cultivation of the fourth dhyāna.

Furthermore, the bodhisattva contemplates that the body is equal to space; having gained faith and understanding, they abandon all perceptions of form (*rūpa-saṃjñā*) and extinguish perceptions of resistance (*pratigha-saṃjñā*)—leaving behind various perceptions because they have abandoned perceptions of form, and extinguishing perceptions of resistance because they have left behind perceptions of diversity—and thus enter into infinite space. This is called the cultivation of the sphere of infinite space (*ākāśānantyāyatana*).

Having transcended all of infinite space, there arises the perception of consciousness; entering into infinite consciousness is called the cultivation and dwelling in the sphere of infinite consciousness (*vijñānānantyāyatana*).
Having transcended all of infinite consciousness, one enters into nothingness; this is called the cultivation and dwelling in the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*).
Transcending the sphere of nothingness, they dwell having cultivated the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
Furthermore, because bodhisattvas have distanced themselves from the mind that takes perception and feeling as its objects, it is called dwelling in the meditative absorption of cessation.
Although he enters that concentration, he never takes delight in or becomes attached to it.

Having emerged from that concentration, he dwells with a mind imbued with loving-kindness (*maitrī*), abandoning thoughts of enmity and resentment, free from perceptions of harm, vast, immeasurable, impartial, and non-dual; having cultivated this well, he pervades one direction with a resolute understanding, entering and abiding in concentration, and likewise pervades the other three directions, the four intermediate points, and the zenith and nadir throughout the entire world.

Accompanied by compassion, abandoning thoughts of enmity and ill will, free from harmful intent, vast and immeasurable, impartial and non-dual, thoroughly cultivated, one directs the mind to pervade an entire world-system in one direction; having entered meditative absorption, one dwells there, and likewise pervades the remaining three directions, the four intermediate points, and the zenith and nadir throughout the entire world.

The bodhisattva, endowed with a mind of sympathetic joy, abandons thoughts of enmity and ill will; having cultivated it extensively, immeasurably, impartially, and without duality, he dwells having attained meditative absorption, pervading one direction with a mind of resolute resolve, and likewise the other three directions, the four intermediate points, and the zenith and nadir throughout the entire world.

The bodhisattva, accompanied by a mind of equanimity, free from thoughts of enmity and aversion, having abandoned the intent to harm—vast, immeasurable, impartial, and non-dual—having cultivated it thoroughly, dwells having attained meditative absorption with a mental resolve that pervades one direction, and likewise throughout the remaining three directions, the four intermediate points, and above and below, encompassing the entire world.
"How does a bodhisattva attain non-attachment?
It means that this bodhisattva attains the five supernormal powers yet remains unattached to them, constantly able to seek the provisions for enlightenment and the perfection of all dharmas."
“Good son! Because bodhisattva-mahāsattvas accomplish these ten kinds of dharmas, they attain the perfection of dhyāna. Furthermore, good son!”
When a bodhisattva accomplishes ten dharmas, they attain the perfection of prajñā. What are these ten?
First, skillfulness regarding non-self;
Second, skillfulness regarding the results of karma;
third, skillfulness regarding the conditioned;
fourth, skillfulness regarding the cycle of birth and death.
Fifth, skillfulness in relinquishing birth and death;
sixth, skillfulness in attaining the two vehicles;
seventh, skillfulness in the Mahāyāna.
Eighth, skillfulness in abandoning the activities of Māra;
ninth, attaining non-erroneous prajñā;
tenth, attaining incomparable prajñā.
“Good son! How does a bodhisattva attain skillfulness regarding selflessness?
It means that because bodhisattvas study prajñā, they are able to correctly contemplate form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness.”

When observing form, its arising is unfindable, its accumulation is unfindable, and its cessation is unfindable; likewise, when observing feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, the phenomena of arising, accumulation, and cessation are all unfindable.
Because they cannot be apprehended within the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*), they do not exist in the conventional sense (*saṃvṛti*).
Regarding the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of all phenomena in both the ultimate and conventional senses, there is only verbal expression; in reality, nothing can be apprehended.
For this reason, the bodhisattva does not abandon diligence for a long period of time; desiring to benefit all sentient beings, he acts as if his head were on fire.
By means of this, the bodhisattva attains skillfulness regarding selflessness.
"How does a bodhisattva attain skillfulness regarding the results of karma?
It is when a bodhisattva reflects thus:
'The intrinsic nature of all worlds is empty, like a theatrical stage or a city of gandharvas.'"
"Although all sentient beings do not truly exist, they nevertheless cling to a self; because of this, they are unable to penetrate the Noble Path.
These sentient beings then reflect:

"If there is no self, and no sentient being, no life-principle, no creature, no mind-born, no person, no individual (pudgala), no manava, and no nourisher, then there can be no obtainable essence for the ripening fruit of good and evil karma!"
To understand this as it truly is through right prajñā is called a bodhisattva’s skillfulness regarding the fruits of karma.
What is a bodhisattva’s skillfulness regarding the conditioned?
This means that bodhisattvas, through right prajñā, thoroughly understand all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*) and reflect as follows:
"All conditioned phenomena shift and pass away from moment to moment; they lack the characteristic of long-term endurance, being like dew on a precarious blade of grass or like a rushing torrent."
How can one give rise to craving and attachment toward such dharmas, thereby harboring anxiety and distress?
If one gives rise to grasping, how can one be called wise when these dharmas are easily destroyed?

"By reason of these causes and conditions, one does not delight in clinging to phenomena subject to disintegration, but gives rise to a mind of weary detachment; this is called a bodhisattva’s skillfulness regarding the conditioned."
"What is the bodhisattva’s skillfulness regarding the flow and revolution of birth and death?
It is when the bodhisattvas reflect thus:
'All the world is shrouded by ignorance, constantly dwelling in birth and death, bound by the snare of craving.'"
With craving as the cause, grasping arises;
with grasping as the cause, wholesome and unwholesome karma arise;
because karma arises, existence continues.
With conditioned phenomena as cause, birth arises;
with birth as cause, there come old age and death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, and distress, through the accumulation of all these sufferings.
"In this way, they continue in succession without interruption, like the buckets of a waterwheel revolving up and down; the continuity of birth and death is likewise so.
By means of right prajñā, the bodhisattva understands this as it truly is; this is called the bodhisattva’s skillfulness regarding the flow and revolution of birth and death.
"What is the skillful means by which a bodhisattva attains liberation from birth and death?
It is when a bodhisattva reflects thus:
'Because one is free from ignorance, one does not cling to formative activities (saṃskāra);'"
By relinquishing all conditioned formations (*saṃskāra*), craving (*tṛṣṇā*) ceases;
by being free from craving, grasping (*upādāna*) ceases;
and by being able to abandon grasping, existence (*bhava*) does not continue.
"Because one abandons that existence, there is no further birth;
because one can depart from birth, one forever severs old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, and affliction.
Thus, by means of right prajñā, the bodhisattva understands things as they truly are; this is called the bodhisattva’s skillfulness in abandoning and departing from saṃsāra.
"How does a bodhisattva attain skillfulness regarding the two vehicles?
It is when a bodhisattva reflects thus:

'Because this dharma can lead to the fruits of stream-entry, once-returning, non-returning, and arhatship; because it exhausts all outflows forever, severs all fetters and habitual tendencies, and brings about the end of the continuous cycle of birth and death, one wanders in nirvana.'"
By contemplating this Dharma, one becomes a pratyekabuddha, wandering alone like the rhinoceros horn;
yet all bodhisattvas, through right prajñā, thoroughly understand this Dharma and never take its realization as a final attainment.
Why is this? If Bodhisattvas reflect thus:

"I shall utter the lion’s roar for the benefit of the realm of sentient beings; I shall deliver all classes of sentient beings dwelling in saṃsāra," they make a great vow, never intending to transcend saṃsāra alone!
This is called the bodhisattva’s skillfulness regarding the two vehicles.
What is the bodhisattva’s skillfulness regarding the Great Vehicle?

It means that among the training in the precepts, the bodhisattva observes that the trainee is unapprehendable, the training itself is unapprehendable, and even the fruit obtained through the precepts is unapprehendable; yet, they do not cling to emptiness nor fall into the view of nihilism. This is called the bodhisattva’s skillfulness regarding the Great Vehicle.
"How does a bodhisattva attain skillfulness in abandoning the activities of Māra?
It means that bodhisattvas distance themselves from all unwholesome persons and do not dwell in those evil lands."
Furthermore, they are able to remain far removed from worldly views and the cultivation of incantations for the sake of seeking gain, profit, respect, and offerings.
Moreover, they are able to distance themselves from all afflictions that obstruct the factors of enlightenment and are able to cultivate the various paths of antidotes.
This is called skillfulness in abandoning the deeds of Māra.
How does a bodhisattva attain non-perverted *prajñā*?

It means that when bodhisattvas cultivate *prajñā*, regarding all worldly scriptures, incantations, and arts and crafts, they always do so for the sake of teaching and transforming sentient beings; they never do so for the sake of seeking personal understanding, nor for the sake of gaining fame for themselves, nor for the sake of obtaining gain and offerings. Rather, it is for the sake of expounding the great majesty of the Noble Teaching, and never with the desire to manifest their own virtues. They single-mindedly give rise to reflection upon the supreme and correct teaching, manifesting its merits within the Vinaya established by the Tathāgata, and never falling into the various views of heterodox paths.
This is called the bodhisattva’s skillful means that are free from inversion.
What is the bodhisattva’s attainment of peerless prajñā?

It refers to the prajñā studied by bodhisattvas, which surpasses that of the two vehicles, all worldly beings—including devas, māras, brahmās, the world at large, and all non-Buddhist brāhmaṇas—as well as the eight classes of beings and all sentient beings; yet there is nothing equal to the bodhisattva’s prajñā, except for the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha.
This is called the peerless prajñā of a bodhisattva. "Good son!
When a bodhisattva can accomplish these ten kinds of dharmas, they attain the perfection of prajñā."

Translated by the Tang Dynasty Indian Tripitaka Master Dharmaruci:
"Furthermore, son of good family, when a bodhisattva accomplishes ten kinds of dharmas, they attain the perfection of skillful means."
What are the ten? First, skillful means for attaining dedication;
second, skillful means for causing all non-Buddhists to turn toward [the path];
Third, skillful means for turning away from and abandoning sense objects;
fourth, skillful means for dispelling regret;
fifth, skillful means for rescuing and protecting sentient beings.
Sixth, skillful means regarding the provision of livelihood for sentient beings;
seventh, skillful means regarding receiving and taking;
eighth, skillful means regarding abandoning what is improper and abiding in what is proper.
Ninth, skillful means in manifesting, instructing, encouraging, and gladdening;
tenth, skillful means in making offerings and serving.
"How does a bodhisattva attain skillful means in dedication?

It is when a bodhisattva takes flowers and fruits that do not belong to others and, during the six periods of day and night, offers them to all Buddhas and bodhisattvas, dedicating these roots of goodness toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

Furthermore, the bodhisattva takes fragrant trees, various jewel trees, or *kalpa* trees that do not belong to others, and during the six periods of day and night, makes offerings to all Buddhas and the assembly of bodhisattvas, dedicating these roots of goodness toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*."

Furthermore, when a bodhisattva hears of all the vast services and offerings described in the sūtras, they give rise to a mind of pure faith and joy, and dedicate these offerings to all buddhas and bodhisattvas.

Furthermore, a bodhisattva is able to cause the accumulations for enlightenment to be fully perfected through the virtuous deeds performed by other bodhisattvas in the ten directions as well as by other sentient beings; generating a pure intention and rejoicing with a profound heart, they dedicate these roots of virtue toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

If a bodhisattva offers incense and flowers to the stūpas of the Tathāgata and to the images of the Buddha, dedicating this merit so that all sentient beings may be freed from the defilement of broken precepts and attain the fragrance of the Buddha’s ethical discipline;

and if the bodhisattva further constantly sprinkles water, sweeps, and anoints the ground, dedicating this so that all sentient beings may abandon improper conduct and cultivate virtuous practices with perfect and complete decorum;
and if the bodhisattvas offer flower canopies, dedicating this so that all sentient beings may relinquish their feverish afflictions.
Furthermore, when that bodhisattva enters a monastery, he gives rise to this thought: "May all sentient beings enter the city of nirvāṇa.
When he leaves the monastery, he makes the vow: "May all sentient beings be born from the prison of saṃsāra.
If he opens the door to his room, he vows: "May all sentient beings open the doors to the various happy realms and the supramundane wisdom."
When closing the door of the chamber, may all sentient beings be caused to close the gates to the miserable realms.
When the Bodhisattva sits, may all sentient beings attain the seat beneath the wondrous Bodhi tree.
When lying on his right side, may all sentient beings abide peacefully in nirvāṇa.
When rising from bed, may all sentient beings be freed from the fetters and hindrances that bind them;
when going to relieve myself, may all sentient beings turn toward the path of great awakening;
while actually relieving myself, may all sentient beings extract the arrows of all poisons.
When washing [the body], may all sentient beings wash away the stains of afflictions and all faults;
when washing the hands, may all sentient beings be freed from defiled and turbid karma;
when washing the feet, may all sentient beings be freed from the dust and grime of obstructions.
When chewing a tooth-stick, may all sentient beings be freed from defilements and impurities.
Regarding all actions performed by the Bodhisattva himself, he dedicates them for the benefit, welfare, and happiness of all sentient beings.
When the Bodhisattva prostrates before a stūpa of the Tathāgata, he vows that all sentient beings shall always receive the homage of devas and the world.
This is called the bodhisattva’s skillful means of dedication (*pariṇāmanopāyakauśalya*).
What is the bodhisattva’s skillful means of causing non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) to turn toward [the Dharma]?

It is when this bodhisattva, within various classes of non-Buddhist assemblies, is able to manifest in the forms of those non-Buddhists—namely, the Carakas, Parivrājakas, Nirgranthas, and Vatsīputrīyas—and therein accepts, maintains, reads, and recites their teachings.
A bodhisattva, desiring to bring sentient beings to maturity, reflects in this way:
"If I were to first act as an ācārya, I would be unable to cause arrogant sentient beings to become compliant and disciplined."
"Therefore, I went among the followers of non-Buddhist paths (*tīrthika*) and manifested leaving the household life to become their disciple.

Having thus gone forth, I practiced with courageous diligence, training in various modes of conduct according to them; I became extensively learned and widely heard, exhausting the depths of their doctrines. I begged for coarse and impure food, yet in all that I did, my deportment and practice surpassed those of the non-Buddhists.
Consequently, the Bodhisattva becomes a revered teacher and model for all non-Buddhists (tīrthikas), and they all accept and believe whatever he says, following his guidance and being tamed by him.

Once the Bodhisattva knows that these sentient beings have turned toward him, he explains the faults and errors of those non-Buddhists' wrong views and demonstrates that the doctrines they study are not the authentic teaching, because they cannot explain the renunciation of craving nor lead to its total eradication.
Consequently, the non-Buddhists were transformed by the Bodhisattva; they abandoned their heterodox paths and entered into the True Dharma.
Furthermore, among all the non-Buddhists who practiced the five supernormal powers and the Brahma-conduct, the Bodhisattva applied himself with diligent effort and realized the five superknowledges.

Furthermore, by cultivating and perfecting the meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*), various *samādhis*, and *samāpattis*, he surpasses the five supernormal powers attained by non-Buddhists; being wise and transcendent, he acts as their teacher and guide.

Once the Bodhisattva has understood that those non-Buddhists to be converted have all been brought to maturity, he points out the various faults of their meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*), concentrations (*samādhi*), and attainments (*samāpatti*), as well as the fact that the teachings they study are not the authentic doctrine, because they do not teach the path of renunciation and the counteractive removal of desire.
Consequently, the non-Buddhists were transformed by the Bodhisattva; they abandoned their heterodox paths and entered into the Buddha-dharma.
This is called the Bodhisattva’s skillful means for causing all non-Buddhists to turn toward the Dharma.
“What is the bodhisattva’s skillful means for transforming and abandoning sense objects?

It is when this bodhisattva, seeing sentient beings who are largely full of desire, employs skillful means to subdue them by manifesting as a female form—exquisite, magnificent, and surpassing all other women—so that those sentient beings who see it develop a mind of passionate attachment.”

Seeing them thus stained by attachment, the Bodhisattva immediately manifested his death in that very place where they were lying; in a single kṣaṇa, a single muhūrta, he displayed the appearance of bloating and putrefaction, foul-smelling, loathsome, and repulsive.
Upon seeing them, sentient beings are struck with great terror and give rise to a mind of suffering and distress;
with deep-seated revulsion, they think: "Who can cause me to leave such a foul and evil place!"

At that time, the Bodhisattva immediately expounded these various dharmas before them according to their individual capacities, such that they would certainly realize one of the three types of enlightenment.
This is called the Bodhisattva’s skillful means of transformative relinquishment.
"What is the bodhisattva’s skillful means for dispelling remorse?

It is when this bodhisattva sees sentient beings who have committed the crimes of immediate retribution, or who have given rise to all manner of unwholesome karmas, and who lose their composure out of grief and regret."
The Bodhisattva went to him and spoke these words:
"Good son! Why do you remain here with a distracted mind, dwelling in sorrow and regret?"
That sentient being said: "O Great Being!

I have committed various unwholesome deeds of immediate retribution; I fear that throughout the long night I shall undergo all manner of suffering and affliction, as it brings neither benefit nor peace."
For these reasons, they lose their composure and fall into grief and remorse.
At that time, the Bodhisattva extensively expounded the True Dharma for those sentient beings, causing them to deeply repent their transgressions and receive the Bodhisattva precepts.

If these sentient beings have not yet been able to repent their transgressions, at that time the Bodhisattva, wishing to cause those people’s minds to give rise to faith and submission, manifests supernatural powers and extensively explains the matters regarding that person’s reflections.
By this means, sentient beings develop a mind of faith and submissiveness toward the Bodhisattva, feeling joy, confidence, and delight.

Once they have developed such faith and delight, their faculties and dispositions reach maturity; the Bodhisattva then extensively expounds the sublime Dharma for them, and those individuals are able to receive and comprehend it accordingly.
Furthermore, the Bodhisattva manifested as the parents before that person and spoke these words:
"Look at this; I am your companion, your husband."
"Do not regret your actions; the karma you have created will ultimately not cause you to fall into the hells, nor will it lead to the loss of your benefit and happiness!
Having spoken thus, he immediately killed the parents who had appeared before him.
The Bodhisattva manifests miraculous transformations before those sentient beings, and they reflect:

"If even one possessed of wisdom kills his parents yet does not lose his supernormal powers, how much more so for me, who am devoid of wisdom? Having committed such karma, I shall fall into hell and be deprived of benefit and happiness!"
At that time, the Bodhisattva expounds the sublime Dharma for those sentient beings, causing their evil karma to gradually become as slight as a mosquito’s wing.
This is called the Bodhisattva’s skillful means for dispelling regrettable actions.
“What is the bodhisattva’s skillful means for rescuing and protecting sentient beings?
It is when this bodhisattva perceives that the faculties of sentient beings have matured and are capable of receiving the teaching.”

Those sentient beings commit all manner of extremely unwholesome deeds; yet, desiring to benefit them, the Bodhisattva employs skillful means to subdue them by manifesting as various kinds of sentient beings. To those who are to be subdued by the body of a great king, he manifests as a great king and preaches the Dharma to them.
To those who are to be subdued by the body of a minor king, he manifests as a minor king and preaches the Dharma to them.
To those who are to be subdued by the bodies of brahmins or kṣatriyas, he manifests as a brahmin or a kṣatriya and preaches the Dharma to them.
To those who are to be disciplined by a celestial body, he manifests a celestial body and preaches the Dharma;
to those who are to be disciplined by a Vajrapāṇi body, he manifests a Vajrapāṇi body and preaches the Dharma;
to those who are to be disciplined through fear, he manifests as something terrifying and preaches the Dharma.
To those who should be tamed through binding, killing, beating, or scolding, he manifests such things as these and teaches them the Dharma;
to those who should be tamed through kind speech, he manifests kind speech and teaches them the Dharma.

If there are classes of sentient beings who, when about to commit various immediate transgressions (*ānantarya-karma*), give rise to harmful intentions toward the person of a Bodhisattva, that Bodhisattva who has attained supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) will immediately manifest various skillful means: sometimes he obstructs them, sometimes he restrains them, or sometimes he moves them to another direction.

Furthermore, before those individuals, he manifests what appears to be the very act of the immediate transgression they intend to commit, or he manifests the appearance of the hells (*naraka*), thereby suppressing the karma of their immediate transgression so that it does not manifest.

There are bodhisattvas who have not yet attained supernatural powers, yet are skillfully able to observe the length of the lifespans of those sentient beings; seeing that those beings are about to commit an act of immediate retribution, they reflect:
"These sentient beings are about to incur grave offenses."
Thus, giving rise to great compassion, he felt sorrow and distress.
The Bodhisattva observed that being as clearly as an amra fruit held in the palm of his hand and reflected:

"For the sake of benefiting even a single sentient being, I am able to undergo great suffering and affliction in the Avīci hell; until this very being has attained nirvana without remainder, I shall constantly employ such means—without resorting to any other expedient—to prevent their harm."

When these sentient beings, having committed evil karma, were about to be born in that hell, because I had not yet attained mastery over supernatural powers, I lacked the means to transfer those faithless, short-lived, and wicked beings to another region, fearing that those beings might be reborn in the Avīci Hell due to their unwholesome karma!

Thus, the Bodhisattva gives rise to a heart of compassion and reflects that sentient beings each follow their own karma and cannot be rescued by any other expedient means; therefore, he merely gives rise to a mind of loving-kindness to provide impartial instruction and demonstration of disciplinary measures.
This is called the bodhisattva’s skillful means of rescuing and protecting sentient beings.
What is the bodhisattva’s skillful means of providing for the livelihood of sentient beings?

It refers to when bodhisattvas observe that sentient beings are incapable of receiving the Dharma, seeking only food and clothing as their sole sufficiency, and being unable to understand the taming of the noble Dharma.

The Bodhisattva instructs these sentient beings in such activities as arithmetic, arts and crafts, writing, and record-keeping, so that they may accomplish what is wholesome and not accomplish unwholesome dharmas.
This is called the bodhisattva’s skillful means regarding the bestowing of life-sustenance upon sentient beings.
What is the bodhisattva’s skillful means regarding receiving and taking?

It is that this bodhisattva, even if they obtain a heap of precious jewels as vast as Mount Sumeru, does not accept them; yet, if they obtain inferior goods for sustaining life, they immediately accept them.
Why is this? It is because this bodhisattva reflects as follows:

"These sentient beings are obscured by stinginess, envy, and craving; they cherish their own and others' possessions and do not allow themselves or others to enjoy them. Due to these causes and conditions, they remain within the ocean of birth and death, constantly being swept away and submerged."

Because the Bodhisattva desires to bring those sentient beings full benefit and happiness throughout the long night [of saṃsāra], he accepts their offerings; yet, though he accepts these things, he gives rise to no craving or attachment, nor does he harbor any sense of ownership. He does so solely to make offerings to the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha, so that all sentient beings may likewise attain supreme victory, and to benefit those sentient beings who are poor and suffering—thereby causing the donors to rejoice and exult.
This is called the bodhisattva’s skillful means in receiving and accepting.
What is the bodhisattva’s skillful means in abandoning what is inappropriate and abiding in what is appropriate?

This refers to when bodhisattvas perceive that sentient beings are capable of receiving the Dharma and should manifest equal enlightenment in *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, yet those sentient beings, for the sake of attaining the vehicles of the śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas, initiate skillful means and constantly and diligently practice them.
When a bodhisattva teaches the Dharma so that those sentient beings abandon the two vehicles and are guided toward dedication within the Mahāyāna,
this is called the bodhisattva’s skillful means of abandoning what is not the proper sphere and abiding in what is the proper sphere.
"What is the bodhisattva’s skillful means of manifesting, instructing, encouraging, and gladdening?
It refers to how bodhisattvas cause sentient beings who have not yet resolved upon bodhicitta to resolve upon it;

and for those who have already resolved upon bodhicitta, even if they maintain ethical discipline, their minds may easily become complacent, or they may practice little diligence while being largely indolent—therefore, the bodhisattva teaches them to constantly cultivate diligence."

If sentient beings, though they maintain a small portion of the precepts, frequently violate them, then by reason of this, their faith is not pure; they constantly lack joy and dwell with their minds shrouded by the defilement of broken precepts.
The Bodhisattva expounds various sublime teachings for those sentient beings, causing their minds to give rise to pure faith and to experience joy and gladness.
This is called the Bodhisattva’s skillful means of manifesting, instructing, encouraging, and gladdening.
"How does a bodhisattva attain skillful means in receiving service and making offerings?
It means that once these bodhisattvas have gone forth, they know moderation and contentment regarding all gains and offerings, and the offerings they receive are not contrary to the Dharma."
Furthermore, when bodhisattvas dwell alone in seclusion, remaining in meditative concentration and conforming to the conduct of the Buddhas and bodhisattvas, they reflect in this way:
"I wish to serve and make offerings to the Tathāgatas."

That is to say, having engaged in such contemplation, this bodhisattva performs various services and offerings to all Tathāgatas, thereby attaining the perfection of the six sublime pāramitās through the completion of their practice.
How does one bring the practices of the six pāramitās to perfection? It is as follows:
when preparing the necessary provisions for service, worship, and so forth, this is the bodhisattva’s perfection of generosity (dāna-pāramitā);
when, amidst such service and worship, one resolves to benefit all sentient beings, this is the bodhisattva’s perfection of ethical discipline (śīla-pāramitā).
That which consists in the mind being able to abide in joy and gladness amidst service and offerings is the bodhisattva’s perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*);
that which consists in the mind being free from weariness amidst service and offerings is the bodhisattva’s perfection of diligence (*vīrya-pāramitā*);
and that which consists in single-minded reflection amidst service and offerings is the bodhisattva’s perfection of meditative concentration (*dhyāna-pāramitā*).
That which refers to the mind’s ability to engage in various forms of analytical observation regarding service, offerings, and so forth—this is the bodhisattva’s *prajñāpāramitā*.
This is called the bodhisattva’s skillful means (*upāyakauśalya*) in serving and making offerings.
“Good son! When a bodhisattva accomplishes these ten kinds of dharmas, they attain the perfection of skillful means. Furthermore, good son!”
When Bodhisattvas accomplish ten kinds of dharmas, they attain the fulfillment of their vows. What are these ten?
First, they possess vows that are not inferior.
Second, the vow free from cowardice;
third, the vow to diligently practice for the sake of benefiting all sentient beings;
fourth, the vow made to be praised by all Buddhas and Tathāgatas.
Fifth, the aspiration to skillfully subdue all māras;
sixth, the accomplishment of an aspiration that does not depend on others;
seventh, the attainment of boundless aspirations.
Eighth, the vow of being without fear or terror;
ninth, the vow of being without weariness or fatigue;
tenth, the vow of attaining fulfillment.
"What is the bodhisattva’s non-inferior vow?
It means that this bodhisattva does not take delight in the various realms of existence when making vows; this is called the bodhisattva’s non-inferior vow."
"What is the bodhisattva’s vow free from cowardice?

It means that this bodhisattva does not weary of the triple world, seeks liberation from craving, and dwells in tranquility while making their vow; this is called the bodhisattva’s vow free from cowardice."
"What is the bodhisattva’s diligent cultivation of vows for the sake of benefiting all sentient beings?
It is when a bodhisattva makes this vow:
'Until the realm of sentient beings has fully realized nirvana without remainder, I myself shall subsequently realize great parinirvāṇa!'"
This is called the bodhisattva’s diligent cultivation of vows out of a desire to benefit all sentient beings.
What is the vow that a bodhisattva makes so as to be praised by the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas?
That is to say, this bodhisattva makes such a vow:
"May all beings in the realm of sentient beings who have not yet resolved upon awakening resolve to do so;
and having resolved, may they gradually practice the branches of conduct conducive to awakening."

After completing these practices, when he sits beneath the Bodhi tree and has already attained his seat at the site of enlightenment, I shall serve, revere, and make offerings to him, and entreat him to turn the wheel of Dharma;
and if he enters parinirvāṇa, I shall entreat him to remain long in the world for the sake of benefiting all sentient beings!
This is called the vow made by a bodhisattva that is praised by all Buddhas and Tathāgatas.
What is the vow of a bodhisattva that is well able to crush and subdue all Māras?
That is to say, this bodhisattva makes such a vow:
"When I attain manifest, perfect enlightenment in the future, may there never be any hosts of celestial Māras within my buddha-field, nor shall even the names of various Māras ever be heard!"
This is called the Bodhisattva’s skillful ability to subdue all the aspirations of Māra.
What is the accomplishment of an aspiration that does not depend on others?
It means that this Bodhisattva does not only after being prompted by another that he generates the aspiration for *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

Nevertheless, by means of prajñā, one observes the realm of sentient beings undergoing suffering and affliction; having observed this, and desiring to rescue and protect them, one resolves to attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
This is called a bodhisattva who is able to accomplish vows that do not depend on others.
How does a bodhisattva attain boundless vows?

This means that this bodhisattva does not generate a vow for the sake of a mere fraction of the provisions for enlightenment; rather, this bodhisattva generates a great vow. Draping one shoulder, with the right knee touching the ground, and giving rise to pure faith, he contemplates all the Buddhas currently dwelling in the worlds of the ten directions and all the bodhisattvas—whether there are bodhisattvas abiding in ascetic practices or seated at the site of enlightenment, or whether he sees various Buddhas, or those manifesting equal enlightenment, or turning the wheel of Dharma. Having observed them, he generates a pure intention and, regarding each of those Buddhas and bodhisattvas in the ten directions—whether they abide in ascetic practices, manifest equal enlightenment, or turn the wheel of Dharma—the bodhisattva develops faith and understanding toward each one, rejoices from the depths of his heart, and dedicates [this merit] toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
This is called the bodhisattva attaining boundless vows.
What is the bodhisattva’s attainment of the vow free from alarm and fear?

It is when bodhisattvas who have newly resolved their minds hear the profound Dharma, hear of the vast majesty and virtue of the Buddhas, hear of the playful supernatural powers of the bodhisattvas, and hear of the profound skillful means; having heard these, the bodhisattvas are neither startled nor afraid, but reflect as follows:

"It is said that the enlightenment realized by all Tathāgatas, the realm in which they abide, and their maturation of sentient beings are all boundless; within those dharmas, I am unable to know them, yet I should know them as the Buddhas realize and know them."
This is called the bodhisattva’s vow of being free from fear and dread.
What is the bodhisattva’s vow of being free from weariness?
It means that although bodhisattvas see that sentient beings are stubborn, foolish by nature, and difficult to subdue, they never become weary or disheartened toward these sentient beings.
There may be bodhisattvas who, seeing that sentient beings are stubborn and ignorant by nature and difficult to subdue, become weary and disheartened;
because of this weariness, they abandon those sentient beings and make such a vow:
"I shall seek birth in a pure world, where I shall never again hear the names of such evil sentient beings."
"Even though one may vow to be born in a pure world, one will ultimately not be born there because of having abandoned sentient beings who have not yet reached maturity.
Regarding this meaning, furthermore, a wise bodhisattva gives rise to this thought:

"Among all sentient beings in all worlds, those whose diligence is inferior, those who are indolent, and those who are as stubborn, dull, deaf, and blind as a mute sheep—such sentient beings are observed and selected by all Buddhas and bodhisattvas; and throughout the entire realm of sentient beings, those who lack the nature for parinirvāṇa are all abandoned."

I now desire that all such sentient beings be gathered together within my buddha-field, and I further desire that these sentient beings sit at the site of enlightenment and attain unexcelled, perfect, and complete awakening.
When this bodhisattva gives rise to such thoughts and reflections, in every moment of thought all the palaces of the māras tremble, and he is praised by all the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas.
In this way, such a bodhisattva will certainly be born in a pure buddha-field and will also swiftly manifest equal enlightenment in anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
This is called the bodhisattva’s vow of non-exhaustion.
How does a bodhisattva attain the fulfillment of their vows?

It means that once this bodhisattva has sat upon the seat of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa), they defeat the hosts of Māra and manifests perfect awakening (abhisambodhi) in the path of unexcelled, complete, and perfect enlightenment (anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi).
Since his vows are already fulfilled, he no longer generates further aspirations. Good son!

It is like clarified butter in a bowl: once it is filled to the brim, it cannot accommodate even a single drop of butter as minute as a speck of dust. For this reason, it is said that he has attained the fulfillment of his vows.
The Bodhisattva is like that bowl filled with clarified butter; having manifested equal enlightenment in bodhi and fulfilled his vows, he no longer further utters any sublime vows.
This is called a bodhisattva attaining the fulfillment of their vows. "Good son,
when a bodhisattva accomplishes these ten kinds of dharmas, they attain the fulfillment of their great vows."
"Furthermore, son of good family,
when bodhisattvas accomplish ten dharmas, their power of cultivation is perfected. What are these ten?
First, the perfection of the power of cultivation through being unobscured by others;
second, the perfection of the power of spiritual majesty through being unsubdued;
third, the perfection of the cultivation of the power of merit.
Fourth, the perfection of cultivation in the power of wisdom;
fifth, the attainment of perfection in the power of retinue;
sixth, the attainment of perfection in the power of supernormal faculties.
Seventh, the power of mastery is cultivated to perfection;
eighth, the power of dhāraṇī is attained to perfection;
ninth, the power of miraculous transformations that cannot be altered by others is perfected.
Tenth, the perfection of the power of his teaching being uncontradicted by others.
"Good son, how is it that a bodhisattva’s perfection of the power of cultivation is such that he is not eclipsed by others?

It means that this bodhisattva cannot be eclipsed by any heterodox practitioners or proponents of divergent doctrines; this is called the perfection of the power of cultivation through being unobscured by others.
"What is the perfection of the power of being unsubdued by a bodhisattva?"
This means that among all sentient beings, there is ultimately none capable of crushing the power of this bodhisattva; this is called the perfection of the power of being uncrushable and unsubdued.
"How does a bodhisattva achieve the perfection of cultivation in the power of merit?"

It means that this bodhisattva cultivates all mundane and supramundane merits, fully accumulating all the provisions for enlightenment such that not even the slightest portion remains incomplete; this is called the bodhisattva’s perfection in the cultivation of the power of merit.
"What is meant by a bodhisattva’s perfection in the cultivation of the power of wisdom?

It means that this bodhisattva perceives all the Buddha-dharmas through right wisdom; with the exception of the Tathāgata’s knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*), there is nothing he has not realized and nothing he does not fully understand. This is called a bodhisattva’s perfection in the cultivation of the power of wisdom."
"How does a bodhisattva achieve perfection through the power of similarity with their retinue?

It means that all the members of this bodhisattva’s retinue are fully perfected in ethical discipline, view, deportment, and pure livelihood; and all members of the retinue act in complete accordance with the bodhisattva’s own conduct. This is called a bodhisattva achieving perfection through the power of similarity with their retinue."
"How does a bodhisattva cultivate the perfection of the power of supernormal knowledges?

It means that this bodhisattva’s superior power of supernormal knowledges transcends the spheres of supernormal knowledge of all worldly beings and those of the two vehicles. By his own desire, the bodhisattva can place Jambudvīpa, or even the four continents, a thousand-world system, a two-thousand-world system, or a three-thousandfold great thousand-world system upon the tip of a single hair."

Furthermore, a bodhisattva desires to place immeasurable *gaṅgā*-sands of world-systems within the measure of a single atom; likewise, two, three, four, or five such worlds, or ten, twenty, thirty, forty, or fifty, up to unspeakably unspeakably unspeakable numbers of *gaṅgā*-sands of world-systems, he places them within a single infinitesimal atom.

The quantity of those atoms neither increases nor decreases; within a single atom, all those worlds are each situated without mutual obstruction, and the sentient beings therein likewise experience no state of disturbance or crowding.
This is called the Bodhisattva’s cultivation and attainment of perfection in the power of supernormal knowledges (*abhijñā*).
How does a Bodhisattva cultivate and attain perfection in the power of mastery (*vaśitā*)?

It means that this Bodhisattva, by the mere inclination of his will, causes the seven treasures to fill the great trichiliocosm to benefit sentient beings, and even desires to cause various kinds of jewels to fill unspeakably unspeakable numbers of world-systems.
This is called the bodhisattva’s fulfillment of the power of mastery.
How does a bodhisattva fulfill the power of dhāraṇī?

It is when this bodhisattva, even regarding all the Tathāgatas expounding the True Dharma within unspeakably unspeakable numbers of Buddha-fields—wherein the meanings and phrases differ and the names and principles vary—is able, within a single kṣaṇa, or a single lava, or a single muhūrta, to comprehend, understand, and practice them all in their meanings, phrases, names, and principles.
This is called a bodhisattva attaining perfection in the power of dhāraṇī.
What is the bodhisattva’s perfection in the majestic power of miraculous transformations that cannot be altered?

It means that regarding all the miraculous transformations of this bodhisattva, with the sole exception of a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, no sentient being whatsoever will ever be able to alter the bodhisattva.
This is called the bodhisattva’s attainment of the perfection of the majestic power of unalterable spiritual transformations.
What is the bodhisattva’s attainment of the perfection of the power of non-contradictory instruction?

It means that whatever instructions this bodhisattva issues are without contradiction; sentient beings believe and comply with them, and none transgress them, except as a skillful means for their benefit and happiness.
This is called the bodhisattva’s attainment of the perfection of the power of non-contradiction with the teachings. "Good son!
When a bodhisattva accomplishes these ten dharmas, their power of cultivation is perfected."
"Furthermore, son of good family,
when a bodhisattva accomplishes ten kinds of dharmas, they attain the perfection of wisdom. What are these ten?
First, attaining perfection in the wisdom of the selflessness of persons;
second, attaining perfection in the wisdom of the selflessness of phenomena;
third, attaining perfection in immeasurable wisdom.
Fourth, the perfection of the knowledge of the objective sphere of samādhi;
fifth, the perfection of the cultivation of the knowledge of supernormal transformations;
sixth, the perfection of the cultivation of the knowledge of non-appropriation.
Seventh, the perfection of the wisdom that observes the conduct of sentient beings;
eighth, the perfection of effortless wisdom;
ninth, the perfection of the cultivation of the wisdom of the characteristics of all phenomena.
Tenth, they attain the perfection of supramundane wisdom.
How does a bodhisattva perfect the wisdom of the selflessness of persons?
It means that this bodhisattva, in accordance with the characteristics of the aggregates, observes their arising and further observes their disintegration.
When a bodhisattva correctly contemplates the arising of the aggregates, they see that their nature is not solid and they lack any real activity; this is emptiness.
Furthermore, when correctly observing the cessation of the aggregates, he sees that their essential nature is disintegrated.
The bodhisattva reflects in this way:
"The aggregates are ultimately without self; they are also without a sentient being, without a life-principle, without a nourisher, and without a person."
"Foolish ordinary beings cling to a self. Thus he reflects:

"The aggregates are not the self, and the self is not the aggregates; yet, within the aggregates they falsely conceive of a self. Because they cannot understand the true nature of phenomena, they wander through birth and death like a spinning wheel."
“When a bodhisattva understands all phenomena as they truly are, this is called the bodhisattva’s perfection of the wisdom regarding the selflessness of persons.
How does a bodhisattva attain perfection in the wisdom regarding the selflessness of phenomena?”
This means that this bodhisattva understands, as it truly is, the nature of phenomena (dharmas) as being subject to superimposition and denial.
Furthermore, the bodhisattva reflects in this way: "Phenomena and names are mutually adventitious;

they are established as phenomena and names solely through false conceptualization, and both lack intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). Based on the measure of the mind of ideation (*vikalpa-citta-mātra*) and in accordance with worldly convention, phenomena and names are mutually adventitious. It is not that they lack substance or function; rather, the nature of these phenomena is said to exist based on dependence upon others, because they arise only by depending upon various other conditions."
The Bodhisattva understands, as it truly is, that all things arise in dependence upon conditions and cease when conditions are exhausted.
This is called the Bodhisattva’s perfection of the wisdom regarding the selflessness of phenomena (*dharmanairātmya*).
“How does a bodhisattva attain perfection in immeasurable wisdom?
It is because this immeasurable wisdom of the bodhisattva does not arise in the first moment and fail to arise in subsequent moments;
nor does it arise in this place and fail to arise in other places.”
Because they constantly and continuously arise, pervading all moments and all locations through unimpeded wisdom,
this is called the Bodhisattva’s attainment of perfection in immeasurable wisdom.
"How does a bodhisattva attain perfection in the wisdom regarding the spheres of activity of samādhi?

It means that this bodhisattva is able to fully understand all the samādhis attained by those of the two vehicles, is able to fully understand all the samādhis attained by bodhisattvas, and is also able to understand all the samādhis of all Tathāgatas."

Furthermore, this bodhisattva is also able to understand the meditative absorptions (samādhi) cultivated and dwelled in by those of the two vehicles, as well as the objects of experience within those meditative absorptions; he is also able to understand the meditative absorptions dwelled in by all bodhisattvas, as well as the objects of experience within those meditative absorptions; and he is also able to understand the various meditative absorptions in which the Tathāgatas dwell, as well as the objects of experience within those meditative absorptions.
Because the Bodhisattva is empowered by the sustaining power (*adhiṣṭhāna*) of the Tathāgata’s strength, they are able to fully comprehend the Buddha’s samādhis.
If a Bodhisattva were to rely solely on the wisdom that is the matured fruit (*vipākaphala-jñāna*) achieved through their own efforts, they would be unable to know the Buddha’s samādhis;
however, by means of that very wisdom of the matured fruit achieved through their own efforts, they can fully comprehend all other samādhis.
This is called the bodhisattva’s perfection of the knowledge regarding the objective sphere of practice within samādhi.
How does a bodhisattva cultivate the knowledge of supernormal transformations (ṛddhividhi-jñāna) so as to attain its perfection?

That is to say, this bodhisattva is able to correctly understand the miraculous transformations of śrāvakas, is able to correctly understand the miraculous transformations of pratyekabuddhas, and is able to correctly understand the miraculous transformations of bodhisattvas; how much more so, then, could they not know all the miraculous transformations possessed by all sentient beings!
This is called the bodhisattva’s cultivation of the wisdom of supernormal transformations (ṛddhi-jñāna) to the point of perfection.
What is the bodhisattva’s cultivation of the wisdom of non-appropriation to the point of perfection?

It refers to the wisdom accomplished by this bodhisattva, which cannot be appropriated by any outsiders (tīrthika), evil Māras, śrāvakas, or pratyekabuddhas; this is called the bodhisattva’s cultivation of the wisdom of non-appropriation to the point of perfection.
"How does a bodhisattva attain perfection in the wisdom that observes the conduct of sentient beings?

It is because this bodhisattva, with pure wisdom, observes the realm of sentient beings and perceives within it those who have not yet resolved for enlightenment, those who have already resolved for enlightenment, those who have not yet attained the resolve for enlightenment, or those who have already attained it; those dwelling in the first through the tenth stages (*bhūmi*); those who have already manifested perfect awakening (*abhisambuddha*), those currently manifesting perfect awakening while turning the wheel of Dharma, or those among those to be converted who have completed all tasks and entered *parinirvāṇa*; those entering *parinirvāṇa* by way of the Śrāvaka vehicle, or those entering *parinirvāṇa* by way of the Pratyekabuddha vehicle; and those born in the happy realms or the miserable realms—the bodhisattva perceives them all."
This is called the bodhisattva’s perfection of the wisdom that observes the conduct of sentient beings.
How does a bodhisattva attain perfection in effortless wisdom (*anābhoga-jñāna*)?
It means that whether this bodhisattva is walking, standing, going, or coming, or whether they are in motion or at rest, they spontaneously and constantly give rise to effortless wisdom.

Just as a person who is asleep has no volitional effort regarding exhalation and inhalation, one should know that the bodhisattva’s effortless wisdom (*anābhoga-jñāna*) is likewise: it arises without obstruction toward all objects and all forms of knowledge.
This is called the Bodhisattva’s attainment of perfection in effortless wisdom (*anābhoga-jñāna*).
How does the Bodhisattva attain perfection in the wisdom regarding the characteristics of all phenomena?

It means that this Bodhisattva realizes that all phenomena share a single characteristic—that is, they are able to realize the single characteristic as being without characteristics (*animitta*) and as illusory characteristics and characteristics of false conceptualization.
This is called the Bodhisattva’s perfection in the cultivation of the wisdom regarding the characteristics of all phenomena.
What is the Bodhisattva’s perfection in the cultivation of supramundane wisdom?

It refers to this Bodhisattva attaining untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-jñāna*) that transcends all mundane forms of knowledge; this is called the Bodhisattva’s perfection in the cultivation of supramundane wisdom.
“Good son! When a bodhisattva accomplishes these ten kinds of dharmas, they attain the perfection of wisdom. Furthermore, good son!”
When Bodhisattvas accomplish ten kinds of dharmas, they attain the state of being like the great earth. What are these ten?
First, they are vast and immeasurable.
Second, it is that which is enjoyed by all sentient beings;
third, it is the relinquishing of both enmity and favor;
fourth, it is the universal capacity to receive the great rain-clouds of the Dharma.
Fifth, it is that upon which all sentient beings rely;
sixth, it is the locus where the seeds of all virtues depend;
seventh, it is like a great vessel for precious jewels.
Eighth, they are like a great vessel for medicine;
ninth, they attain imperturbability;
tenth, they attain freedom from alarm and fear.
“Good son! How is it that a bodhisattva is vast and immeasurable?
It is like the great earth, which is universally expansive and without limit or measure.”
In this way, the bodhisattva is all-pervasive and vast; the provisions of merit and wisdom are without limit.
This is called the bodhisattva attaining the vast and immeasurable.
How is it that the bodhisattva becomes an object of enjoyment for all sentient beings?
Just as the great earth serves as various provisions for the enjoyment of all sentient beings,

so too does the bodhisattva gather those various accumulations— such as the perfections of generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom— for the enjoyment of all sentient beings.
This is called the Bodhisattva being that which is enjoyed by all sentient beings.
"How does a Bodhisattva abandon both enmity and gratitude?
Son of good family!
For example, just as the great earth impartially sustains all beings without thoughts of gratitude or resentment, without anger or joy;
so too is the Bodhisattva, who harbors no sense of gratitude or resentment toward sentient beings and gives rise to neither anger nor joy.
This is called the bodhisattva’s relinquishing of both enmity and gratitude.
How does a bodhisattva universally receive the great rain-clouds of the Dharma?
It is like the great earth, which universally receives vast clouds and rains, containing them all within itself.
In this way, the bodhisattva receives from the Tathāgata the initiation of vast clouds and rains of wholesome dharmas, being able both to endure and to maintain them.
This is called the bodhisattva’s universal capacity to receive the great clouds and rains of the Dharma.
"How does a bodhisattva become a refuge for all sentient beings?
Son of good family!
It is like the great earth, which serves as the basis for the coming and going of all sentient beings."
In this way, the bodhisattva is equally and universally the basis for all sentient beings to proceed toward the happy realms and advance toward nirvāṇa;
thus, the bodhisattva is called the refuge for all sentient beings.
"How is it that a bodhisattva serves as the locus for all seeds of goodness?
Son of good family!
It is like the great earth, which can serve as the locus for all seeds."
In this way, the bodhisattva is able to serve as the foundational locus for the seeds of all wholesome dharmas for sentient beings;
this is called the locus upon which the various seeds of the bodhisattva’s virtues depend.
"How is it that a bodhisattva is like a great vessel for jewels?
Good son! It is, for example, as the great earth serves as a vessel for all jewels, because it can manifest all kinds of precious treasures."
In this way, a bodhisattva can manifest various kinds of jewels of merit.
This is called the bodhisattva being like a great vessel for jewels.
"How is it that a bodhisattva is like a great vessel for medicine?
"Good son! Just as the great earth is that upon which all medicinal herbs depend for their appearance, and these are able to eliminate all diseases of the world;
so it is with the Bodhisattva—upon him all the great medicinal dharmas emerge, and the medicinal dharmas thus manifested are able to extinguish the diseases of afflictions in the world."
This is called the bodhisattva being like a great vessel for medicine.
"How does a bodhisattva attain immovability? Good son!
Just as the great earth cannot be diminished by the strength of mosquitoes, gnats, and the like, nor can it be shaken by the various winds of the world;
so too the Bodhisattva is not moved or disturbed by any internal or external sufferings of sentient beings.
This is called a bodhisattva attaining imperturbability.
"How does a bodhisattva attain freedom from fear? Good son!
For example, just as the great earth is not startled or terrified by the roaring sounds of various dragons or the kings of beasts,
so too the bodhisattva, upon hearing the roaring sounds of those māras and all the non-Buddhists, gives rise to no fear.
This is called the bodhisattva attaining freedom from fear and dread. "Good son!
When a bodhisattva accomplishes these ten kinds of dharmas, they become like the great earth."
The Sūtra of the Precious Rain Spoken by the Buddha, Volume Three;
The Sūtra of the Precious Rain Spoken by the Buddha, Volume Four.
Translated by the Tang Dynasty Indian Tripiṭaka Master Dharmaruci.
"Furthermore, noble son, when a bodhisattva accomplishes ten qualities, they become like water.
What are these ten?
First, they accord with wholesome dharmas."
Second, they are always able to give rise to and grow all pure dharmas (*śukla-dharma*);
third, they possess joyful, pure faith, which is moistened by delight;
fourth, they cause the continuity of all afflictions (*kleśa*) to decay and rot.
Fifth, its intrinsic nature is lucid, free from turbidity, and pure;
sixth, it extinguishes the burning heat of all afflictions;
seventh, it relinquishes all craving and thirst for desires.
Eighth, it is profoundly deep and difficult to fathom;
ninth, it fills all places, whether level or uneven;
tenth, it extinguishes the dust of all afflictions.
"What is meant by a bodhisattva conforming to wholesome dharmas?
It is like a great body of water: whether moving, flowing, or emerging, it is able to conform to and moisten all grasses and trees."
In this way, the bodhisattva practices in accordance with all wholesome dharmas, propagates them in accordance with them, and attains liberation in accordance with them.
This is called the bodhisattva’s conformity to wholesome dharmas.
“How does a bodhisattva give rise to all pure and wholesome dharmas?
Good son, it is like the nature of water, which can produce all grasses, trees, thickets, and forests.”
Once born, they grow.
In this same way, the Bodhisattva, by means of the water of samādhi, can produce all factors conducive to enlightenment (bodhipakṣadharma);
once produced, they grow until they can become the tree of sarvajña, attaining the tree of wisdom that is the fruit of all Buddhas.
All various kinds of pure, wholesome dharmas are made available for the enjoyment of all sentient beings;
this is called the bodhisattva’s ability to give rise to all pure, wholesome dharmas.
“How does a bodhisattva attain joyful pure faith and the moisture of delight?
Son of good family!
It is like water, whose nature is to flow and moisten, and which is able to moisten all others.”

In this way, the bodhisattva constantly maintains pure faith, joy, and delight, with a nature that is moistened; furthermore, they are able to cause all other sentient beings to likewise experience joy, pure faith, delight, and moistening.
What is joy? It is the constant aspiration for supramundane dharmas.
What is pure faith?
This refers to being able to take refuge in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha.
What is meant by "joyful delight"?
It refers to that pure mind of theirs which is constantly joyful and delighted.
This is called the bodhisattva’s joy, pure faith, delight, and nourishment.
How does a bodhisattva cause all the roots and sprouts of the continuity of afflictions to completely decay?
"Good son! Just as water can cause the roots of all trees and grasses to rot and decay, so too does the Bodhisattva,
by means of the water of the samādhi upon which their practice relies, cause the continuous succession of the root-seeds of all afflictions to rot and decay."
Once they have rotted away, the continuity of the afflictions cannot be found as a substantial entity; the foul stench of the afflictions leaves no residual habit-energy behind.
This is called the Bodhisattva causing the roots and sprouts of the continuity of all afflictions to completely rot away.
“What is meant by a bodhisattva whose intrinsic nature is transparent, free from turbidity, and pure?
Son of good family!
It is just as water, which is by its very nature transparent, free from turbidity, and pure.”
What is meant by "the intrinsic nature is lucid"?
It refers to being able to remain far removed from both active outbursts (*paryavasthāna*) and latent tendencies (*anuśaya*).
What is meant by "being free from turbidity"?
This means being able to remain far removed from greed, hatred, and delusion.
How is it pure? It is because it can cause the sense faculties to attain purity.
This is called the bodhisattva’s intrinsic clarity, freedom from turbidity, and purity.
"How does a bodhisattva extinguish the burning of all afflictions?
Son of good family!
Just as the nature of water completely extinguishes the heat of sentient beings' afflictions, as well as physical heat and hot places,
so too does the Bodhisattva, by means of the water of the Dharma, extinguish the heat of all the afflictions of sentient beings.
This is called the bodhisattva’s extinguishing of the burning of all afflictions.
“How does a bodhisattva abandon all thirst for desire? Good son!
Just as sentient beings, when oppressed by thirst, find relief from their thirst as soon as they obtain water, so it is with Bodhisattvas:
because all sentient beings are oppressed by the thirst for the objects of desire, they give rise to various forms of suffering and affliction.
The Bodhisattva then rains down the great rain of the Dharma, by which sentient beings are freed from the thirst for sense objects.
This is called the Bodhisattva’s relinquishing of all thirst for sensual desires.
“What is meant by ‘the bodhisattva’s profound and difficult-to-cross’?
Good son, it is like a great body of deep water, which is extremely difficult to cross.”
In this way, the bodhisattva achieves the perfection of profound prajñā and cannot be overcome by any māras or externalists.
This is called the bodhisattva’s profundity that is difficult to fathom.
“How does a bodhisattva fill equal and unequal places?
Son of good family!
Just as a torrential stream of water completely fills all places, whether they be level or uneven.”
In this way, the Bodhisattva is able to completely fill the realms of all sentient beings—both those who are equal and those who are unequal—with a torrential stream of the water of Dharma.

Because the Bodhisattva feels compassion for all sentient beings, they give rise to a vast torrent of the water of Dharma without oppressing the realms of sentient beings; thus, they are not like ordinary water.
This is called the Bodhisattva filling equal and unequal places.
"How does a Bodhisattva extinguish all the dust of the afflictions?
Son of good family!
Just as water can cause all hard and rigid places to become universally supple and can settle all dust and grit, so too does the Bodhisattva,
by means of the water of samādhi based upon prajñā, cause the hard and rigid defiled minds of all sentient beings to become entirely supple and can extinguish the dust and grit of the afflictions.
This is called the bodhisattva’s quelling and extinguishing of all the dust of afflictions. "Good son,
when a bodhisattva accomplishes these ten kinds of dharmas, they are equal to water."
"Furthermore, son of good family!
A bodhisattva who accomplishes ten qualities is equal to fire. What are these ten?
First, it can burn away the mass of all afflictions;
second, it can bring the Buddha-dharma to maturity;
third, it can dry up the mud of all afflictions.
Fourth, it is like a great mass of fire;
fifth, it is like the radiance of fire;
sixth, it is able to cause terror and dread.
Seventh, it can bring about peace and security;
eighth, it can cause all sentient beings to obtain [it] together;
ninth, it can cause [them] to make offerings.
Tenth, one attains freedom from being slighted or deceived.
"How is it that one can incinerate the mass of all afflictions? Good son!..."
Just as a great fire can burn away all grasses, trees, thickets, and heaps of filth and impurity,
so too does a bodhisattva, by means of the fire of wisdom, burn away all fetters, latent tendencies, and the heap of afflictions such as greed, hatred, and delusion.
This is called a bodhisattva being able to incinerate the entire mass of all afflictions.
"How does a bodhisattva bring the Buddha-dharmas to maturity? Good son!
Just as the nature of fire ripens all kinds of food, drink, medicinal herbs, and other such things,
so too does the bodhisattva, through the wisdom realized within, ripen the Buddha-dharmas without ever falling away from them.
This is called the Bodhisattva’s maturation of the Buddha-dharmas.
“How does a Bodhisattva dry up the mud of all afflictions? Good son!
Just as a great fire can dry up mud,
so too does the bodhisattva completely dry up the mud of all afflictions (*kleśa*).
This is called the bodhisattva’s ability to dry up the mud of all afflictions.
“How is it that a bodhisattva is like a great mass of fire? Good son!
For example, suppose there is a person oppressed by the suffering of extreme cold who, by kindling a great mass of fire, succeeds in escaping that cold suffering.”
In this way, when sentient beings are oppressed by the cold suffering of the afflictions (*kleśa*), the Bodhisattva causes them to be extinguished by the fire of *prajñā*.
This is called the Bodhisattva being like a great mass of fire.
"How is it that a bodhisattva is like the radiance of fire? Good son!

It is, for example, as if someone were to kindle a great mass of fire upon the peak of the Snowy Mountains or the peak of Mount Mithila; blazing and fiercely radiant, its light would pervade one *yojana*, or two *yojanas*, or three *yojanas*."

In this way, the Bodhisattva, with the brilliant radiance of wisdom, pervades a hundred *yojanas*, or a thousand *yojanas*, or a hundred thousand *yojanas*, and even throughout immeasurable *asaṃkhyeya* worlds; all sentient beings therein are likewise graced by the pervasive brilliance of his wisdom-light.
Because sentient beings encounter this light of wisdom, they destroy all the darkness of ignorance.
This is called the Bodhisattva being like the light of fire.
"How does a Bodhisattva cause [others] to be struck with awe and fear?"

Good son! For example, when the king of beasts and various other fierce predators see a great mass of fire, they immediately give rise to fear; having become terrified, they abandon this place and travel far away to another region.

It is the same for all the Māra kings and their demonic hosts: if they see a bodhisattva, fear arises in their hearts because they perceive their own majesty and radiance to be inferior; they abandon the bodhisattva and flee to other places, not even wishing to hear the bodhisattva’s name, let alone behold him closely.
This is called a bodhisattva who can cause [others] to be struck with awe and fear.
"How does a bodhisattva bring about peace and security? Good son!

It is like a person in a vast wilderness, exhausted by hunger and thirst, beset by peril and hardship, and having lost their sense of direction, who upon seeing a great mass of fire approaches it; or perhaps they encounter a village or a cattle-pasture, and having seen these, they leave behind all fear and their mind attains peace and security.
Sentient beings are likewise!

Dwelling in the wilderness and perilous difficulties of birth and death, parched with thirst and exhausted by fatigue, they lose their way on the correct path; yet upon seeing the Bodhisattva, they are freed from all the terrors of affliction, and their minds attain peace and security.
This is called a bodhisattva being able to bring about peace and security.
"How does a bodhisattva enable all sentient beings to attain this together? Good son!
For example, the warming power of a mass of fire is something shared by all sentient beings; whether it be kings, their ministers, or even the sons of caṇḍālas, they all partake of it together.
The Bodhisattva is likewise!
All the power of his grace is shared by all sentient beings—whether they be kings, those equal to kings, or even the sons of caṇḍālas.
This is called the Bodhisattva’s ability to cause all sentient beings to share in it together.
"How can a bodhisattva cause offerings to be made?
Good son, it is like a mass of fire that causes people in cities, towns, and villages— such as Agnihotra Brahmins and Kṣatriyas— to offer worship."
The Bodhisattva is likewise!
They should be honored by the gods, humans, asuras, and others of the world with the same regard one has for a Buddha;
this is called the Bodhisattva’s ability to inspire offerings.
"How does a bodhisattva become one who cannot be slighted or deceived? Good son!
It is like a tiny spark of fire that cannot be slighted, because its nature is to burn."
The Bodhisattva is likewise!

Abiding in the stage of practice through understanding and newly training in the Mahāyāna, although they may not yet possess vast power and majesty, they are never looked down upon or treated with contempt by any in the world—whether devas, humans, or asuras.

Why is this? Because the world’s devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, and others know that before long the Bodhisattva will sit at the site of enlightenment and attain unexcelled, perfect, and complete awakening (anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi).
This is called the bodhisattva attaining freedom from being slighted or deceived. "Good son!
When a bodhisattva accomplishes these ten kinds of dharmas, they become like fire."
"Furthermore, son of good family,
when bodhisattvas accomplish ten qualities, they are equal to the wind. What are these ten?
First, it is equal to the movement of the wind in that it has no fixed location;
second, it is equal to the course of the wind in that it is ultimately inexhaustible;
third, it is able to shatter the mountain peaks of the self-conceit of sentient beings.
Fourth, they are able to raise the great clouds and rain of the Dharma;
fifth, they are able to eliminate all the feverish afflictions and delusions of sentient beings;

sixth, they are able to universally bestow upon all sentient beings the pure dharmas that flow equally from them, as well as the skillful means of sustaining life through the out-breath and in-breath.
Seventh, they are able to sustain the rain from immeasurable great Dharma-clouds;
eighth, they are able to establish the most supreme Great Dharma, with all palaces adorned in various ways;
ninth, they are able to definitively expound various sublime Dharmas within the assemblies, just as when the wind blows upon the kalpavṛkṣa trees, causing delightful flowers to fall like rain.

Tenth, having accumulated immeasurable pure wheels of Dharma (*dharmacakra*), samādhis, liberations (*vimokṣa*), and dhāraṇīs over incalculable eons (*asaṃkhyeya-kalpa*), he brings forth the wind-circle of wisdom (*jñāna-vāyu-maṇḍala*) in those assemblies surrounded by great oceans, Mount Sumeru, and the Cakravāḍa mountains; for any sentient beings who are capable of being tamed and can be matured, he causes their bases of existence (*āśraya*) to be turned and extinguished, leaving nothing behind.
“Good son! How is it that one is equal to the wind in moving without a fixed location? Good son!”

For example, like the movement of wind, it dwells nowhere and has no fixed location; it has no basis of reliance and possesses no form or characteristic, yet it can perform its own function—namely, causing all palaces, Mount Sumeru, and the various oceans to tremble—and accomplishes these tasks so that others may perceive them.
The Bodhisattva is also like this: practicing in all places, they attain non-attachment.
What are these "all places"? They are the aggregates (skandhas), the elements (dhātus), and the sense bases (āyatanas).

Among all phenomena (*dharmas*), the aggregates (*skandhas*) are the aggregate of form, the aggregate of feeling, the aggregate of perception, the aggregate of formations, and the aggregate of consciousness.

The elements (*dhātus*) are the eye element, the form element, and the eye-consciousness element; the ear element, the sound element, and the ear-consciousness element; the nose element, the odor element, and the nose-consciousness element; the tongue element, the taste element, and the tongue-consciousness element; the body element, the tangible object element, and the body-consciousness element;

the mind element, the mental-object element, and the mind-consciousness element. The sense bases (*āyatanas*) are the eye base and the form base; the ear base and the sound base; the nose base and the odor base; the tongue base and the taste base; the body base and the tangible object base; the mind base and the mental-object base.

Furthermore, regarding mundane and supramundane phenomena—including the flourishing wealth and nobility of all devas and humans, the status of a wheel-turning sage king (cakravartin), Śakra, Brahmā, the World-Protectors (lokapāla), Maheśvara, as well as śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, bodhisattvas of the various stages, and even up to omniscience—the bodhisattva attains non-attachment toward all such states.

Furthermore, they are able to remain far removed from the conceptualizations of immeasurable discrimination—such as being neither existent nor non-existent, neither identical nor different, neither real nor false—and because there is no objective referent, the liberation in which Bodhisattvas practice is unimpeded.

Furthermore, they are able to manifest throughout the infinite and boundless worlds of the ten directions, appearing in the forms of Śakra, Brahmā, the World-Protectors (Lokapālas), and so forth. Desiring to benefit all sentient beings, they travel everywhere; yet even after many kalpas have passed, they can never be seen, because they are free from limits and because their Dharma-nature body is far removed from both the conceptualizer and the conceptualized.
“Good son! This is called the bodhisattva’s practice that is equal to the movement of the wind, having no fixed location. Good son!”
"How does the practice of the Bodhisattva equal that of the wind, reaching its ultimate limit without exhaustion? Good son!
Just as the wind moves through immeasurable worlds, able to blow upon all things, swiftly causing them to revolve, each performing its respective function."
The Bodhisattva is likewise!

Just as the wind touches all things and swiftly moves through every direction and place without ever reaching an end, so too is he able to travel to the assemblies at the bodhimaṇḍas of all Tathāgatas and the assemblies at the bodhimaṇḍas of all Bodhisattvas;

furthermore, he establishes himself universally within all the palaces of the world, proclaiming and expounding the teachings, and thoroughly observing the infinite phenomena of both the conventional and the ultimate truth.
This is called the bodhisattva’s practice of equanimity like the wind, which is ultimately inexhaustible. "Good son,
how does a bodhisattva succeed in shattering the mountain peaks of the pride of all sentient beings?"
Good son! Just as the wind can cause the peaks, forests, and groves of Mount Mandara to bend low, break, and fall,
so too is it with the Bodhisattva!
Just as that wind can cause the mountain peaks of sentient beings’ pride, intoxication, and heedlessness to be shattered and cast down.
What is called the mountain peak of pride?
