It refers to those sentient beings who, relying upon their own physical form, strength, and other such attributes, enjoy them with mastery; who possess long life and freedom from illness, are capable of sustaining their livelihood, and are skilled in crafts, learned, clever, and wise; who have excellent retinues and possess eloquent speech that delights the audience—thereby becoming intoxicated with pride and praising their own capabilities.

Because Bodhisattvas wish to shatter the mountain peaks of the self-conceit (*asmimāna*) of sentient beings, they are able to manifest signs of physical power and such matters as the enjoyment of wealth; being most supreme and sovereign, surpassing those ordinary people, they preach the True Dharma to shatter the high mountains of sentient beings' self-conceit and are able to establish them all in the pure and wholesome states.
This is called a bodhisattva being able to shatter the mountain peaks of self-conceit. "Good son!
How does a bodhisattva become able to raise the great clouds and rain of the Dharma?"
"Good son! It is like the power of the wind pervading the four directions, giving rise to great clouds;
those clouds are like wheels with various colors, their thunderous sound resounding afar like the roar of the ocean—exquisite, clear, profound, and soft."
Furthermore, various musical sounds and songs emerge that are able to gladden the mind; garlands of lightning flash with brilliant adornment, and great rains fall constantly day and night.
Moreover, rains of various kinds of jewels pour down everywhere, covering hundreds of thousands of koṭi-nayuta worlds and causing all sentient beings to rejoice and find delight;
furthermore, they cause all the grasses, trees, forests, and crops in the world to grow and flourish.

The Bodhisattva is likewise! Taking great compassion as the wind, they give rise to various bodily forms throughout the boundless worlds of the ten directions, using them as clouds. The light they emit is dazzlingly brilliant and sublime; its radiant appearance is adorned and purified like the light of a garland of lightning, beloved by all sentient beings. They produce great sounds that proclaim the true Dharma, like the majestic resonance of thunder, deep and far-reaching. With sixty thousand varieties of distinct speech, they use these sounds to rain down the great Dharma rain upon all sentient beings throughout the entirety of space and the pervasiveness of the Dharma realm. They provide protection for all sentient beings in the world who dwell in evil destinies, unfavorable conditions, or those suffering pain, causing them all to be free from suffering.

Furthermore, they are able to empower these sentient beings, establishing them in all pure and adorned worlds, causing them all to attain supreme joy, giving rise to a mind of peace and happiness, and becoming prosperous and flourishing; they cause them to obtain various marks and signs of excellence and a halo of light, that light being pure, distinct, and brilliantly radiant.

Furthermore, within all assemblies of the Dharma, he sprinkles the rainwater of the Dharma upon the crowns of the heads of humans and devas, causing them to attain supreme joy and bliss. He brings to fulfillment all mundane and supramundane pure dharmas, causing them all to grow and flourish, just as clouds and rain enable medicinal herbs, thickets, forests, and crops to grow.
This is called a bodhisattva’s ability to extensively give rise to the great rain from the clouds of the Dharma. "Good son,
how is it that a bodhisattva is able to eliminate the feverish afflictions and delusions of all sentient beings?"

"Noble son! Just as when the wind blows upon the masses of clouds, it causes pure fragrant rain to flow everywhere, which brings about coolness and eliminates all the feverish afflictions of sentient beings."
The Bodhisattva is likewise!

With great compassion as the wind, he uses the True Dharma as water and the fragrance of pure precepts and the fragrance of unfailing vows to benefit sentient beings. This means that when one draws near to and dwells together with a Bodhisattva—whether hearing their teaching of the Dharma, seeing them, or touching them—one receives benefit; this is called the "fragrance of the Bodhisattva’s unfailing vow."

By means of this peerless, harmonious perfumed water, all sentient beings in the evil realms—such as their afflictions of greed, hatred, and delusion; their wrong views and evil conduct; their poverty and suffering; their separation from what they love and union with what they dislike within their spheres of experience; their unrighteous cravings; and the various fevers that give rise to manifold diseases—are all caused to be extinguished. Furthermore, it can establish them upon the ground free from sorrow and affliction.
This is called the bodhisattva’s ability to extinguish all the burning heat of the afflictions of the world.

How is it that a bodhisattva is able to universally bestow upon all sentient beings the pure dharmas of their own kind, and possesses skill in the life-sustaining techniques of exhalation and inhalation?
"Good son! Just as there are inhalations and exhalations due to the power of the wind, which enable all sentient beings to sustain their lives,
so it is with the bodhisattva!"
Just as the power of that wind can bestow all pure and white dharmas, can grant various forms of wealth, honor, and fulfillment, and can cause sentient beings to each attain joy.
"Furthermore, good son!

For example, the power of the wind is extensively able to establish all the various adornments of the worlds. That is to say, the wind can support the vajra-rimmed wheel and so forth, the seven-jeweled continents and oceans, the Cakravāḍa mountains, the Mahācakravāḍa mountains, the four great continents, Mount Sumeru, the Great Sumeru, and other jewel mountains, the Fragrant Mountains, the Snowy Mountains, the palaces of Śakra, Jambudvīpa and so forth, as well as the small thousand-fold, middle thousand-fold, and great trichiliocosm worlds."
The Bodhisattva is likewise!

Great compassion is the wind, meaning it is able to bestow upon all sentient beings throughout the ten directions the entire mass of their merits, causing them all to grow, be established, and reach fulfillment.
Just as the Snowy Mountains are brought into existence by the power of the wind, one should know that the Bodhisattva’s bestowing of gifts upon the world as a field of merit is likewise so.
Just as the wind brings about the four great continents, Mount Sumeru, and so forth, one should know that the Bodhisattva’s accomplishment of Śrāvakas is likewise so.
Just as the wind can sustain a small chiliocosm, one should know that the Bodhisattva’s ability to accomplish the fruit of a Pratyekabuddha is likewise so!
Just as the wind establishes a medium chiliocosm, one should know that the establishment of the fruit of the Bodhisattva vehicle is likewise so!

Just as the wind establishes the great trichiliocosm, so too does the Bodhisattva establish the marks of the Tathāgata’s body endowed with the hundred merits; surpassing all worlds and all realms, profoundly deep and pure, ultimately perfect, pervading the entire realm of space—know that it is likewise when one hears the Buddha’s name, makes all offerings, and at all times remains established in *samāhita*, ever-present before them.
Just as the wind can produce the waters of all great oceans, one should know that the Bodhisattva’s production of the ocean of samādhis is likewise.

Just as the wind establishes the small, medium, and great continents, as well as the various mountains and so forth, one should know that the Bodhisattva’s accomplishment of the various dhāraṇīs, through skillful means, matures the assembly of disciples and all sentient beings is likewise.
Just as the wind establishes the palace of Śakra, one should know that it is likewise with the Bodhisattva’s ability to establish pure Buddha-fields adorned with merit!

Just as the wind can bring forth the groves of kalpavṛkṣa trees, one should know that it is likewise with the Bodhisattva’s accomplishment of the stages, the pāramitās, the mastery of samādhis and supernormal powers, the various dhāraṇīs, the light of wisdom of the three knowledges, the power of manifesting perfect enlightenment, the fearlessnesses, the unique qualities, and great compassion—attaining supreme mastery over all phenomena!
“Good son! What are called the marks of the hundred merits of the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones? Good son!”

For example, suppose that in each of the ten directions there were worlds as numerous as the sands of incalculable *gaṅgā* rivers, and every single sentient being within them were to individually achieve a mass of merit equal to that of all the universal monarchs (*cakravartin*) existing within thirteen thousand great thousandfold world systems.
If the mass of merit possessed by all those sentient beings were gathered into a single collection, it would equal the amount of merit of one great universal monarch (*cakravartin*).

Beyond the number of worlds previously described in the eastern direction, there are again as many worlds as before; in each of those worlds, every sentient being possesses an amount of merit equal to that of the aforementioned great universal monarch.

In this same sequence, it is likewise for the south, west, north, the four intermediate directions, and the zenith and nadir; even unto every single sentient being within all worlds throughout the entirety of the realm of space, each one attains a measure of merit equal to that of a single great wheel-turning monarch as previously described.

"Good son! Suppose that in each of the ten directions there were worlds as numerous as the sands of incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) Gaṅgā rivers, and every single sentient being within them were to individually achieve a mass of merit equal to that of all the Śakras residing within thirteen thousand great thousand-world systems."
The aggregate of merit consisting of the merit of Śakra possessed by all those sentient beings, when combined, constitutes the measure of the merit of one great Śakra.

To the east, beyond the number of worlds previously described, there are again as many worlds as were mentioned before; every sentient being within those worlds individually attains a measure of merit equal to that of one Great Śakra as previously described.

In this same sequence, it is likewise for the south, west, north, the four intermediate directions, and the zenith and nadir; even unto every single sentient being in all worlds throughout the entirety of the realm of space, each shall achieve a measure of merit as previously described.

"Good son! Suppose that in each of the ten directions there were worlds as numerous as the sands of incalculable Gaṅgā rivers; and suppose every single sentient being within them were to achieve a mass of merit equal to that of all the Brahmā kings existing within thirteen thousand great thousandfold world systems."
The total measure of the merit of those sentient beings who constitute such Brahmā kings, gathered together as a single mass, forms the measure of the merit of one great Brahmā king.

To the east, beyond the number of worlds previously described, there are further worlds in a number equal to that; every sentient being within those worlds individually achieves a measure of merit equal to that of one great Brahmā king as previously described. In this same sequence, it is likewise in the south, west, north, the four intermediate directions, and above and below, until all sentient beings throughout the entirety of the realm of empty space have each achieved a measure of merit equal to that of one great Brahmā king as previously described.

"Good son! By this same calculation, the measure of the mass of merit of all sentient beings in all worlds who have attained the state of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, who have realized the light of great wisdom of the ten stages and received the empowerment of the Dharma-cloud, and who have become great bodhisattvas possessing the ten masteries, is likewise the same."

“Good son! Taking all sentient beings throughout all worlds as numerous as the atoms within the entirety of space across the ten directions and three periods of time, and gathering the mass of merit from all such various types of sentient beings, when this number is multiplied a hundredfold, it constitutes the mass of merit within a single pore of a Tathāgata.

If the mass of merit from all the pores of that Tathāgata were multiplied by a number equal to ten *asaṃkhyeya* hundreds of thousands, it would constitute the measure of merit for a single secondary mark (*anuvyañjana*) among the eighty secondary marks.

By means of all those merits from the secondary marks (*anuvyañjana*), when accumulated to a number ten times as many as an unspeakable of unspeakables, one accomplishes twenty-nine of the Tathāgata’s marks (*lakṣaṇa*); when accumulated to a number ten times as many as an unspeakable of unspeakable *koṭis*, one accomplishes the mark of the white tuft of hair (*ūrṇā-kośa*) between the eyebrows of the Tathāgata.
The radiance of his white tuft mark (ūrṇā-kośa) is pure and majestic, exceeding a perfectly pure lunar disc by a thousandfold.

When such numbers are accumulated to a full ten times an unspeakable number of unspeakable thousands of koṭis, it accomplishes the Tathāgata’s mark of the invisible crown of the head (anavalokitamūrdha-lakṣaṇa). Adorned with the uṣṇīṣa, this mark of the invisible crown surpasses all worldly accumulations by a full ten times an unspeakable number of unspeakable koṭi-nayuta hundreds of thousands. It accomplishes the Tathāgata’s mark of the Brahma-like voice (brahma-svara-lakṣaṇa).

The characteristics of the Brahma-voice produced by that Buddha consist of sixty thousand aspects; it is spontaneous and sovereign, capable of various modes of expression, with a diction and melody so harmonious and elegant that all in the world hear it equally, further causing sentient beings to rejoice and be fully satisfied.
"Good son! This is called the mark of the hundred merits of all Buddhas. Good son!"
The Tathāgata is universally adorned with these inexhaustible provisions of merit and wisdom, enabling all sentient beings to partake of them.
O son of good family!

If all sentient beings throughout the worlds of the ten directions, pervading the entire dharma-realm and the full extent of space, were all to abide on the tenth stage, the Cloud of Dharma; if they were all adorned with various supreme refinements of the three karmas and had attained mastery among the ten masteries; and if there were vessels made of Jambudvīpa gold, adorned with various jewels, equal in measure to space and as numerous as the sands of the Ganges River—[if even such beings and objects were to exist...]

Using this precious vessel to take up the mass of merit within a single pore of the Tathāgata, one might carry it away in a single kṣaṇa; though one were to continue taking it away until the end of the future, the mass of merit within a single pore of the Tathāgata would neither increase nor decrease.
"Good son! The physical marks of all Tathāgatas, which embody a hundred merits, are inconceivable.
What are the twelve kinds found in the various stages?
1. The stage of not yet having generated the mind of enlightenment;
2. The stage of extreme joy;
3. The stage free from defilement;
4. The Ground of Radiant Light;
5. The Ground of Blazing Wisdom;
6. The Ground of Utmost Difficulty to Conquer;
7. The Ground of Presence;
8. The Ground of Far-Going;
9. The Immovable Ground;
Tenth, the Stage of Excellent Intelligence (Sādhumatī-bhūmi);
eleventh, the Stage of the Cloud of Dharma (Dharmameghā-bhūmi);
twelfth, the Stage of the Buddha of Universal Radiance (Samantaprabhā-buddhabhūmi).

What is the first stage, the ground of the bodhisattva who has not yet set out? It refers to this bodhisattva who has transcended all the phenomena of destruction practiced by ordinary fools; who excels all those in the three realms—humans, devas, Śakra, Brahmā, the World-Protectors, śrāvakas, and pratyekabuddhas; who surpasses all that is attained in the world; who is adorned with the various ornaments of the three karmas; whose radiant halo shines brilliantly throughout all the boundless worlds of the ten directions; and who, through the power of diligence, in a single kṣaṇa, comes and goes without obstruction across incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) worlds;
and who, within the four great continents of every world, universally manifests lotuses as great radiance, adorned with jeweled nets to support his feet.

Within a thousand worlds, there were infinite and boundless adorned jewel thrones; he diligently practiced *vipaśyanā* and was well able to thoroughly understand all phenomena. Regarding the objects of his focus, he encountered no obstacles;

according to what his mind delighted in, he could manifest ten kinds of vast auspicious signs, even manifesting incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) and supreme auspicious signs. He attained non-retrogression and traveled through all directions without hindrance, emitting inconceivable great nets of light that adorned immeasurable Buddha-fields with skillful miraculous transformations.

Within unspeakable numbers of worlds, he manifested as the sovereign of infinite and boundless worlds; appearing like a shadow-body of a Buddha, he exercised mastery as a lord, received the consecration (*abhiṣeka*), and became a great donor.

They are able to rain down the light of immeasurable Dharma-treasures throughout all mundane and supramundane realms, performing great sacrificial assemblies; like clouds, they bestow [benefits] universally and everywhere without end or obstruction, with vast adornments that cause all who see them to rejoice, satisfying the inclinations of all sentient beings in accordance with their wishes;
furthermore, they can shake all incalculable worlds, traveling back and forth out of compassion for all sentient beings in the boundless evil destinies and elsewhere.
Furthermore, they are able to make offerings to boundless Buddhas and are fully capable of receiving and upholding all dharma-gates;

moreover, they constantly sport within incalculable samādhis, dhāraṇīs, liberations, and the luminous wisdom of supernormal powers, delighting in the pleasures of the boundless gardens of the Dharma without any expectation of reward.

Throughout countless *koṭi* great eons, one attains effortlessness (*anābhoga*), free from conceptual discrimination and endowed with supreme radiance. Having passed through immeasurable hundreds of thousands of *koṭi-nayuta* lotus-eon periods, one enters the Mahāyāna and practices various forms of altruistic conduct. One extracts the accumulations of merit and wisdom that lead to liberation; because the causes previously cultivated were of infinite kinds, they now increase by hundreds of thousands of times. Through this supreme and most excellent resolve regarding the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), one attains the first stage (*prathamā bhūmi*) in an uninterrupted moment.
This is the stage where the Bodhisattva has not yet set out to realize the ground of the nature of bodhicitta. Good son!
It is like a wheel-turning sage king who has already surpassed the physical forms of human beings, yet has not yet attained the pure and wondrous physical forms that transcend those of the devas.
In this way, the bodhisattva has already transcended all worldly stages, as well as those of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, yet has not yet attained the ultimate stage of a bodhisattva.

"Furthermore, regarding the stage of the Buddha Universal Radiance (*Samantaprabhā-buddhabhūmi*): it is the realization of being free from the extremes of the middle and the periphery, such that no further defilements remain; it is the attainment of mastery over all phenomena; and within a single instant, it is the universal observation of all sentient beings and the acquisition of the signs of all meaningful benefits."
"Furthermore, what are called the various samādhis?
It refers to the ten kinds of samādhis realized by bodhisattvas:
first, the Jewel-Emergence Samādhi;..."
2. The samādhi of abiding well;
3. the samādhi of immovability;
4. the samādhi of non-retrogression;
5. The Jewel Heap Samādhi; 6. The Sunlight Samādhi;
7. The Accomplishment of All Aims Samādhi;
8. The Samādhi of the Torch of Wisdom;
9. The Samādhi of Abiding Before the Buddhas of the Present;
10. The Samādhi of Heroic Stride.
These bodhisattvas have realized immeasurable and boundless samādhis, with those such as these serving as their foremost.
Furthermore, there are twelve kinds of bodhisattva dhāraṇīs:
first, the consecration dhāraṇī;...
2. The dhāraṇī of the wise; 3. the dhāraṇī of pure sound;
4. the dhāraṇī of the inexhaustible casket;
5. The Boundless Revolving Dhāraṇī; 6. The Ocean-Seal Dhāraṇī;
7. The Peak of Eloquence Dhāraṇī;
8. The Lotus Adornment Dhāraṇī;
9. The Entrance into the Gate of Non-attachment Dhāraṇī;
10. The Determined Entrance into Unimpeded Understanding Dhāraṇī;
11. The Dharani of the Miraculous Transformation of the Adornments of All Buddhas;
12. The Dharani of the Manifestation in the World of the Boundless Colors and Forms of the Buddha-body.
These bodhisattvas have realized immeasurable and boundless dhāraṇīs, with these as their foremost.
What are the six kinds of supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) of a bodhisattva?
1. The supernormal knowledge of the divine eye;
2. The supernormal knowledge of the divine ear;
3. The supernormal knowledge of others' minds;
4. The supernormal knowledge of recollecting past lives;
5. The supernormal knowledge of the power of transformation;
6. The supernormal knowledge of the exhaustion of outflows.
"What are the ten kinds of mastery of a bodhisattva?
First, mastery over life, by which one can maintain and sustain this lifespan throughout immeasurable asaṃkhyeya kalpas;
second, mastery over mind, by which, through the skillful means of mental mastery and subjugation, one enters unspeakable samādhis and attains sovereignty."
3. Mastery over wealth, by which one manifests all the magnificent adornments of every world;
4. Mastery over karma, by which one can manifest in accordance with various karmas and their maturation;
5. Mastery over birth, by which one can manifest taking birth in all worlds.
Sixth is mastery over resolve (*adhimukti-vaśitā*), which means being able to manifest the physical forms of all Buddhas, filling all worlds so that they may be seen;
seventh is mastery over vows (*praṇidhāna-vaśitā*), which means being able to manifest perfect enlightenment at any time and in any world as one desires;
eighth is mastery over supernormal powers (*abhijñā-vaśitā*), which means manifesting infinite varieties of miraculous transformations in all worlds.
Ninth, mastery over phenomena (*dharmavaśitā*), which means being able to clearly manifest those dharma-gates that are free from the extremes of the middle and the peripheries;

tenth, mastery over knowledge (*jñānavaśitā*), which means being able to universally and fully comprehend, within a single instant, the ten powers, the fearlessnesses, the unimpeded deliverances, the unique qualities of a Buddha, and all the primary and secondary marks of the Tathāgatas of the three periods of time,
and furthermore being able to manifest unsurpassed perfect enlightenment.
Furthermore, in a single instant, they are able to fully comprehend the number of atoms within all the buddha-fields of the Buddhas of the three periods of time;
they can also manifest the arising of all-knowledge and the realization of perfect enlightenment, accomplishing various qualities and being endowed with the most supreme excellence.
These are the ten kinds of mastery of a bodhisattva.
What are the ten powers of a bodhisattva?
First, the power of intention;
2. the power of superior intention;
3. the power of application;
4. the power of wisdom;
5. The power of aspiration;
6. The power of cultivation;
7. The power of the vehicle;
8. The power of supernormal knowledges; 9. The power of awakening;
10. The power of being able to turn the wheel of Dharma.
"What are the four fearlessnesses of a bodhisattva?
First, having heard the dhāraṇīs, receiving, upholding, reading, and reciting them, and expounding their meaning, one attains fearlessness.

Second, by realizing selflessness, one does not disturb others nor manifest evil signs; being naturally free from fault and guarding one's deportment, the three karmas are pure, and thus one attains fearlessness."

Third, by taking prajñā as the means (upāya), they are well able to penetrate the teachings they have received and upheld, never forgetting them; furthermore, they can manifest non-negligence, enabling all sentient beings to attain liberation and purity without obstruction, thereby attaining fearlessness.

Fourth, they do not seek liberation through other vehicles, never forgetting the mind of omniscience (sarvajñā-citta); they are able to perfect various forms of mastery and benefit all sentient beings through skillful means, thereby attaining fearlessness.
These are called the four fearlessnesses of a bodhisattva.
What are the eighteen unique qualities of a bodhisattva?
First, when practicing generosity, bodhisattvas do not follow the instructions of others.
2. Maintaining ethical discipline without following the instructions of others;
3. Cultivating patience without following the instructions of others;
4. Exerting diligence without following the instructions of others;
Fifth, meditative concentration that does not rely on the instruction of others;
sixth, wisdom that does not rely on the instruction of others;
seventh, practicing the means of integration (*saṃgrahavastu*) so as to be able to gather all sentient beings.
8. The ability to understand and dedicate [merit];
9. Skillful means and mastery as a leader, enabling all sentient beings to engage in practice and further manifesting the attainment of liberation through the Supreme Vehicle;
10. Non-retrogression from the Mahāyāna.

Eleventh, they are skillfully able to manifest within saṃsāra and nirvāṇa while attaining peace and happiness; their speech is skillful, able to follow worldly conventions where the phrasing is identical yet the meaning differs.
Twelfth, with wisdom as their precursor, although they manifest various forms of rebirth before them, they act without effort and remain free from all faults.
Thirteenth, they are fully endowed with the ten wholesome actions of body, speech, and mind.
14. To gather in all sentient beings, never abandoning them, and being constantly able to endure all aggregates of suffering;
15. Being able to manifest all that is cherished and delighted in by all worlds;
16. Although dwelling among many afflicted fools and śrāvakas, not forgetting the mind of omniscience, which is as firm as a jewel and pure and magnificent.
Seventeenth, when assuming the royal throne of all dharmas, his crown is consecrated with silk and water;
eighteenth, he is able to never abandon the true Dharma of the Buddhas, manifesting a yearning for it.
These are called the eighteen unique qualities of a bodhisattva.
*The Sūtra Spoken by the Buddha on the Precious Rain*, Fascicle Four.

Translated by the Tang Dynasty Indian Tripiṭaka Master Dharmaruci:
"Good son! What are called the ten powers of the Tathāgata? First, the power of knowledge regarding what is possible and what is impossible;..."
2. The power of knowing the ripening of karmic causes throughout the past, future, and present;
3. The power of knowing various inclinations;
4. The power of knowing various elements.
Fifth, the power of knowing the superior and inferior faculties;
sixth, the power of knowing the paths leading to all destinations;
seventh, the power of knowing the defilement and purification of all meditative concentrations, liberations, samādhis, and samāpattis, as well as their transcendence.
8. The power of knowledge regarding the recollection of past abodes;
9. The power of knowledge regarding death and rebirth;
10. The power of knowledge regarding the exhaustion of the outflows.
These are called the ten powers of knowledge of the Tathāgata.
What are the four fearlessnesses of the Tathāgata?
First, the fearlessness of having attained perfect awakening to all phenomena.
2. Fearlessness regarding the knowledge that all outflows are exhausted;
3. Fearlessness regarding the definitive bestowal of prophecy based on the fact that obstructive dharmas are not in vain;
4. Fearlessness regarding the attainment of renunciation through the perfection of practice.
These are called the Tathāgata’s four fearlessnesses.
What are the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha?
First, the Tathāgata is free from error.
2. No harsh or abrupt sounds;
3. No loss of mindfulness; 4. No unconcentrated mind;
Fifth, the absence of diverse perceptions;
sixth, the absence of equanimity lacking discernment;
seventh, the non-diminution of aspiration;
8. No decrease in vigor; 9. No decrease in mindfulness;
10. No decrease in concentration;
Eleventh, his wisdom does not diminish;
twelfth, his liberation does not diminish;
thirteenth, regarding the past, his knowledge and vision are unattached and unimpeded.
14. Unattached and unimpeded knowledge and vision regarding the future;
15. Unattached and unimpeded knowledge and vision regarding the present;
16. All bodily actions are preceded by wisdom and proceed in accordance with wisdom.
Seventeenth, all verbal actions are preceded by wisdom and proceed in accordance with wisdom;
eighteenth, all mental actions are preceded by wisdom and proceed in accordance with wisdom.
These are called the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha.
"Good son, what is the great compassion of the Tathāgata?"

"Good son! The Tathāgata’s accomplishment of great compassion consists of thirty-two kinds, by which he gives rise to various inconceivable forms of great compassion toward all sentient beings throughout the infinite and boundless worlds of the ten directions."
What are the thirty-two kinds of great compassion?
First, all dharmas are devoid of self, yet sentient beings do not believe that all dharmas are selfless; therefore, the Tathāgata gives rise to great compassion for those sentient beings.
Second, all dharmas have no real sentient beings, yet living beings themselves claim there are real sentient beings; therefore, the Tathāgata gives rise to great compassion for all sentient beings.

Third, all dharmas have no real life-principle (*jīva*), yet sentient beings claim that there is a real life-principle; therefore, the Tathāgata gives rise to great compassion for the sake of these sentient beings.
Fourth, all dharmas have no person (*pudgala*), yet sentient beings cling to the existence of a person; therefore, the Tathāgata gives rise to great compassion for the sake of these sentient beings.

Fifth, all dharmas have no substantial intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), yet sentient beings hold that dharmas truly possess an intrinsic nature; therefore, the Tathāgata gives rise to great compassion for the sake of these sentient beings.
Sixth, all dharmas have no real locus, yet sentient beings cling to them as having a real locus; therefore, the Tathāgata gives rise to great compassion for these sentient beings.

Seventh, all dharmas have no real storehouse of grasping, yet sentient beings falsely cling to them as having a real storehouse of grasping; therefore, the Tathāgata gives rise to great compassion for these sentient beings.

Eighth, all dharmas are without self or what belongs to a self, yet sentient beings cling to them as having a real self and what belongs to a self; therefore, the Tathāgata gives rise to great compassion for those sentient beings.

Ninth, all dharmas have no real sovereign, yet sentient beings falsely cling to the existence of a real sovereign; therefore, the Tathāgata gives rise to great compassion for the sake of all sentient beings.
Tenth, all dharmas have no real entities, yet sentient beings falsely cling to the existence of real entities; therefore, the Tathāgata gives rise to great compassion for those sentient beings.
Eleventh, all dharmas are unborn, yet sentient beings falsely cling to the notion that dharmas are born; therefore, the Tathāgata gives rise to great compassion for the sake of all sentient beings.

12. All phenomena are without arising and without cessation, yet sentient beings falsely cling to them as having arising and cessation; therefore, the Tathāgata gives rise to great compassion for all sentient beings. 13.
All phenomena are without defilement, yet sentient beings falsely cling to them as truly being defiled; therefore, the Tathāgata gives rise to great compassion for all sentient beings.
14. Phenomena are without greed, yet sentient beings give rise to greed; therefore, the Tathāgata gives rise to great compassion for all sentient beings.
15. All phenomena are free from hatred, yet sentient beings give rise to hatred; therefore, the Tathāgata gives rise to great compassion for all sentient beings. 16.

All phenomena are free from delusion, yet sentient beings give rise to delusion; therefore, the Tathāgata gives rise to great compassion for all sentient beings. 17. All phenomena arise from causes and conditions;

their intrinsic nature is quiescent and their intrinsic nature is pure, yet sentient beings falsely cling to them as having a real, obtainable existence; therefore, the Tathāgata gives rise to great compassion for all sentient beings.
18. All dharmas have no coming, yet sentient beings falsely cling to the notion that they come; therefore, the Tathāgata gives rise to great compassion for those sentient beings. 19.
All dharmas have no going, yet sentient beings falsely cling to the notion that they go; therefore, the Tathāgata gives rise to great compassion for those sentient beings. 20.
All dharmas have no real agency, yet sentient beings falsely cling to the notion of real agency; therefore, the Tathāgata gives rise to great compassion for all sentient beings.

21. All phenomena are free from conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*), yet sentient beings delight in and cling to conceptual proliferation; therefore, the Tathāgata gives rise to great compassion for those sentient beings. 22.
The essence of all phenomena is empty, yet sentient beings cling to them as having existence; therefore, the Tathāgata gives rise to great compassion for all sentient beings. 23.

All phenomena are signless (*animitta*), yet sentient beings falsely cling to them and act as if they possessed signs; therefore, the Tathāgata gives rise to great compassion for those sentient beings.
24. All phenomena are wishless (*apraṇihita*), yet sentient beings falsely cling to phenomena as having wishes; therefore, the Tathāgata gives rise to great compassion for those sentient beings. 25.

Sentient beings in this realm dwell in the world, and due to their respective attachments, they engage in mutual disputes, giving rise to greed, hatred, and delusion. Observing such sentient beings, [the Tathāgata thinks]: "I shall now preach the Dharma for these sentient beings so that they may forever sever greed, hatred, and delusion."
For this reason, the Tathāgata gives rise to great compassion for all sentient beings;

twenty-sixth, seeing that sentient beings dwell in the world, possessed of inversions, fallen onto perilous and evil paths, and dropped into improper places, [he thinks]: "I should cause those sentient beings to enter the path of reality."
"Because of this, the Tathāgata gives rise to great compassion for all sentient beings;

twenty-seventh, these sentient beings of this realm are attached to the world, obscured by craving, plundering the wealth of others with insatiable minds. 'I shall cause those classes of sentient beings to obtain the wealth of the noble Dharma—namely, generosity, ethical discipline, learning, and so forth.'"
For this reason, the Tathāgata gives rise to great compassion for those sentient beings;

twenty-eighth, all sentient beings are driven and enslaved by craving and attachment, becoming infatuated with and stained by their dwellings, wives, children, wealth, and various grains such as rice and wheat; they labor to seek and protect them, acting as slaves to their own possessions. "I should expound the sublime Dharma for them, showing that dwellings and such are ultimately impermanent and unsubstantial phenomena, yet these sentient beings falsely conceive of them as substantial."
For this reason, the Tathāgata gives rise to great compassion for all sentient beings;

twenty-ninth, because the sentient beings of this world deceive one another, mutually encroach upon and seize from one another, and sustain themselves through evil livelihoods, I preach the Dharma so that all sentient beings may attain a pure livelihood.
For this reason, the Tathāgata gives rise to great compassion for all sentient beings.

(30) Sentient beings in this realm associate with evil friends and receive benefits such as offerings and praise, whereby they consider these to be their true spiritual teachers (*kalyāṇamitra*). [The Tathāgata thinks: "I should act as a true spiritual teacher for all those sentient beings; I should act as their ultimate good friend, so that the manifold sufferings of those sentient beings may be extinguished and they may attain the ultimate peace and bliss of *nirvāṇa*."
For this reason, the Tathāgata gives rise to great compassion for all sentient beings;

(31) furthermore, sentient beings within the three realms dwell in households, constantly beset by weariness and toil, and at all times delight in and are attached to this vessel of manifold sufferings. [The Tathāgata thinks: "I should preach such a Dharma for them, so that these sentient beings may attain liberation from within the three realms."
For this reason, the Tathāgata gives rise to great compassion for those sentient beings;
thirty-second, the Noble One who has attained liberation has declared:
"All phenomena arise from causes, are nurtured by various conditions, and their resultant characteristics flourish."
"If sentient beings give rise to indolence, they will abandon the supreme, distinguished, and untainted right knowledge as well as the most excellent nirvana.

Although these sentient beings may seek the inferior vehicles of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, "I should preach such a Dharma for them so that all sentient beings delight in vast wisdom and aspire to the Buddha-knowledge."
"For this reason, the Tathāgata gives rise to great compassion for all sentient beings.
Son of good family!

This is the great compassion achieved by the Tathāgata, which arises toward sentient beings in thirty-two ways. You should know that these are the true fields of merit for Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas; their majestic radiance is blazing, they possess non-retrogression, and they are further able to benefit all sentient beings."

“Good son! All the merits of all Tathāgatas and Bodhisattvas who have attained mastery are immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*), with these marks of a hundred merits as their foremost.”
If all Tathāgatas were to expound such marks of immeasurable and boundless merit for incalculable eons, they could never reach their end.

I now speak of them in brief for the sake of inspiring joy and happiness in sentient beings; this is called the bodhisattva’s skill in sustaining life through the inhalation and exhalation of breath, which comprises all dharmas that are the pure outflow of the gathering-in of sentient beings.
“Good son! How is it that a bodhisattva is able to sustain the immeasurable great clouds and rains of the Dharma? Good son!”

For example, the wind-circle is vast and boundless, pervading the world; it is firm and immovable, and during the periods of formation and destruction, it is able to sustain the clouds and rain, the oceans and the continents, Mount Mucilinda, Mount Mahāmucilinda, the Cakravāḍa mountains, the Mahācakravāḍa mountains, all the fragrant mountains, as well as the rivers, forests, and palaces, taking that wind-circle as their support.

The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva is also like this: using immeasurable and boundless *dhāraṇīs* as the wind-circle, they give rise to the clouds of all-enlightened ones (*samyak-saṃbuddha*), just as at the time of the formation eon (*vivartakalpa*) the world is established—namely, Mount Sumeru, the Cakravāḍa mountains, the Mahācakravāḍa mountains, the Fragrant Mountain, the Snowy Mountains, the oceans and great continents, the rivers, forests, and palaces.

Furthermore, it pours down the great rain-clouds of the Dharma, which are able to sustain the infinite aggregates of phenomena—both mundane and supramundane—including the marks of a hundred merits, the stages (*bhūmi*), the perfections (*pāramitā*), all samādhis, the various dhāraṇīs, the superknowledges (*abhijñā*), the masteries (*vaśitā*), the powers (*bala*), the fearlessnesses (*vaiśāradya*), as well as the analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*), the unique qualities (*āveṇika*), and great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*), thereby bringing to fulfillment all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.
This is called the bodhisattva’s ability to sustain the immeasurable rain from the clouds of the Great Dharma. "Good son,
how does a bodhisattva succeed in establishing the most excellent palace with its various adornments?"

Good son! It is like the power of the wind, which universally establishes and sustains all palaces with their various adornments; it causes the sprouts of all grasses and trees to grow, making their roots, stems, branches, leaves, flowers, and fruits flourish; and furthermore, it enables the differentiation of the limbs of all sentient beings.

In this way, the Bodhisattva, by means of boundless wisdom, unattached wisdom, the wisdom of unhindered analytical knowledge, and the wisdom of eloquence, arrays all manner of mundane and supramundane perfections like the wind; furthermore, they are able to fully comprehend and manifest the various distinctions of their bestowal.
Now, this shall be explained briefly:
these various phenomena are capable of producing rebirth in the evil realms as well as rebirth in the good realms, with the latter being predominant;
that is to say, these phenomena produce rebirth in the hells (*naraka*) and among the animals (*tiryagyoni*).
That is to say, these dharmas cause one to be born in the realm of Yama, or among humans and devas, or among the gods Śakra, Brahmā, and the World-Protectors;

that is to say, in whatever place these dharmas cause one to be born, one’s physical form is upright and majestic, pleasing for others to behold, and one possesses intelligence, wisdom, and a favorable retinue.

Furthermore, the bodhisattva skillfully understands these dharmas: the various arts and sciences (*vidyāsthāna*), the diverse crafts and skills, all categories of material forms, and all heterodox treatises.
Furthermore, it can manifest that because there is the lineage of the śrāvaka, the Śrāvakayāna arises;
because there is the lineage of the pratyekabuddha, the Pratyekabuddhayāna arises;
and because there is the lineage of the Mahāyāna, the Bodhisattvayāna arises.
Now, this shall be briefly explained:
by initiating various sublime qualities for one's own benefit and the benefit of others, one attains the stage of Samantabhadra and all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*).

Furthermore, one is able to discern: "This is the [various] stages; this is the perfections (*pāramitā*); these are the samādhis; these are the dhāraṇīs; these are the supernormal powers (*abhijñā*); these are the vidyās; these are the masteries (*vaśitā*); these are the liberations (*vimokṣa*); these are the powers (*bala*); these are the fearlessnesses (*vaiśāradya*); these are the analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*); and these are the unique qualities of the Buddhas (*āveṇika-buddhadharma*)."
"Good son! By means of the skillful mastery of dhāraṇīs numbering as many as lotuses and so forth, the bodhisattva establishes such infinite dharmas with various adornments. Good son!"
This is called the Bodhisattva’s ability to establish the most supreme Dharma and its various adornments within all palaces. "Good son,

how is it that a Bodhisattva can definitively expound various sublime Dharmas amidst the assemblies, just as the wind blows upon the kalpavṛkṣa trees, causing delightful flowers to rain down at all times like a shower?"

"Good son! Just as when the wind blows upon the kalpavṛkṣa trees, delightful flowers fall like rain, along with various precious ornaments, garments, food, and drink—all fully provided. Stirred by gentle breezes, these things appear in succession, pervading the realms of devas and humans."
Once sentient beings have attained this, they are no longer subject to grief or affliction, and their hearts give rise to joy;
they obtain superior delight, with body and mind at peace and blissful;
they sport and play in merriment, experiencing the joy of the Dharma garden.
At all times, their physical appearance is majestic and dignified, and their power is swift;
they experience supreme bliss without any decline.
The Bodhisattva is also like this!

Just as that wind, in pure worlds, requests the Tathāgatas and Bodhisattvas to definitively expound the corresponding sublime Dharma within the great assemblies, raining down flowers of the Dharma-treasure like falling rain—namely, the sūtras, geyas, vyākaraṇas, gāthās, udānas, nidānas, avadānas, itivṛttakas, jātaka-s, vaipulyas, adbhuta-dharmas, and upadeśas—expounding them in various ways, whether ascending or descending, in direct or reverse order.

Furthermore, they are able to manifest all conventional worldly discourse; regarding their objects of focus, they expound and explain the selflessness of phenomena, their quiescence and purity, free from all defiled characteristics.
Furthermore, they can manifest the dharma-gate of the equality of all phenomena, causing sentient beings to enter it;
they can also manifest all inconceivable phenomena that are like illusions, causing them to be directed toward illusory-like wisdom.
Furthermore, they cause sentient beings to increase in all manner of ways regarding all phenomena, playing with spiritual powers (*abhijñā*) with joy and delight;
through mere question and answer, they enable them to attain contentment;
and, being free from the extremes of the middle and the peripheries, they give rise to vast and skillful spiritual powers.
Because they are always able to delight in the garden of the Dharma, their bodies never experience weariness;
their verbal and mental actions never transgress [the precepts];
and the majestic power and virtue of all humans and devas become vast and great.
Fully enjoying all phenomena, they never decline;
constantly giving rise to the brilliant illumination of prajñā for observation, they advance toward the superior and sublime Dharma.
This is called the bodhisattva’s ability to definitively expound various sublime dharmas within the assembly, like a kalpavṛkṣa tree that constantly rains down pleasing flowers, falling like rain.

“Good son! How does a bodhisattva, having accumulated immeasurable wheels of the pure Dharma, samādhis, liberations, and dhāraṇīs over incalculable eons, give rise to the wind-wheel of wisdom within that assembly surrounded by the great oceans, Mount Meru, and the Cakravāḍa mountains, so as to turn and extinguish all bases of existence without remainder for those sentient beings among them who are capable of being tamed and matured?”

Good son! It is like when the world is destroyed at the end of a kalpa: by the power of unimpeded winds, the hundreds of thousands of nayutas of Sumeru mountains, Cakravāḍa mountains, and so forth within the trichiliocosm are swiftly blown apart; and all the great oceans are shattered and dispersed until they are entirely non-existent, like empty space.
The Bodhisattva is likewise!

Adorned by the accumulation of various provisions of merit and wisdom gathered over many eons, he is able to stir up the wind-circle of wisdom within all assemblies, manifesting miraculous transformations through his swift supernatural power;
he utters great sounds to proclaim the aggregates of all dharmas and the unimpeded wheel of Dharma.
May the mountain peaks of the conceit (*asmimāna*) arising in all sentient beings be completely extinguished.
Furthermore, may they be able to realize the radiant light of the sublime Dharma, and may *vipaśyanā* be constantly present before them;
may they contemplate all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) according to reality, with their inner minds correctly abiding in *samāhita*, and may they fully attain all *samādhis*.
One destroys and disperses the aggregates, elements, and sense bases, as well as all conditioned formations and this non-substantial body;
by thoroughly understanding all false conceptualizations, one is able to transcend all worlds;
being devoid of formal characteristics and inconceivable, one increases and perfects supramundane merit.
Furthermore, they are able to manifest all forms and appearances, thoroughly understanding how to attain a purified basis that abides for all time until the end of the future.

This is called a Bodhisattva’s accumulation over incalculable eons (*asaṃkhyeya-kalpa*) of immeasurable wheels of the pure Dharma, as well as samādhis, liberations, and dhāraṇīs. Within those great assemblies surrounded by the great oceans, Mount Meru, and the Cakravāḍa mountains, among those sentient beings who are capable of being tamed and matured, they raise the wind-wheel of wisdom to completely eliminate the basis of existence without remainder.
“Good son! When bodhisattvas accomplish these ten kinds of dharmas, they are equal to the wind.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Vighuṣṭaśabda addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
To expound these ten dharma-gates, complete in all their various aspects, is truly most rare!
All sentient beings are fully satisfied and delighted.”

"Bhagavān! If there are devas or humans who are able to give rise to pure faith in this Dharma, and who practice with resolute understanding as taught by the Buddha, they shall realize the fulfillment of both this life and future lives; they will attain all the peace and happiness of Śakra and Brahmā, and be consistently devoted to the benefit of others."
The Buddha said to the Bodhisattva Nivaraṇaviṣkambhin: “Excellent man! So it is, so it is!”
Contemplate that those sentient beings shall transcend all worlds.
If there are those who can practice within these dharmas, they will forever sever all unwholesome dharmas, accomplish all pure wholesome dharmas, and become a refuge for all the world.

Those who slander it are called fools; they fall into evil realms and undergo various sufferings and afflictions, and furthermore, they are held in contempt by all the world, including gods, humans, and asuras.
"Furthermore, son of good family,
because a bodhisattva accomplishes ten qualities, he is equal to space. What are these ten?
First, attaining freedom from defilement;
second, attaining non-attachment;
third, being able to realize tranquility.
Fourth, realizing boundless prajñā;
fifth, attaining boundless wisdom;
sixth, being able to practice in accordance with the equal dharma-realm;
Seventh, they attain pure resolve, believing that all phenomena are like empty space;
eighth, they attain non-abiding;
ninth, they transcend all spheres of activity.
Tenth, they transcend conceptual calculation.
Son of good family,
because bodhisattvas accomplish these ten kinds of dharmas, they are equal to space.
"Furthermore, son of good family,
when a bodhisattva accomplishes ten kinds of dharmas, they are equal to space. What are these ten?
First, one is neither greedy nor hateful toward forms that are pleasant or unpleasant;
second, one is neither greedy nor hateful toward sounds that are pleasant or unpleasant;
third, one is neither greedy nor hateful toward odors that are pleasant or unpleasant.
Fourth, they are neither greedy nor hateful toward pleasant or unpleasant tastes;
fifth, they are neither greedy nor hateful toward pleasant or unpleasant tangibles;
sixth, they are neither greedy nor hateful toward pleasant or unpleasant mental phenomena.
Seventh, one is neither greedy nor angry amidst gain and loss;
eighth, one is neither greedy nor angry amidst defamation and praise;
ninth, one is neither greedy nor angry amidst honor and ridicule.
Tenth, they are neither attached to nor resentful toward suffering or pleasure.
Son of good family,
when a bodhisattva accomplishes these ten dharmas, they are equal to space.
"Furthermore, noble son,
when a bodhisattva accomplishes ten qualities, they are equal to the moon. What are these ten?
First, it enables all sentient beings to attain physical pleasure;
second, it enables them to attain the joy of seeing [the Buddha];
third, it increases all pure and wholesome dharmas.
Fourth, it can sever the dharmas of darkness;
fifth, it can cause one to be praised;
sixth, it attains purity of body.
Seventh, they attain the supreme vehicle;
eighth, they constantly obtain adornment;
ninth, they attain delight in the Dharma.
Tenth, they attain great majestic power and great majesty.
"Good son! How does a bodhisattva cause the bodies of all sentient beings to obtain joy and happiness?"
"Good son! Just as the moon appears and can bring about coolness, its nature being lovely and delightful, causing the bodies of all sentient beings to attain joy;
so too it is with the Bodhisattva!"

Appearing in the world, they are able to remove all the burning afflictions of sentient beings; their nature is lovely and delightful, causing the bodies of all sentient beings to attain joy and pleasure.
"How does a bodhisattva attain a joyful and pleasant appearance?"
"Good son! Just as the moon appears with a radiance and color that are fresh and pure, causing all sentient beings to rejoice and delight in beholding it, so too is the appearance of a Bodhisattva:
with the sense faculties stilled and majestic deportment and merit fully purified, he causes all sentient beings to rejoice and delight in beholding him."
"How does a bodhisattva succeed in increasing all pure and wholesome dharmas? Good son,
it is like the waxing moon, which increases day by day until it becomes full, endowed with every variety of radiance and color."
The Bodhisattva is likewise!

From the first generation of the mind until sitting at the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa), all pure and white dharmas gradually increase, until they reach the perfection of the knowledge of all modes (sarvākārajñatā).
“How does a bodhisattva sever all dark dharmas? Good son,
it is like the light and color of the dark fortnight, which diminish day by day until on the fifteenth day, none of the characteristics of light or color can be found.”
In this way, the bodhisattva realizes supramundane wisdom; all unwholesome dharmas are gradually eliminated until, when sitting at the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa), not a single one remains.
"How does a bodhisattva cause others to offer praise?
Good son, it is like the appearance of the moon, which causes all the kṣatriyas, brāhmaṇas, and others— whether men or women— in the cities, towns, and villages of the human world to offer praise."
In this way, the Bodhisattva is like the appearance of the moon, praised by all the world—gods, humans, asuras, gandharvas, and so forth.
“How does a bodhisattva attain purity of body?
Son of good family!
Just as the son of the gods, Candra, attains a pure body through the fulfillment of the fruits of his karma, its radiance and color being brilliant and clear.”

In this way, the Bodhisattva appears in the world, realizes the nature of phenomena (dharmatā), and is born through transformation from the Dharma; because he is not produced from the impurities of the parents' kalala and so forth, his body attains purity, and its radiance is brilliant and clear.
"How does a bodhisattva attain the Supreme Vehicle?
Good son! It is like the Moon Deva-son, who, riding upon the Supreme Vehicle, radiates light across the four continents."
In this way, the bodhisattva rides upon the supreme vehicle, and the radiance of their wisdom shines throughout all infinite and boundless worlds.
"How does a bodhisattva always achieve adornment?"
"Good son! Just as the celestial son Candra is adorned with majestic power, and his ornaments never wither or fade,
so too does the bodhisattva constantly adorn himself with the dharmas of merit."
"How does a bodhisattva attain delight in the Dharma?
Good son, it is like the Moon Deva-son, who at all times delights in sensual pleasures."
The Bodhisattva is like the moon; at all times, he delights in the joy of the garden of the Dharma and does not delight in sensual pleasures.
How does a Bodhisattva attain great majestic power and great majesty?
"Good son! Just as the Moon Deva possesses great supernormal powers and great majestic virtue,
so too does the bodhisattva!"
They possess great supernormal powers and great majestic virtue, namely, the nature of great merit and the nature of great wisdom. "Good son,
because bodhisattvas accomplish these ten kinds of dharmas, they are equal to the moon."
"Furthermore, noble son,
when a bodhisattva accomplishes ten qualities, they are equal to the sun. What are these ten?
First, it can destroy all the darkness of ignorance;
second, it can subdue sentient beings and cause them to attain awakening;
third, it can radiate light throughout the ten directions.
Fourth, it is able to bring forth wholesome dharmas;
fifth, it is the complete extinction of all outflows;
sixth, it is able to produce radiance.
Seventh, it is able to eclipse all the heterodox arguments of external paths;
eighth, it is able to manifest high and low [distinctions];
ninth, it initiates the karma that is performed, namely, all pure and wholesome dharmas.
Tenth, he gains the affection and joy of virtuous people.
"How does a bodhisattva manage to shatter all the darkness of ignorance? Good son!..."
Just as the rising sun dispels all darkness, so too is the rising of the Bodhisattva-sun: it is able to shatter the darkness of all ignorance.
"How does the Bodhisattva discipline sentient beings and cause them to attain awakening?"
"Good son! Just as the appearance of the sun causes all lotuses to bloom,
so too does the rising of the Bodhisattva-sun subdue sentient beings and cause them to attain awakening."
"How does a bodhisattva illuminate the ten directions? Just as the sun appears and illuminates the ten directions, so too does the sun that is the bodhisattva appear;
through the majestic power and radiance of *prajñā*, he shines brilliantly throughout the worlds of the ten directions without disturbing sentient beings."
"How does a bodhisattva manifest wholesome dharmas?
Son of good family!
Just as when the Sun Deity appears, light becomes available throughout Jambudvīpa."
When a Bodhisattva appears in the world, they manifest all wholesome dharmas through the light of wisdom.
How is it that a Bodhisattva’s outflows are exhausted?
It is like when the sun sets; in Jambudvīpa, it is said that the sunlight has vanished.
When a bodhisattva’s afflictions are extinguished, it is called the permanent severance of all outflows (*āsrava*).
"How is it that a bodhisattva can produce light? Good son!..."
Just as the sun appears and creates various kinds of light for all sentient beings in Jambudvīpa,
so too does the Bodhisattva appear and radiate the light of wisdom for all sentient beings, capable of destroying all darkness and obscurations of ignorance.
"How does a bodhisattva outshine all the heterodox arguments of external paths?
Just as when the sun appears, it completely outshines them all, yet that sun does not think:
'I am able to outshine all ignorance!'"
"However, such is the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*).
When the Bodhisattva-sun rises, it can manifest its majestic radiance, eclipsing the various heterodox and erroneous doctrines of the outsiders; yet the Bodhisattva does not engage in such thought:
'I am able to eclipse these various heterodox and erroneous doctrines!'"
"However, such is the nature of phenomena (dharmatā).
How then can a bodhisattva manifest high and low?
O son of good family!..."
Just as the sun appears over Jambudvīpa, revealing all beings, whether high or low;
so too does the sun of the bodhisattva appear, perceiving all beings—whether equal or unequal—through the light of wisdom.
That is to say, entering the various noble paths is called "equality," while abiding in what is not the path is called "inequality.
How does a bodhisattva initiate the karma that is to be performed?
"Noble son! Just as the appearance of the sun causes all farmers to undertake their labors,
so too does the appearance of the Bodhisattva-sun initiate the activity of all wholesome dharmas."
"How does a bodhisattva become beloved by virtuous people?
Son of good family, it is like the rising sun: it is loved and cherished by all virtuous people, yet it is collectively hated and envied by those of an evil nature."

The Bodhisattva Sun appears, beloved by those who are wise and virtuous, yet universally detested and envied by those of foolish nature, the ignorant and evil, those who follow false paths, those who turn their backs on Nirvana, and those who delight in the cycle of birth and death.
“Good son! When a bodhisattva accomplishes these ten kinds of dharmas, he is equal to the sun.
Furthermore, good son!”
When Bodhisattvas accomplish ten dharmas, they are like lions. What are these ten?
First, they attain freedom from alarm and fear.
Second, they attain freedom from timidity and fear;
third, they attain the non-retrogressive path;
fourth, they roar like a lion.
Fifth, attaining fearlessness;
sixth, wandering through groves and gardens;
seventh, dwelling in mountain caves.
Eighth, they attain the state of non-appropriation;
ninth, their power is so courageous and fierce that they can defeat the armies of others;
tenth, they protect the sprouts and crops of all wholesome dharmas.
"How does a bodhisattva attain freedom from fear?
Good son, it is like a lion:
wherever it roams, there is never any cause for alarm or terror, for it sees that there is no one equal to itself."
In this way, wherever the bodhisattva goes, there is no fear or terror, as he perceives himself to have no equal.
"How does a bodhisattva attain freedom from timidity and fear?"

Good son! Just as a lion feels no fear whatsoever upon hearing the sounds of jackals or other malevolent beasts, so too the bodhisattva remains entirely without fear during all occasions of dispute with others; he neither sinks into despondency nor displays arrogance.
"How does a bodhisattva not retreat from the path? Good son!
It is like a lion that, when called to come forward, its mind never retreats or avoids the path."
In this way, a bodhisattva is able to summon other bodhisattvas to any place of dispute without their minds ever becoming discouraged.
How is it that a bodhisattva roars like a lion?
"Good son! For example, when a lion roars, the wild beasts and jackals flee in terror from every direction.

In the same way, when a Bodhisattva proclaims the Unsurpassed Vehicle with a lion’s roar, he causes all the wild beasts of external paths—those who cling to 'self' and 'what belongs to self'—to flee and disperse in every direction."

Although the bodhisattva makes this lion’s roar, he never disturbs or troubles any sentient beings; rather, he desires only to bring those classes of sentient beings who cling to "I" and "mine" to subjugation, so that they may forever abandon such attachments.
“How does a bodhisattva attain fearlessness? Good son!
It is like a lion that surveys all directions and attains fearlessness.”
In this way, the bodhisattva is able to universally observe the realm of all sentient beings with pure deportment and attains fearlessness.
"How does a bodhisattva roam through gardens and groves?"
For example, just as a lion is by nature fearless and can manifest its majestic power while roaming through various gardens and groves, so too is the Bodhisattva:
by nature serene, they are always able to sport within the forest of unimpeded dharmas.
"How does a bodhisattva rely upon mountain caves?
Good son! It is, for example, like a lion that relies upon a mountain cave."
In this way, the bodhisattva is always able to dwell securely in the cave of wisdom.
"How does a bodhisattva attain non-appropriation? Good son!
Just as a lion casts off its hoarded stores and attains a state of having nothing to grasp,
so too does the bodhisattva cast off the heavy burden of all afflictions, forever having nothing to grasp.
"How does a bodhisattva become like that lion—naturally courageous and valiant, possessing great power, solitary and peerless, capable of defeating the armies of others?"
“Good son! When a bodhisattva sits at the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa), alone and without a second, his power is able to crush and destroy all the hosts of Māra.
How does a bodhisattva protect the crops of all wholesome dharmas?
Good son! For example, wherever a lion roams in proximity to a village or town, no evil beasts can damage the crops near it.
In this way, wherever a bodhisattva dwells among humans or travels, no non-Buddhists or malevolent beasts can destroy the sprouts of their wholesome dharmas.
“Noble son! When a bodhisattva accomplishes these ten kinds of dharmas, they become like a lion.
Furthermore, noble son!”
If a bodhisattva accomplishes ten dharmas, they are able to skillfully tame and subdue [the mind]. What are these ten?
First, the resolve for enlightenment (bodhicitta) is firm and steadfast.
Second, their actions are able to purify the mind of enlightenment;
third, they closely guard the sense faculties;
fourth, they are able to advance toward the right path.
Fifth, they are able to bear heavy burdens;
sixth, they never grow weary or indolent;
seventh, they attain right livelihood and benefit sentient beings.
Eighth, abandoning all deceptive speech;
ninth, being forever free from flattery and deceit;
tenth, having a nature that is upright and straightforward.
"Noble son! When a bodhisattva accomplishes these ten kinds of dharmas, they are able to skillfully subdue [the mind].
Furthermore, noble son!"
When a bodhisattva accomplishes ten dharmas, they attain natural quiescence.
What are these ten? First, they become a yoga practitioner.
Second, extensively practicing emptiness;
third, developing the noble path and becoming free from all entanglements without obstruction;
fourth, following the Tathāgata’s teachings and practicing without contradiction.
Fifth, they accord with the principle of the equality of all phenomena, penetrate the true nature of reality, and dwell within the world with a mind always as humble as that of a candāla’s son;
sixth, at all times they are able to maintain the thought of being a beggar, remaining far removed from pride, arrogance, and heedlessness;
seventh, they have no doubt regarding the Buddha-dharma and are able to realize the manifest presence of the Buddha’s perfect wisdom.
Eighth, they have no hesitation regarding any phenomena, because they know the nature of phenomena through their own internal realization;
ninth, they do not attain awakening through others, because they have personally seen the Path;
tenth, they serve as a field of merit for the world, because they are directed toward Bodhi.
"Noble son! When bodhisattvas accomplish these ten kinds of dharmas, they attain the tranquility of their own nature.
Furthermore, noble son!"
When a bodhisattva accomplishes ten dharmas, they become like a lotus flower. What are these ten?
First, being free from all defilement and attachment;
Second, they are not defiled by even minor stains of transgression;
third, they attain the sublime fragrance of precepts;
fourth, they are constantly pure.
Fifth, his face is always smiling;
sixth, he is free from coarseness and rudeness;
seventh, he can manifest auspiciousness.
Eighth, awakening through development; ninth, maturing awakening;
tenth, being taken into care by others.
“How does a bodhisattva remain unstained? Good son,
it is like a lotus flower that emerges from the water yet remains unstained by it.”
Why is this? It is because the nature of that lotus is pure.
In the same way, although a bodhisattva emerges from the waters of birth and death, once emerged, they are free from any defilement or attachment.

Why is this? Because Bodhisattvas are able to realize the intrinsic nature of the dharmas of skillful means (*upāya*) and wisdom (*prajñā*); for by virtue of their skillfulness, they dwell within the cycle of birth and death (*saṃsāra*) without being defiled or attached by its faults and afflictions, since skillful means and wisdom are able to encompass them.
"How does a bodhisattva remain unstained by even the slightest defilements of sin? Good son,
it is like a lotus flower, which is not defiled by even the smallest amount of water."
In this way, the bodhisattva is not defiled by even the slightest stain of sin.
"How does a bodhisattva obtain the fragrance of sublime precepts? Good son!
Just as wherever there is a place capable of producing lotus flowers, their fragrance pervades that particular location, so it is with the Bodhisattva;
as he travels through all regions of the human world, the fragrance of his precepts fills those places where he wanders.
"How does a bodhisattva always attain purity? Good son!
Just as any place where lotuses grow is regarded by all the villages of the world, including the brahmins and kṣatriyas, as a pure place."

In this way, wherever a bodhisattva is born, because that place is tranquil and pure, they are always protected and remembered by all Buddhas and praised by all bodhisattvas; furthermore, devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, humans, non-humans, and others all flock to them.
"What is meant by 'the bodhisattva’s face smiles'?
Good son, it is like a lotus flower that has blossomed all over; if any sentient beings see it, their hearts are all filled with joy."
In this way, the bodhisattva at all times maintains a serene countenance and smiles, free from frowning, with the sense faculties purified.
How does a bodhisattva attain freedom from coarseness and rudeness?
Good son! For example, the nature of the lotus flower is supple and not coarse or harsh.
So it is with the bodhisattva: their nature is always supple; their speech is neither coarse nor harsh, and they are free from hypocrisy and deceit.
"How does a bodhisattva manifest auspiciousness?
Son of good family!
It is like a person who, whether awake or dreaming, for even as long as one muhūrta, sees a lotus flower and regards it as an auspicious sign of a favorable omen, praising and extolling it."
In this way, at all times, for those who see the Bodhisattva, it is auspicious and virtuous; they shall praise and extol him, which brings great benefit, even unto the attainment of omniscience.
"How does a bodhisattva develop awakening?
Good son! It is like a lotus flower; when it is in full bloom, it is said to have 'developed.'"
In this way, when a bodhisattva attains the blossoming of the flowers of the factors of awakening (bodhipākṣika-dharma) through prajñā, it is called "awakening" (bodhi).
How does a bodhisattva bring awakening to maturity?
Good son! For example, when a lotus flower is fully matured, if anyone sees it, it causes the faculty of the eye to experience supreme delight;
if anyone smells it, it causes the faculty of the nose to experience supreme delight.
If there are those who touch it, it can cause the faculty of the body to experience supreme joy;
if there are those who rejoice, it can cause the faculty of the mind to experience supreme joy.

So it is with the Bodhisattva: if they achieve the radiance of prajñā, they can cause the faculty of the eye to become pure for all who see them, the faculty of the ear to become pure for all who hear them, the faculty of the body to become pure for all who touch them or make offerings to them, and the faculty of the mind to become pure for all who extol and praise their virtues or contemplate them.
“How is it that a bodhisattva is taken up by others? Good son!
It is like a lotus flower when it is in full bloom; it is able to be taken up by all humans and non-humans.”
In this way, wherever a bodhisattva is born, they are taken into the care of all buddhas, as well as by all bodhisattvas, Śakras, Brahmās, and the World-Protectors. "O noble son!
When Bodhisattvas accomplish these ten kinds of dharmas, they become like a lotus flower.
*The Sūtra Spoken by the Buddha on the Precious Rain*, Scroll Five;
*The Sūtra Spoken by the Buddha on the Precious Rain*, Scroll Six.
Translated by the Tang Dynasty Indian Tripitaka Master Dharmaruci:
"Furthermore, son of good family, when a bodhisattva accomplishes ten dharmas, they attain a vast mind.
What are these ten?"
First, "I shall accumulate all the equal pāramitās"—this is called generating the vast mind;
second, "I shall fulfill all the Buddha-dharmas"—this is called generating the vast mind;
third, "I shall subdue all sentient beings"—this is called generating the vast mind.
Fourth, "I shall sit at the seat of enlightenment and manifest perfect awakening in unsurpassed, complete, and perfect enlightenment"—this is called generating the vast mind;

fifth, "Having manifested perfect awakening, I shall turn the wheel of Dharma such that no śramaṇas, brahmins, devas, Māras, Brahmās, or worldly beings can turn it as I do"—this is called generating the vast mind;
sixth, "For the benefit of all sentient beings, I shall go to immeasurable and boundless worlds to perform acts of benefit for each and every sentient being"—this is called generating the vast mind.
Seventh, I shall accumulate prajñā to serve as a boat or raft, ferrying all sentient beings across the ocean of birth and death to the further shore; this is called generating the vast mind.

Eighth, seeing that sentient beings have no master, no refuge, no savior, no protector, and no dwelling place, I shall act as their kinsman and provide them with protection and so forth; this is called generating the vast mind.
Ninth, regarding the most supreme activities of all Buddhas, I shall manifest the ability to perform those most supreme activities of all Buddhas.
Where the Buddha roars the lion’s roar, I shall likewise roar the great lion’s roar;
where the Buddha sports, I shall likewise sport;
where the Great Dragon observes, I shall likewise observe.

"Whatever I have attained, may all devas, Māras, Brahmās, the world, śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, and all those in the world—gods, humans, and asuras—likewise attain it; this is called generating the vast mind. Tenth:

the Buddha, with his great majesty and virtue, tames sentient beings; I shall likewise tame them, not through coarse or evil conduct, nor through unbeneficial asceticism, nor through inferior practices; this is called generating the vast mind."
"Noble son! When a bodhisattva accomplishes these ten kinds of dharmas, they attain the vast mind.
Furthermore, noble son!"
When a bodhisattva accomplishes ten dharmas, they attain a pure mind. What are these ten?
First, they attain a perfectly fulfilled intention, because this intention is by nature immovable, constantly abiding, and free from hypocrisy.

Second, he is far removed from improper mental attention (*ayoniśo-manasikāra*), meaning that while thinking, "I shall make the lion's roar of a Buddha," he never gives rise to the mental attention of a śrāvaka, nor does he give rise to the mental attention of a pratyekabuddha, nor does he give rise to limited mental attention;
third, he is eternally free from all dust and defilement, meaning he is able to eliminate the dust of all afflictions (*kleśa*);
fourth, he is eternally free from physical hypocrisy, meaning he is able to remain far removed from all deceptive postures and unusual appearances.
Fifth, they are forever free from verbal hypocrisy and never display untruthful speech;
sixth, they are forever free from mental hypocrisy—meaning that because their bodies are without attachment, their speech is contented, and their minds have no longing;
seventh, they repay kindness, never forgetting even the slightest favor, let alone failing to remember and repay great ones.
Eighth, they recognize kindness; toward those who have been kind to them, they never conceal anything nor treat them with contempt;
seeing their virtues, they leap for joy and praise them aloud, setting aside those in the world who lack a sense of shame and remorse;
ninth, they act according to their words, meaning that these bodhisattvas manifest pleasant speech that accords with the hearts of others.
The mind is always tranquil and free from resentment;
one respects others and does not give rise to contempt;
one speaks with truth and is devoid of deceit.
They are not pursued by stinginess, envy, flattery, or deception;
the Bodhisattva never incites others to fight, nor does he engage in mutual destruction with others;
he speaks the meaning of reality and provides whatever is beneficial to all.

Tenth, they are forever free from slandering the teachings of the Tathāgata; that is to say, having resolved upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, these bodhisattvas shave their hair and beards, don the saffron robes, and with right faith go forth into homelessness within the teachings of the Tathāgata. They do not go forth under the compulsion of royal power, nor are they forced to go forth by thieves, nor do they go forth through the expedient of debt, nor do they seek to go forth out of fear. They do not go forth out of dread of failing to make a living or for the sake of a wrong livelihood; rather, they go forth out of faith, seeking the true Dharma.
A bodhisattva constantly seeks spiritual friends (kalyāṇamitra), attending to and serving them, listening to the true Dharma, and practicing it after having heard it.
Furthermore, a bodhisattva is not obscured by the conceit of self (māna), because they are free from such conceit;
nor do they grasp things erroneously, because their nature is to receive [the teachings] without inversion.
They realize the path of penetration because they have attained penetration;
they realize the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) because they have attained the nature of phenomena.
Having realized the nature of phenomena, they are certain to attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
This is called a bodhisattva’s freedom from all slander within the Buddha’s teaching. Noble son,
when a bodhisattva accomplishes these ten kinds of dharmas, they attain a pure mind.
"Furthermore, noble son,
when a bodhisattva accomplishes ten dharmas, he attains a mind free from hesitation. What are these ten?
First, profound faith in the Tathāgata’s secret of bodily action;
second, profound faith in the Tathāgata’s secret of verbal action;
third, profound faith in the Tathāgata’s secret of mental action.
Fourth, profound faith in the accumulation of the bodhisattva path;
fifth, profound faith in bodhi;
sixth, the ability to believe in the appearance of the Tathāgata.
Seventh, they are able to believe in the exposition of the true reality (*dharmatā*) of the One Vehicle;
eighth, they are able to believe in the proclamation of the various kinds of true reality;
ninth, they are able to believe in the profound and far-reaching speech and sounds of the Tathāgata.
