Tenth, they have deep faith that the Tathāgata knows the inclinations of sentient beings and tames them accordingly.
"How does a bodhisattva have deep faith in the secret of the Tathāgata’s bodily actions?

"Good son! When bodhisattvas hear of the nature of the Tathāgata’s dharma-body, the nature of his tranquil body, the nature of his unequaled body, the nature of his immeasurable body, the nature of his unshared body, and the nature of his vajra-body, they reflect:
'This is the reality; it is not false or deceptive.'"
This means that when this bodhisattva has no doubt or hesitation regarding those teachings, it is called the bodhisattva’s profound faith in the Tathāgata’s secret of bodily action.
What is the bodhisattva’s profound faith in the Tathāgata’s secret of vocal action?
That is to say, when bodhisattvas hear that the Tathāgata grants prophecies to sentient beings—whether in their presence, not in their presence, or as secret prophecies—they reflect thus:
"The speech and voice of the Tathāgata are ultimately never false or deceptive; they are free from error!"
For this reason, his speech attains truthfulness. Why is this?

Because the Tathāgata has forever severed all faults and afflictions, forever severed all defilements and impurities, forever severed all burning torments, and because he is eternally free from all mental disturbances, he has attained mastery; he is bright, pure, and clear, devoid of all turbidity.
If the words of the Tathāgata were ever false, deceptive, or subject to transgression, such a possibility could not exist; this alone is the truth and is not false or deceptive.
When a bodhisattva attains freedom from hesitation regarding this Dharma, it is called the bodhisattva’s profound faith in the secret of the Tathāgata’s verbal karma.
"How does a bodhisattva have deep faith in the Tathāgata’s secret mental activity?

If a bodhisattva hears of the Tathāgata’s mental secrets—that is, all the Tathāgata’s intentions and the basis for the meaning of the Dharma that reside in the mind and abide by way of the mind—and realizes that no bodhisattvas, śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, or any sentient beings can know them, except through the empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*) of the Tathāgata."

Why is this? The Tathāgata is profoundly deep and difficult to measure; he transcends all conceptualization and the sphere of conceptualization. Vast and immeasurable, like space, he surpasses the entire realm of those who engage in false conceptualization.
The bodhisattva reflects correctly in this way: "This is the truth; it is not false!
Thus, they attain freedom from hesitation regarding those teachings. This is called the bodhisattva’s profound faith in the Tathāgata’s secret of mental action.
"What is the profound faith in the accumulation of the bodhisattvas?

It refers to hearing that these bodhisattvas manifest for the benefit of all sentient beings, being able to accomplish whatever tasks those sentient beings require, never becoming weary, and never feeling alarm or fear."

Furthermore, they are able to bear the heavy burden of great vows; possessing great power, they are courageous and firm, capable of universally accumulating all the *pāramitās* and successively accumulating all the Buddha-dharmas. They attain unimpeded wisdom, the nature of boundless wisdom, the nature of incomparable wisdom, and the nature of unique wisdom. Their diligence is firm, their armor is firm, and their vows are firm—vows that are immovable and vows that are unique—serving as the causes and conditions for unsurpassed *bodhi*.
These bodhisattvas practice in successive stages, causing [the qualities] to arise, increase, and become perfected and vast.
The bodhisattva reflects thus:
"This is the truth; it is not false!"
When a bodhisattva attains freedom from hesitation regarding all those dharmas, this is called the bodhisattva’s ability to accumulate profound faith.
How does a bodhisattva deeply believe in the awakening and the appearance of the Tathāgata?
It refers to when bodhisattvas reflect in this way:
"I have heard that once bodhisattvas have sat at the seat of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa), they become unattached, unimpeded, and free from obstruction;

they attain the supernormal knowledge of the divine eye, the supernormal knowledge of the divine ear, the supernormal knowledge of others' minds, the supernormal knowledge of recollecting past lives, the supernormal knowledge of miraculous powers, and the supernormal knowledge of the exhaustion of outflows."
Having attained supreme wisdom, they comprehend each and every moment of the three periods of time—unattached, unimpeded, and unobstructed.
By virtue of these causes and conditions, they are able to universally observe the realms of all sentient beings.

These types of sentient beings accomplish misconduct of body, accomplish misconduct of speech, and accomplish misconduct of mind; they receive various false teachings, give rise to wrong views, and slander the noble ones. Due to these causes and conditions, when their bodies perish and their lives end, they fall into the evil destinies and are born among the denizens of hell.

Furthermore, he is able to observe that such sentient beings have accomplished virtuous conduct of body, accomplished virtuous conduct of speech, and accomplished virtuous conduct of mind; they receive the true Dharma, give rise to right view, and do not slander the noble ones. By these causes and conditions, after the end of their lives, they are born in the various happy realms and attain rebirth among the devas.
Having thus truly observed the realms of sentient beings and their wholesome and unwholesome karma, the bodhisattva reflects:
"In the past, when I was practicing the conduct of a bodhisattva, I made this vow:
'If I awaken myself, I shall cause others to awaken;'"
"My vows are fulfilled and my aspirations are satisfied!
This alone is the truth; it is not false.
When a bodhisattva can attain freedom from hesitation regarding those dharmas, by means of this, the bodhisattva is able to realize bodhi, which is called perfect enlightenment (samyak-saṃbodhi).
“Good son! This is called a bodhisattva’s profound faith in bodhi and the appearance of the Tathāgata.
How does a bodhisattva profoundly believe in the exposition of the true reality (*dharmatā*) of the One Vehicle?
That is to say, bodhisattvas reflect in this way:
"Having heard the Single Vehicle (ekayāna) of the Tathāgata, I know that only this is true, not false, and it is eternally unchanging."
Why is this? Because it is from the One Vehicle that all vehicles emerge. Good son!

For example, within Jambudvīpa there are various minor continents; although they each have different names, they all equally depend upon Jambudvīpa, and for this reason it is called "a single Jambudvīpa."

The teaching of the One Vehicle is likewise so: because all vehicles appear from the Tathāgata-vehicle, although these various vehicles have different names, they are called the "One Vehicle" because they all equally rely upon the Tathāgata-vehicle.
When a bodhisattva is able to attain freedom from doubt regarding that True Dharma, this is called the bodhisattva’s profound faith in proclaiming the true reality of the One Vehicle.
"How does a bodhisattva have profound faith in proclaiming the various aspects of true reality?"
It refers to when bodhisattvas reflect in this way:
"Having heard the Tathāgata proclaim such various aspects of reality within the sūtras, only this is true; it is not false or deceptive."
Why is this? Because the Tathāgatas are able to subdue beings, they expound the sublime Dharma according to the various inclinations of sentient beings.
When a bodhisattva is free from hesitation regarding this true Dharma, it is called a bodhisattva being able to have deep faith in and expound the various aspects of reality.
"How does a bodhisattva attain deep faith in the profound and far-reaching nature of the Tathāgata’s speech?
It is when a bodhisattva reflects thus:
'Having heard that the Tathāgata’s speech is profound and far-reaching, this alone is true; it is not false.'"

Why is this? Because even the sons of the gods, possessing but meager roots of merit and virtue, obtain such profound, far-reaching, and exquisite voices; how much more so for the Tathāgata, who has accumulated sublime practices throughout immeasurable hundreds of thousands of kalpas!
By this, the bodhisattva attains freedom from hesitation regarding those teachings; this is called the bodhisattva’s profound faith in the Tathāgata’s speech as being deep and far-reaching.
How does a bodhisattva attain profound faith that the Tathāgata knows the intentions and inclinations of sentient beings and thereby disciplines them?
It refers to when bodhisattvas reflect as follows:

"I have heard that the Tathāgata is able to know the mental dispositions, various latent tendencies, and various inclinations of all sentient beings; by preaching the Dharma with a single voice, he brings them all to subdual, causing each to understand according to their own intent, severing doubts and delusions, and bringing sentient beings to maturity."
Each and every sentient being thinks thus:
"The Tathāgata has preached the sublime Dharma solely for my sake.
Yet, in this regard, the Tathāgata is truly without discrimination—neither thinking "I am the speaker" nor "sentient beings are those to be converted."
"This alone is the truth; it is not false.

When a bodhisattva can attain freedom from hesitation regarding those teachings, this is called a bodhisattva’s profound faith that the Tathāgata knows the inclinations of sentient beings and disciplines them accordingly.
“Good son! When a bodhisattva accomplishes these ten kinds of dharmas, his mind is free from hesitation. Furthermore, good son!”
If a bodhisattva accomplishes ten dharmas, they attain wisdom like the ocean. What are these ten?
First, attaining that which is like a place of jewels;
Second, it is profoundly deep and difficult to fathom;
third, it is vast and immeasurable;
fourth, it accords with gradual deepening.
Fifth, not dwelling together with the corpses of afflictions;
sixth, being of a single flavor;
seventh, accommodating swift currents.
Eighth, its tides do not exceed their appointed time;
ninth, it serves as a refuge for great sentient beings;
tenth, it is inexhaustible.
"How does a bodhisattva obtain that which is like a treasure trove?
Good son, it is like the great ocean, which has many treasure troves; people from Jambudvīpa all come to take its treasures, yet they are never exhausted."
In this way, the Bodhisattva is a repository for jewels of merit; all sentient beings may take from these jewels of merit without them ever being exhausted.
How is it that the Bodhisattva is profound and difficult to fathom?
"Good son! Just as the great ocean is extremely deep and difficult to cross,
so it is with the bodhisattva, who has accomplished the wisdom of a profound great ocean that no sentient being can transcend."
"How is it that a bodhisattva is vast and immeasurable?
Good son, it is like the great ocean, which is universally vast and expansive."
In this way, the ocean of a bodhisattva’s wisdom is vast and boundless.
"How does a bodhisattva follow it as it gradually deepens?
Son of good family!
Just as the great ocean follows the downward slope, becoming gradually lower and deeper, so too does the Bodhisattva;
following the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), the ocean of all-knowledge becomes gradually lower and deeper.
"How does a bodhisattva not dwell together with the corpses of afflictions?
Good son, it is like the great ocean, which does not harbor corpses."
Why is this? Because it is the inherent nature of the ocean.
In the same way, the Bodhisattva does not dwell in the company of those who are like corpses of men—the afflictions.
Why is this? Because the Dharma of Bodhisattvas is thus.
"In what way are all Bodhisattvas of one single flavor?"
"Good son! It is like the great ocean: all the torrential waters that pour into it become of one and the same salty nature.
In the same way, when a bodhisattva accumulates immeasurable pure dharmas until they reach omniscience, they all come to share the single flavor of omniscience."
“How does a bodhisattva accommodate swift currents? Good son!
It is like the great ocean, which accommodates immeasurable swift currents of water without increasing or decreasing.”
In this way, the bodhisattva receives the torrential flow of the immeasurable rain of Dharma without increase or decrease.
"How does a bodhisattva not miss the timing of the tides? Good son!
Just as the tide of the great ocean does not miss its appointed time,
so too the bodhisattva teaches and transforms sentient beings according to their individual capacities, never missing the proper time.
How does a bodhisattva serve as a refuge for great sentient beings?
Just as the great ocean serves as the support for great sentient beings,
so too does the bodhisattva serve as the support for all the pure and white dharmas of all sentient beings.
"How does a bodhisattva attain inexhaustibility?
Son of good family!
It is like the great ocean, which provides water for all sentient beings to draw from, yet its waters never become exhausted."
In this way, the bodhisattva expounds various teachings for the sake of all sentient beings without end.
"Good son, when a bodhisattva accomplishes these ten kinds of dharmas, they attain wisdom like the ocean."
"Furthermore, son of good family,
when a bodhisattva accomplishes ten dharmas, they attain skillfulness in subtle wisdom. What are these ten?
First, attaining skillfulness in seeking renunciation;
second, attaining skillfulness in penetrating all phenomena;
third, attaining skillfulness in realizing the equality of all phenomena.
Fourth, attaining skill in realizing that all phenomena have the characteristic of an illusion;
fifth, attaining skill in the thorough knowledge of all phenomena;
sixth, attaining skill in the profound and difficult-to-penetrate nature of dependent origination.
Seventh, they attain the skillful means of the inconceivability of karma;
eighth, they attain the skillful means of thoroughly knowing the meanings according to what is taught;
ninth, they attain the skillful means of realizing and knowing the meaning as it truly is.
Tenth, attaining skillfulness in reality.
"Good son, how does a bodhisattva attain skillfulness in seeking renunciation, and so on, up to how does he attain skillfulness in reality?"

That is to say, this bodhisattva observes all these sentient beings dwelling in the world, constantly burning with desire, obscured and surrounded by hatred, and blinded by the darkness of ignorance; the bodhisattva then reflects:
"How can these sentient beings attain skillfulness in liberation?"
For the sake of those beings, the Bodhisattva aspires to attain thorough penetration of all phenomena.
By means of such penetration, they enter into the equality of all phenomena;
by means of such entry, they realize the illusory nature of all things.
Through thorough understanding, one knows all phenomena as they truly are;
through such universal knowledge, one contemplates profound dependent origination in accordance with reality;
and through such contemplation, one observes the inconceivable nature of karma in accordance with reality.
The Bodhisattva contemplates in this way:
"Within all phenomena there is nothing at all that is real, yet karma manifests in various and diverse ways.

By means of this, the Bodhisattva is able to awaken to and enter subtle wisdom, and immediately understands the meaning of the essential teachings on the Dharma heard from the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.
Because of this definitive meaning, one attains the vision of reality;
because of seeing reality, one delivers sentient beings from the ocean of birth and death. Good son!
This is called the bodhisattva’s skill in seeking the departure from suffering, up to and including skill in the ultimate reality.
Son of good family,
when a bodhisattva accomplishes these ten dharmas, they attain subtle and wondrous wisdom.
"Furthermore, noble son,
when a bodhisattva accomplishes ten kinds of dharmas, they attain appropriate eloquence (*pratibhāna*). What are these ten?
First, the designation of non-self among all phenomena;
second, the absence of a sentient being;
third, the absence of a life-principle.
Fourth, there is no nourisher; fifth, there is no *pudgala*;
sixth, it is far removed from an agent and a recipient.
Seventh, it is far removed from a knower or a seer;
eighth, it is empty, non-existent, and without a master;
ninth, it is empty of false conceptualization.
Tenth, all phenomena are designated as dependently originated.
Son of good family!

Because all phenomena are without self, without sentient beings, without life-force, without nourisher, and without person (pudgala); because they are devoid of an agent and a recipient, and devoid of a knower and a seer; because they are empty, non-existent, and without a master; and because they arise from false conceptualization based on conditions—in this way, one should accord with the nature of phenomena (dharmatā).

“Good son! All those dharmas that accord with the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), do not contradict the nature of phenomena, correspond to the nature of phenomena, penetrate the nature of phenomena, and clarify the nature of phenomena—all such natures of phenomena a bodhisattva mahāsattva should fully know; this is called ‘that which should be analyzed.’”
"Noble son! When a bodhisattva accomplishes these ten dharmas, they attain appropriate eloquence.
Furthermore, noble son!"
When bodhisattvas accomplish ten dharmas, they attain the eloquence of liberation. What are these ten?
First, they attain unattached eloquence.
Second, attaining inexhaustible eloquence;
third, attaining the eloquence of awakening;
fourth, attaining the eloquence of fearlessness.
Fifth, one attains the eloquence of humility;
sixth, one attains the eloquence of fearlessness;
seventh, one attains the unshared eloquence.
Eighth, they attain unobscured eloquence;
ninth, they attain boundless eloquence;
tenth, they attain unimpeded eloquence.
"Noble son! When bodhisattva-mahāsattvas accomplish these ten kinds of dharmas, they attain the eloquence of liberation.
Furthermore, noble son!"
When a bodhisattva accomplishes ten dharmas, they attain pure eloquence. What are these ten?
First, they attain an eloquence that is free from hoarseness and stammering.
Second, attaining unconfused eloquence;
third, attaining non-inferior eloquence;
fourth, attaining non-arrogant eloquence.
Fifth, attaining the eloquence of not losing the meaning;
sixth, attaining the eloquence of non-inferiority regarding syllables;
seventh, attaining the eloquence of non-inferiority regarding skillful means.
Eighth, they attain eloquence that is not inferior;
ninth, they attain eloquence that is not coarse or harsh;
tenth, they attain eloquence that is clear and lucid.
“Good son! Because Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are free from fear amidst the great assemblies, they attain eloquence that is neither faltering nor hoarse.
Because they dwell securely in wisdom, they attain eloquence that is unconfused.”
Because the Bodhisattva is free from fear within the assembly, like a lion king, he is neither startled nor terrified, and thus attains eloquence that is not inferior.
Because he is free from afflictions, he attains eloquence that is not arrogant.
"Good son! One who possesses afflictions (kleśa) is one who possesses arrogance; it is not that one without afflictions possesses arrogance.
Because they have realized the nature of phenomena (dharmatā), they attain the eloquence of never losing the meaning."
"Good son! Those who have not yet realized the Dharma may err regarding its meaning, but those who have already attained it do not suffer such decline.
Because they possess fearlessness regarding all discourse, they attain the eloquence of letters that is never inferior."
"Good son! One who knows only a small portion of treatises may indeed suffer decline regarding the words and letters, but one who knows all treatises is not termed inferior."
Because they have accumulated all skillful means, they attain an eloquence that is not inferior in skillful means.
Those who lack skillfulness will experience decline regarding skillful means, whereas those who possess skillfulness are without inferiority.

"Good son! A bodhisattva-mahāsattva knows the long duration, knows the appropriate time, and knows the times of the beginning, middle, and end. Because he does not speak later what should be said first, nor speak first what should be said later, but speaks according to the proper occasion, he attains timely and non-inferior eloquence."
Because they are forever free from the conceptual proliferation of language, they attain eloquence that is not coarse or harsh. Good son!
That which possesses conceptual proliferation is called coarse and harsh; that which is without conceptual proliferation is not coarse or harsh.
Good son! Because the faculties of a bodhisattva-mahāsattva are sharp and keen, they attain lucid eloquence;
those whose faculties are dull do not possess such lucidity.
Those whose faculties are not sharp do not understand clearly. Good son!
When a bodhisattva accomplishes these ten kinds of dharmas, they attain pure eloquence.
"Furthermore, noble son,
when a bodhisattva accomplishes ten qualities, they bring joy and satisfaction to all sentient beings.
What are these ten?
First, attaining speech that is pleasing;
second, having a smiling countenance and being free from frowning;
third, being able to expound upon the meaning [of the Dharma].
Fourth, they are able to expound the Dharma;
fifth, they are able to teach with impartiality;
sixth, they are free from arrogance.
Seventh, being free from contempt;
eighth, being untainted;
ninth, being without anger.
Tenth, they attain various forms of eloquence.
Good son, how do they attain pleasant speech?
The speech of a bodhisattva is able to gladden the minds of sentient beings.
Why does he smile with a face?
Because the bodhisattva’s serene countenance and comforting presence enable sentient beings to attain peace and security.
How is it that they are able to expound upon the meaning?
Because the Bodhisattva’s speech is measured and appropriate.
How is it that they are able to expound upon the Dharma?
Whatever the Bodhisattva expounds is for the purpose of benefiting sentient beings.
How does he teach with equanimity?
Because the Bodhisattva always bestows the Dharma upon sentient beings with an impartial mind.
What is meant by being without arrogance?
It is that the bodhisattva remains far removed from self-conceit and haughtiness because of their nature of sameness with others.
What is meant by being far removed from contempt?
The Bodhisattva preaches the Dharma out of reverence for the Dharma.
How is he unstained?
Because the Bodhisattva’s ethical discipline (*śīla*) is utterly pure.
What is meant by being free from anger?
It is because the bodhisattva’s nature is to practice patience.
What is meant by attaining various forms of eloquence?
The speech of a bodhisattva is exquisite and beautiful, for it delights sentient beings. Noble son,
when a bodhisattva accomplishes these ten qualities, they are able to cause sentient beings to rejoice and be fully satisfied.
"Furthermore, son of good family!
A bodhisattva who accomplishes ten kinds of dharmas is able to cause sentient beings to receive and understand what is taught. What are these ten?
1. Not preaching the Dharma to those who are not suitable vessels;
2. Not preaching the Dharma to those who harbor malice or seek to cause harm;
3. Not preaching the Dharma to those who possess overweening pride.
Fourth, one does not preach the Dharma for non-Buddhists;
fifth, one does not preach the Dharma for those who do not show respect;
sixth, one does not preach the Dharma for those who lack pure faith.
7. He does not preach the Dharma to those who are deceitful and hypocritical;
8. He does not preach the Dharma to those who are fond of worldly livelihood;
9. He does not preach the Dharma to those who are entangled by the pursuit of gain and offerings, the desire for respect from others, jealousy, and stinginess.
Tenth, one does not preach the Dharma to those who are dull-witted, stubborn, mute, or speech-impaired. Why is this?
It is because a bodhisattva-mahāsattva does not fail to preach out of stinginess regarding the Dharma.
Nor do I withhold it like a teacher’s clenched fist;
nor because sentient beings hold me in contempt; nor because I would abandon the Dharma. I simply do not teach it to them because they are not vessels for the Dharma.
The Bodhisattva Zhigai addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
What kind of sentient beings do the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas teach the Dharma for?”
The Buddha said: “Good son!

If there are sentient beings who are endowed with the faculty of faith, who have matured as vessels for the Dharma, who serve the Buddhas with minds free from flattery and crookedness, and likewise free from deceit and falsehood; whose deportment is without pretension, who do not crave gain or offerings, and who possess noble aspirations; who are virtuous men, awakened upon hearing the Dharma, capable of clear understanding, wise and of sharp faculties, able to comprehend the meaning of what is taught as soon as it is spoken; and who, for the sake of attaining the Dharma, practice with diligent vigor and follow the teachings of the Tathāgata in accordance with the Dharma.”
"Noble son! For sentient beings of such a kind, the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas expound the Dharma. Noble son!"
When a bodhisattva accomplishes these ten kinds of dharmas, they are able to receive and uphold the Dharma that has been taught.
"Furthermore, son of good family,
when a bodhisattva accomplishes ten kinds of dharmas, they are able to serve as a teacher of the Dharma."
What are the ten? First, one preaches the Dharma for the sake of accumulating the Buddha-dharmas; yet the Buddha-dharmas are unattainable, and their accumulation is likewise unattainable.
Second, one preaches the Dharma for the sake of accumulating the various pāramitās; yet the pāramitās are unattainable, and their accumulation is likewise unattainable.
Third, he preaches the Dharma for the sake of accumulating bodhi; yet bodhi is unattainable, and accumulation is likewise unattainable.
Fourth, he preaches the Dharma for the sake of severing afflictions; yet afflictions are unattainable, and severance is likewise unattainable.
Fifth, he preaches the Dharma for the sake of wearying of greed, departing from greed, and extinguishing greed; yet weariness, departure, extinction, and greed are all equally unattainable.

Sixth, he preaches the Dharma for the sake of attaining the fruits of the stage of entering the stream, the once-returner, and the non-returner; yet the stages of entering the stream, the once-returner, and the non-returner are all unattainable.

Seventh, he preaches the Dharma for the sake of attaining the stage of entering arhatship and the fruit of arhatship; yet the stage of entering arhatship and the fruit of arhatship are both unattainable.

Eighth, he preaches the Dharma for the sake of attaining the stage of entering pratyekabuddhahood and the fruit of pratyekabuddhahood; yet the stage of entering pratyekabuddhahood and the fruit of pratyekabuddhahood are both unattainable.
Ninth, he expounds the Dharma for the sake of permanently severing attachment to a self, yet neither the self nor the attachment can be apprehended;
tenth, he expounds the Dharma for the sake of revealing karma and its maturation, yet both karma and its maturation cannot be apprehended.
Why is this? Those bodhisattvas reflect thus:
"It is by means of names that phenomena are said to exist, yet those phenomena which are spoken of are fundamentally unobtainable."

Why is this so? Because the Dharma is not words, and words are not the Dharma; it is only because one accords with worldly convention within the context of conventional truth that names are provisionally established for dharmas that are actually nameless.

In the ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*), there are no names; these are merely false designations and provisional establishments made as names to entice and guide the foolish, and thus it is so said.
"Noble son! Because bodhisattvas accomplish these ten kinds of dharmas, they are able to act as teachers of the Dharma.
Furthermore, noble son!"
When bodhisattvas accomplish ten dharmas, they attain conduct that accords with the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*). What are these ten?

First, the bodhisattva’s conduct that accords with the nature of phenomena does not depart from form (*rūpa*), nor does it depart from feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), mental formations (*saṃskāra*), or consciousness (*vijñāna*).
Second, practicing in accordance with the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) without departing from the desire realm;
third, practicing in accordance with the nature of phenomena without departing from the form realm;
fourth, practicing in accordance with the nature of phenomena without departing from the formless realm.
Fifth, practicing in accordance with the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) without abandoning the Dharma;
sixth, practicing in accordance with the nature of phenomena without clinging to the Dharma;
seventh, practicing in accordance with the nature of phenomena without forsaking sentient beings.
Eighth, practicing in accordance with the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) while not falling into the view of nihilism;
ninth, practicing in accordance with the nature of phenomena while not falling into the view of eternalism;
tenth, practicing in accordance with the nature of phenomena while not abandoning the true path.

Why is this so? Because the bodhisattva has accomplished the skillful means of prajñā, although they accord with the nature of phenomena (dharmatā), they neither abandon nor cling to form and the other aggregates, nor do they engage with them.
"Noble son! When a bodhisattva accomplishes these ten kinds of dharmas, they attain conduct that accords with the nature of phenomena (dharmatā). Furthermore, noble son!"
If a bodhisattva accomplishes ten dharmas, they attain skillfulness regarding the dharma-realm (dharmadhātu).
What are these ten? First, possessing wisdom;
Second, associating with spiritual friends;
third, practicing with diligent perseverance;
fourth, being free from all obstacles.
Fifth, extreme purity;
sixth, honoring instructions;
seventh, frequent cultivation of emptiness.
Eighth, being free from all conceited views;
ninth, tending toward the Path;
tenth, seeing the true meaning.
“Good son! A bodhisattva mahāsattva who possesses wisdom seeks out virtuous friends (kalyāṇamitra).
By seeing virtuous friends, they attain joy, gladness, and delight.”
One should conceive of the spiritual friend as being like the Buddha and rely upon them for their dwelling.
By relying upon them, one attains diligent and energetic application, thereby permanently severing all unwholesome dharmas and bringing all wholesome dharmas to fulfillment.
By virtue of diligently cultivating vigor, one eliminates all hindrances and attains non-obstruction; one reveals the true path and remains far removed from the coarseness of body, speech, and mind.
By being free from hindrances, one attains supreme purity.
Having attained purity, one receives respected instructions.
Having received instructions, one is able to practice emptiness extensively.
Having practiced emptiness, one immediately attains detachment from the view of arrogance.
Having detached from the view of arrogance, one proceeds toward the right path.
Once the bodhisattva has attained abiding on the path, they perceive the true meaning.
The Bodhisattva Nivaranaviskambhin addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
what is called ‘true meaning’?”
The Buddha said:
"Good son! 'True meaning' (bhūtārtha) is a synonym for 'actual meaning' (tattvārtha)."
The Bodhisattva Nivaranaviskambhin addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
what is meant by ‘the meaning of reality’?”
The Buddha said:
"Good son! That which is non-false is the true meaning."
The Bodhisattva Nivṛttāvaraṇa addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
what is meant by ‘non-falsehood’?”
The Buddha said:
"Good son! That which is called True Suchness (tathatā) is non-false and without differentiation!"
The Bodhisattva Zhigai addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
what is meant by ‘suchness’ (tathatā)?”
The Buddha said:
"Good son! This Dharma is realized within oneself; it cannot be established through written words."

Why is this? Because this Dharma transcends all letters, speech, and conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*); it is free from entering and exiting, devoid of speculative calculation, and is not the domain of such calculations. It is signless and free from signs; it is not a place frequented by the foolish, but is far removed from all realms of Māra and all realms of affliction (*kleśa*). It is not the domain of consciousness; it abides in non-abiding, its self-nature is quiescent, and it transcends the entry-points of the wisdom of all noble ones.
By virtue of these causes and conditions, that which is personally realized within is stainless, undefiled, pure, subtle, supreme, peerless, eternally immovable, and by nature indestructible.
Whether Tathāgatas appear in the world or do not appear, this dharmadhātu remains eternally abiding by its very nature. Noble son,
for the sake of benefiting others, these bodhisattvas practice with heroic vigor and undergo immeasurable ascetic austerities to realize this dharmatā.
Having attained the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), one establishes sentient beings so that they abide in such a dharma.
Son of good family!
This is called True Suchness (*tathatā*), and it is also called the Limit of Reality (*bhūtakoṭi*).
"It is called 'all-knowledge' (sarvajñā), and it is also called 'knowledge of all modes' (sarvākārajñā);
it is called the 'inconceivable realm' (acintyadhātu), and it is also called the 'non-dual realm' (advayadhātu).
The Bodhisattva Cihai addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
How is one directly realized within this Dharma?
What is that which is personally realized within?”
The Buddha said:
"Good son, you should realize it within yourself through supramundane prajñā."
The Bodhisattva Nivaranaviskambhin addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
If this is so, is the direct realization of prajñā precisely that which is personally realized within?”
The Buddha said: "No, son of good family!"
“Prajñā perceives phenomena as they truly are; this is the internal realization within one’s own body!
The Bodhisattva Zhigai addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
"If one realizes the Dharma in this way through the wisdom derived from hearing and the wisdom derived from reflection,
is it an internal realization? The Buddha said, "No!"
It is not merely by means of the wisdom derived from hearing and the wisdom derived from reflection that one attains internal realization!
Son of good family,
for this reason, I shall now provide you with a parable.
It is as if there were a person, at the end of the summer heat, in the midst of a wilderness, coming from the east and heading toward the west.
Then another person comes from the west and heads toward the east. This person, exhausted by the heat and oppressed by thirst, says to the person from the east:
"I am now exhausted by the heat and oppressed by thirst; please show me the way."
"Where might there be groves of springs, ponds, and pools of pure, cool water?
If I were to find it, my burning afflictions and parching thirst would all be stilled.
Then the man coming from the east spoke thus to the one coming from the west:
"I am familiar with the road and know where there is water, for I have traveled it and drunk from it myself.
If you proceed eastward from here, you will soon encounter a fork in the path; you should abandon the left road and take the right one."
If you see a green mountain, there will be forests and springs with pure, cool water capable of quenching thirst and exhaustion.
You may go there, and you will surely be able to cast off the affliction of parching heat and thirst!
"Good son! What do you think?
Would that person who is parched with heat and thirst be able to eliminate the affliction of heat and thirst merely by hearing the name of water and contemplating the matter of water?"
The Bodhisattva Śamathatāraṇa addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Those who suffer from heat and thirst must first internally realize the water of coolness; only then can they eliminate the affliction of heat and thirst.”
“Good son! It is so, it is so!
One cannot realize the dharma of suchness realized within oneself merely through hearing and reflection.”
Good son! What is called the "wilderness" is birth and death;
what is called "heat and thirst" refers to all sentient beings who, within the realm of sense objects, are parched and exhausted by the heat of the afflictions.
The one who shows the way is none other than the Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and spiritual friends;
"tasting the path for oneself" refers to skillful means;
and "knowing the path of all-knowledge" refers to the supreme nature of reality (dharmatā) personally realized within.
"Furthermore, good son! I shall now speak another parable to enlighten you.

Suppose the Tathāgata were to remain in the world for an entire kalpa, praising for the people of Jambudvīpa the ambrosia consumed by the devas—its color, fragrance, and exquisite flavor, its pure and subtle nature, and how, when touched, it brings about peace and happiness."
"What do you think? Upon hearing these words, would those sentient beings immediately attain such a taste of the nectar of self-realization within?
The Bodhisattva Zhigai replied to the Buddha, "No."
“World-Honored One!
Although that person hears the Buddha preach the ambrosia, they will ultimately be unable to obtain the flavor of the ambrosia.
The Buddha said:
“Good son! You should understand this analogy in this way: it is not possible to attain that which is realized within one’s own inner experience through hearing and reflection alone. Good son!”
Suppose there is a person who, having eaten a delicious fruit, praises its flavor and fragrance before someone else who has not yet eaten it.
What do you think? Can that person who has not yet eaten it internally realize and know its taste?
"No, World-Honored One. The Buddha said:
“Good son! It is just so with that.
You should understand this analogy in this way: it is not by mere hearing and reflection alone that one can realize what is to be personally realized within.”
When he had spoken thus, the Bodhisattva Nivaranaviskambhin addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
This is truly rare!”
The Tathāgata has now skillfully expounded this essential teaching for my sake.
Should anyone hear such a Dharma-gate as this, they ought to realize it. Why is this?
“World-Honored One!
Because those sons of good family have obtained these causes for the Dharma, they will certainly attain this very nature of the Dharma.
The Buddha said:
"So it is, so it is! Having understood the cause, one shall attain this Dharma. Good son!"
When Bodhisattvas accomplish these ten kinds of dharmas, they attain skillfulness regarding the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*).
The *Sūtra of the Precious Rain* Spoken by the Buddha, Scroll Six.
The *Sūtra of the Precious Rain* Spoken by the Buddha, Scroll Seven.
Translated by the Tang Dynasty Indian Tripitaka Master Dharmaruci:
"Furthermore, son of good family, when a bodhisattva accomplishes ten dharmas, he attains emptiness (*śūnyatā*).
What are these ten?"
First, the ability to know the emptiness of the powers;
second, the ability to know the emptiness of the fearlessnesses;
third, the ability to know the emptiness of the unique qualities (āveṇika-dharma).
Fourth, the ability to know the emptiness of the aggregate of ethical discipline;
fifth, the ability to know the emptiness of meditative concentration;
sixth, the ability to know the emptiness of wisdom.
Seventh, they are able to know the emptiness of the aggregate of liberation;
eighth, they are able to know the emptiness of the aggregate of the knowledge and vision of liberation;
ninth, they are able to know the emptiness of emptiness.
Tenth, they are able to know the emptiness of ultimate meaning (*paramārtha-śūnyatā*).

Although the bodhisattva practices within emptiness, they do not fall into nihilism; furthermore, they do not cling to emptiness, nor do they perceive emptiness, nor do they rely upon emptiness, nor do they enter into the state of non-existence (*abhāva*).
"Noble son! When bodhisattvas accomplish these ten kinds of dharmas, they practice emptiness.
Furthermore, noble son!"
When Bodhisattvas accomplish ten dharmas, they attain the practice of signlessness (*animitta*). What are these ten?
First, they remain far removed from external signs.
Second, distancing oneself from internal signs;
third, distancing oneself from signs of conceptual proliferation;
fourth, distancing oneself from signs of discrimination.
Fifth, to remain far removed from the mark of apprehending anything;
sixth, to remain far removed from the mark of activities performed;
seventh, to remain far removed from the mark of conduct engaged in.
Eighth, the characteristic of being far removed from the objects of perception;
ninth, the characteristic of the non-apprehensibility of the cognizing consciousness;
tenth, the characteristic of the non-apprehensibility of the objects to be known.
"Good son! When a bodhisattva accomplishes these ten kinds of dharmas, they attain the practice of signlessness.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Cihang addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
These ten kinds of dharmas are what a bodhisattva should study.
How should one study them?”
The Buddha said:
"Good son! The sphere of the Buddha’s activity is inconceivable, for it is by nature far removed from the realm of conceptualization."

"Good son! If sentient beings contemplate the realm of the Tathāgata’s dharmatā, their minds become bewildered and distressed; they will ultimately be unable to see either this shore or the other shore of the dharmatā, and will only give rise to weariness."

Why is this? The realm of the Tathāgata is inconceivable, profoundly deep and difficult to fathom; it transcends all realms of false conceptualization and transcends all realms of those who grasp at attainments.
"For this reason, it is not something that can be conceived or measured by those who engage in false conceptualization.
The Bodhisattva Zhigai addressed the Buddha, saying,
"World-Honored One!"
"I now wish to ask a few questions.
I only pray that the Tathāgata will compassionately grant me this request and explain them for my sake.
The Buddha said:
“Good son! All Buddhas permit the posing of questions.
According to what you desire, I shall explain it for you!”
The Bodhisattva Śamatharañjita addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Indeed, self-praise is not the way of a true man!”
“How is it that the Tathāgata’s self-praise regarding the sphere of his own practice transcends all?
The Buddha said, “Excellent, excellent!”
"Good son! Listen attentively, listen attentively!
I shall explain it for you."
Good son! The Tathāgata does not praise himself out of pride, arrogance, greed for gain and offerings, service and attendance, fame and renown, or fear that others might eclipse him.

"Good son! The Tathāgata is without hypocrisy or deceit, and his speech is not flattering; he speaks only for the sake of benefiting all sentient beings so that they may attain peace and happiness and realize the nature of phenomena (dharmatā). Those who develop pure faith toward the Tathāgata, rejoicing with gladness, shall become vessels of the Dharma."
Furthermore, they are able to expound the teachings to benefit sentient beings.
The Bodhisattva Zhigai addressed the Buddha, saying,
“World-Honored One!
"All sentient beings are unable to know the power and majesty of the Tathāgata’s merits; must the Tathāgata now praise himself?
The Buddha said, "Good son!..."

The sentient beings of this land have weak roots of faith and inferior intellectual power; they are unable to know the Tathāgata’s merits and majestic power. For this reason, the Tathāgata praises himself so that they may come to know them.
It is like a physician who is well-versed in prescriptions and medicines and is able to cure all manner of illnesses.
Wherever this physician dwells, there are many ailments, yet no other physician exists who can provide a remedy.
At that time, the physician thought to himself:
"These people are oppressed by the suffering of illness; yet they do not recognize the excellent medicine, nor do they know that I am able to eliminate their disease."
At that time, the physician praised himself before the patient, saying:
"I am able to diagnose illnesses and am also well-versed in medicines!
Thereupon, the patient, having recognized him as a skilled physician, conceived deep reverence and faith; by relying on him for his care, all his ailments were completely cured.
"Good son! What do you think? Would that physician also be called one who praises himself?
Cessation-of-Coverings Bodhisattva said:
"No, World-Honored One! The Buddha said: "Good son!

So it is, so it is! The Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, are unsurpassed and are great kings of physicians; they thoroughly know the causes of the afflictions of sentient beings and can provide the medicine of the Dharma. Yet, sentient beings are unable to understand how the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, skillfully eliminate their illnesses.
At that time, the Buddhas themselves praised their own meritorious virtues and majestic powers.
Upon hearing this, sentient beings gave rise to profound reverence and faith; relying upon the Tathāgata, they were cured of the disease of afflictions.
At that time, the Tathāgata acts as the Great King of Physicians, bestowing the medicine of the Great Dharma so that the diseases of affliction may all be cured.
What is called the medicine of the Great Dharma?
The great medicinal herbs of the Dharma are what are known as the contemplation of impurity, loving-kindness, dependent origination, and so forth. Good son!
For these reasons, the Tathāgata surveys all things and praises himself.
"Furthermore, son of good family,
when a bodhisattva accomplishes ten dharmas, they remain far removed from all reliance on vows. What are these ten?
First, not relying on giving while harboring expectations;
second, not relying on maintaining the precepts while harboring expectations;
third, not relying on patience while harboring expectations.
Fourth, not relying on diligence to have any aspiration;
fifth, not relying on meditative concentration to have any aspiration;
sixth, not relying on wisdom to have any aspiration.
Seventh, not relying on the three realms with any longing or seeking; eighth,
not relying on bodhi with any longing or seeking.
Ninth, not relying on the right path while harboring expectations;
tenth, not relying on nirvana while harboring expectations. Why is this?
Because all bodhisattvas are far removed from all signs of dependence. Good son!
Since bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have nothing upon which to depend, they are able to travel through all worlds.
“Good son! When a bodhisattva accomplishes these ten dharmas, he is able to remain far removed from all reliance on vows. Furthermore, good son!”
When bodhisattvas accomplish ten kinds of dharmas, they practice loving-kindness. What are these ten?
First, directionless loving-kindness;
Second is non-discriminatory loving-kindness;
third is the loving-kindness that attains all dharmas;
fourth is the loving-kindness that attains the definitive contemplation of a single object.
Fifth, the compassion that is free from obstruction;
sixth, the compassion that constantly benefits others;
seventh, the compassion that regards all sentient beings with an impartial mind.
Eighth, the compassion that is free from harm;
ninth, the compassion that is all-pervasive;
tenth, the supramundane compassion.
"Noble son! When a bodhisattva accomplishes these ten kinds of dharmas, this is called the essential nature of cultivating loving-kindness.
Furthermore, noble son!"
When bodhisattvas accomplish ten kinds of dharmas, they practice compassion. What are these ten?
First, seeing sentient beings who are without refuge, without protection, and suffering from affliction, they immediately give rise to pity and resolve to attain bodhicitta.
Second, having generated the bodhicitta, they apply courageous diligence and swiftly enter the nature of phenomena;
third, having entered the nature of phenomena, they bring benefit to sentient beings;
fourth, for the sake of sentient beings who are stingy, they cause them to practice generosity.
Fifth, to cause sentient beings who violate the precepts to uphold them;
sixth, to cause sentient beings who harbor anger and malice to practice patience;
seventh, to cause sentient beings who are indolent to apply diligence.
Eighth, to cause sentient beings who are distracted to attain meditative concentration;
ninth, to cause sentient beings with impaired wisdom to attain wisdom;

tenth, although they undergo various sufferings and afflictions for the sake of sentient beings, their resolve is to rescue them, never becoming weary or fatigued, and never regressing from great enlightenment.
“Noble son! When a bodhisattva accomplishes these ten kinds of dharmas, this is called the cultivation of the intrinsic nature of compassion.
Furthermore, noble son!”
When a bodhisattva accomplishes ten dharmas, they practice sympathetic joy (*muditā*). What are these ten?
First, they give rise to joy, thinking: "I have escaped from the prison of all existences and from the blazing of fierce fires."
Second, I give rise to joy because I am able to sever the bonds of birth and death that have continued for a vast duration;
third, I give rise to joy because I have already been able to cross the great ocean of birth and death, which is turbulent with various discursive thoughts, investigations, and false attachments;
fourth, I give rise to joy because I am able to topple the long-standing banner of pride.
Fifth, I give rise to joy thinking: "I am able to shatter the mountain of afflictions with vajra-wisdom until not even so much as a speck of dust remains.
Sixth, I give rise to joy thinking: "Now that I myself have attained peace and security, I am likewise able to enable others to attain peace and security.

Seventh, I give rise to joy thinking: "While others were sleeping through the long night, I have attained awakening; furthermore, I am able to awaken all sentient beings who, within the long night, are bound by the ropes of craving, shrouded by the veil of ignorance, and blinded by darkness."
Eighth, having attained liberation from all evil realms myself, I am likewise able to bring others to liberation; thus I give rise to joy.

Ninth, throughout the long night of saṃsāra—vast and remote, weary with hunger and thirst, wandering alone without companion, circulating endlessly, failing to recognize the right path, and ignorant of the directions—I have now both recognized the path and am able to show it to others;
thus I give rise to joy. Tenth, I am now able to head toward the city of omniscience; thus I give rise to joy.
"Noble son! When a bodhisattva accomplishes these ten kinds of dharmas, this is called the cultivation of joy.
Furthermore, noble son!"
When a bodhisattva accomplishes ten dharmas, they are able to practice equanimity (*upekṣā*). What are these ten?
First, because they attain the practice of equanimity regarding the forms seen by the eye.
Second, because one attains the practice of equanimity regarding sounds heard by the ear;
third, because one attains the practice of equanimity regarding odors smelled by the nose;
fourth, because one attains the practice of equanimity regarding flavors tasted by the tongue.
Fifth, because one attains the practice of equanimity regarding the tactile sensations experienced by the body;
sixth, because one attains the practice of equanimity regarding the phenomena known by the mind—when practicing in this way, one is not distressed, harmed, or extinguished by objects such as forms;
seventh, because one attains the practice of equanimity regarding the suffering of suffering.
Eighth, because one attains the practice of equanimity regarding the suffering of change;

ninth, because one attains the practice of equanimity regarding the suffering of conditioned formations, when practicing in this way, one does not afflict, harm, or extinguish the nature of the suffering of suffering, the suffering of change, or the suffering of conditioned formations;

tenth, because one attains the practice of equanimity regarding sentient beings for whom what was to be done has been accomplished, one gives rise to a mind of joy, pure faith, and gladness, and reflects as follows:
"Although those sentient beings have already crossed over themselves, I shall cause them to attain liberation"—thus one practices the mind of equanimity (*upekṣā*).
Son of good family!
When a bodhisattva accomplishes these ten kinds of dharmas, this is called the cultivation of equanimity.
"Furthermore, son of good family!
When a bodhisattva accomplishes ten kinds of dharmas, they attain the supernormal power of playful mastery. What are these ten?
First, manifesting disappearance; second, manifesting birth;
third, manifesting youthful play within the inner palace.
Fourth, manifesting the renunciation of the household life;
fifth, manifesting the practice of asceticism;
sixth, manifesting the journey to the site of enlightenment.
Seventh, manifesting the subduing of all Māras;
eighth, manifesting the attainment of equal and perfect enlightenment;
ninth, manifesting the turning of the wheel of the true Dharma.
"Tenth, he manifests great parinirvāṇa.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Cchhāyāpaga (Cessation of Obstructions) addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
"For what causes and conditions do the great bodhisattvas manifest their passing away from the Tuṣita Heaven palace, and even manifest entry into great parinirvāṇa?
The Buddha said, "Good son!"

The Bodhisattva is most honored and most supreme in Tuṣita Heaven; having transcended all worldly realms of desire without any defiled attachment, he manifests his disappearance for the sake of sentient beings.
Having seen sentient beings, one abandons the notion of permanence and gives rise to the notion of impermanence; by relying upon that impermanence, one attains heedfulness. Good son!

Those sentient beings have not yet abandoned negligence; although they have conceived pure faith toward the Bodhisattva, because they are addicted to the objects of desire, they are unable to attend upon or make offerings to him. They think to themselves:
"The Bodhisattva will remain in the world for a long time; we shall go to his presence later to attend upon and make offerings to him—it will not be too late!"
"In order to cause such sentient beings to give rise to a heart of longing and abandon negligence, I have manifested my disappearance!
Yet, once those sentient beings have contemplated impermanence, they will no longer be negligent and shall attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."

"Good son! If there are sentient beings who should be tamed while remaining in the mother’s womb, the Bodhisattva will enter the mother’s womb and manifest his meritorious virtues, majestic spiritual power, and rare wonders, preaching various subtle and wondrous Dharmas for them. Having heard these, those sentient beings shall attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."

"Good son! If there are sentient beings who should be tamed by seeing the Bodhisattva sporting in the inner palace during his youth, the Bodhisattva causes those sentient beings to attain maturity; furthermore, in order to protect inferior sentient beings who possess few roots of faith, he manifests as a youth sporting within the palace."

"Good son! If there are sentient beings who should be brought to maturity by seeing a bodhisattva renounce the household life, the bodhisattva manifests renunciation for the sake of bringing them to maturity."

"Good son! If devas, nāgas, yakṣas, or gandharvas are to be tamed through ascetic practices, the bodhisattva manifests such asceticism for the sake of transforming them and for the sake of subduing the various non-Buddhists."
"Good son! If there are sentient beings who, throughout the long night, have longed for this and made such a vow:
'When a bodhisattva goes to the site of enlightenment, I shall go there and diligently practice offerings! "

For the sake of such sentient beings as these, the Bodhisattva manifests his departure for the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa), so that sentient beings may follow him in making offerings and thereby certainly attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.

"Good son! If there are sentient beings who are arrogant, conceited, haughty, and self-indulgent, in order to cause them to abandon such afflictions and to subdue all Māras, [the Buddha] is able to manifest sitting at the site of enlightenment."

If there are sentient beings who delight in tranquility, the Bodhisattva, in order to cause them to ultimately realize the most excellent, supreme, and most sublime Dharma, manifests sitting at the site of enlightenment and attaining equal and perfect awakening.
Therefore, when the Bodhisattva has manifested perfect enlightenment, the great trichiliocosm becomes entirely tranquil, and all sounds cease.
Upon seeing this event, those sentient beings all say:
"May we, in the future when we realize bodhi, likewise sit at the site of enlightenment and attain equal and perfect awakening!"

"Good son! If sentient beings take those false teachers to be omniscient and receive their false teachings, they will be unable to achieve liberation in this world or the next, nor attain equal and perfect enlightenment.

Desiring to subdue them and to bring their roots of virtue to maturity—and because there are other sentient beings capable of being vessels for the Dharma who can be shown the Way—the Bodhisattva manifests the attainment of equal and perfect enlightenment and proceeds to the city of Vārāṇasī to manifest the turning of the Wheel of Dharma in its three revolutions and twelve aspects."
"Good son! If there are sentient beings who are to be tamed by hearing of nirvāṇa, the bodhisattva then manifests great parinirvāṇa to tame them."
"Good son! For these reasons, the Bodhisattva manifests his disappearance from the most excellent palace in the Tuṣita Heaven, and so forth, even manifesting his Great Parinirvāṇa."
"Noble son! When bodhisattvas accomplish these ten kinds of dharmas, they attain the supernormal power of playful mastery.
Furthermore, noble son!"
If bodhisattvas accomplish ten dharmas, they are able to leave behind the eight states of no leisure. What are these ten?
First, they abandon unwholesome dharmas.
Second, they never transgress the precepts taught by the Tathāgata;
third, they remain far removed from stinginess and greed;
fourth, they have already made offerings to various Buddhas and Tathāgatas.
Fifth, diligently cultivating meritorious deeds;
sixth, perfecting wisdom;
seventh, attaining skillful means.
Eighth, the fulfillment of original vows;
ninth, weariness with and detachment from worldly dharmas;
tenth, diligent and energetic practice.
“Good son! Because a bodhisattva has abandoned all evil karma, he does not fall into hell.
Those sentient beings who are born in the hells are tormented by immeasurable suffering and give rise to a mind of anger.
The Bodhisattva is not like that!
Because they have perfected the nature of the ten paths of wholesome action, they will never be born within the hells. Good son!
Because a bodhisattva does not transgress the training rules of the Tathāgata, they do not fall into the realm of animals.
Those born therein undergo extremely intense and immeasurable suffering and affliction.
Good son! Because bodhisattvas are not stingy or greedy, they are not reborn among the hungry ghosts.
Those who are born there undergo the most intense suffering of hunger and affliction.
"Good son! Because a bodhisattva has already served and made offerings to various Buddhas and Tathāgatas in the past, he is not born into a family of wrong views.
If he were born therein, the necessary conditions would not be complete, and he would be unable to associate with virtuous friends; therefore, the bodhisattva is not born there."

Encountering spiritual friends and practicing wholesome dharmas, one thereby takes birth into a family of right view; with all conditions fulfilled, one increases and expands vast and sublime roots of goodness.
Good son! The faculties of a bodhisattva are never deficient or diminished.
If they were deficient, one would not be a fit vessel for the Buddha-dharma.

Nevertheless, because the bodhisattva has accumulated meritorious deeds and has rendered service and made offerings to the Buddha, the Dharma, the Saṅgha, and the caityas, he attains the perfection of the sense faculties and becomes a fit vessel for the Dharma.
Good son! A bodhisattva is not born in the borderlands. Why is this?

The people of the borderlands are stubborn, dull-witted, and ignorant, like mute sheep; such as these cannot comprehend the meaning of words regarding good and evil, nor do they practice filial piety toward their parents, nor do they show respect for śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas.

For this reason, bodhisattvas are always born in the central lands, possessing sharp faculties and wisdom, being intelligent, discerning, and thoroughly proficient, such that they are capable of serving as vessels for the Buddha-dharma. Good son!

A bodhisattva is not born among the long-lived devas; for if they were so born, they would not encounter the appearance in the world of immeasurable Buddhas, would not attain the fruits of the Path, and would be unable to benefit others.
Therefore, Bodhisattvas are born in the desire realm (kāmadhātu) to encounter the appearance of a Buddha, to serve and make offerings to him, and to bring sentient beings to maturity. Why is this?
Because they are able to attain those skillful means (upāya-kauśalya).

"Good son! A bodhisattva is not born in a world where there is no Buddha; rather, they are always born within a buddha-field that is fully endowed with the Triple Gem—the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha—to whom one should offer worship."
Why is this? Because all bodhisattvas are endowed with their original vows. Good son!

Upon hearing of these states of no leisure, the bodhisattva develops a profound sense of weary detachment; having attained such detachment, they diligently cultivate vigor, acquire all wholesome dharmas, and forever sever all unwholesome dharmas.
"Noble son! When a bodhisattva accomplishes these ten dharmas, they remain far removed from the eight states of no leisure.
Furthermore, noble son!"
If a bodhisattva accomplishes ten dharmas, they will attain non-retrogression from the mind of enlightenment. What are these ten?
First, they remain far removed from falsehood, flattery, and crookedness.
Second, being upright and pure, free from all doubts and delusions;
third, being far removed from the "teacher's fist" (withholding instruction);
fourth, being far removed from stinginess regarding the Dharma.
Fifth, not creating the causes and conditions for the extinction of the Dharma;
sixth, acting in accordance with what one says, never being false or deceptive;
seventh, embracing the Mahāyāna.
Eighth, they always give rise to respect for those who follow the Mahāyāna, because they regard them as fellow practitioners of the Dharma;
ninth, they attain the path toward the Mahāyāna and accord with its realization;
tenth, they regard the Dharma-preachers as spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*).
"Noble son! When a bodhisattva accomplishes these ten dharmas, they attain the non-retrogressive bodhicitta.
Furthermore, noble son!"
When Bodhisattvas accomplish ten dharmas, they attain the wisdom of recollecting past lives.
What are these ten? First, serving all Buddhas;
Second, upholding the true Dharma;
third, maintaining pure ethical discipline;
fourth, being free from remorse.
Fifth, attaining non-obstruction;
sixth, immeasurable joy;
seventh, attaining extensive cultivation of practice.
Eighth, they attain samāhita;
ninth, they attain miraculous birth;
tenth, they attain consciousness free from delusion.
"Good son! Because a bodhisattva serves immeasurable Buddhas, he attains reverence for the True Dharma;
he receives, maintains, reads, and recites all the True Dharmas, and extensively explains them to others."
By disregarding body and life to diligently cultivate the True Dharma, one attains śīla—namely, the purification of the precepts of body, speech, and mind;
because the precepts are pure, one is free from remorse;
and because there is no remorse, one attains freedom from hindrances.
Because there is no obstruction, one attains immeasurable joy;
because of immeasurable joy, one attains extensive practice;
because of extensive practice, one attains samādhi.
Because one attains samādhi, one is able to proceed toward purity;
because one proceeds toward purity, one constantly attains miraculous birth (upapāduka);
because one attains miraculous birth, consciousness is free from delusion.
Because consciousness is free from delusion, one attains the knowledge of recollecting births.
By means of this, one can recollect many births in succession—one birth, two births, and even up to immeasurable hundreds of thousands of births.
“Noble son! When a bodhisattva accomplishes these ten kinds of dharmas, they attain the knowledge of recollecting past lives.
Furthermore, noble son!”
When Bodhisattvas accomplish ten dharmas, they do not depart from spiritual friends. What are these ten?
First, seeing the Buddha, hearing of the Buddha, and recollecting the Buddha;
Second, listening to and hearing the true Dharma;
third, serving and attending upon the Sangha;
fourth, not being separated from the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, and inquiring after their well-being and daily activities.
Fifth, they constantly associate with teachers who are learned and preach the Dharma;
sixth, they always hear the various pāramitās;
seventh, they constantly hear the factors of enlightenment (bodhipakṣadharma).
Eighth, they constantly hear of the three gates of liberation;
ninth, they constantly hear of the four brahma-vihāras;
tenth, they constantly hear of the nature of omniscience.
"Noble son! When a bodhisattva accomplishes these ten kinds of dharmas, they draw near to spiritual friends.
Furthermore, noble son!"
When a bodhisattva accomplishes ten dharmas, they remain far removed from evil associates. What are these ten?
First, remaining far removed from individuals who violate the precepts;
Second, staying far removed from individuals who hold destructive views;
third, staying far removed from individuals who have ruined their dignified conduct;
fourth, staying far removed from individuals who lead a life of wrong livelihood.
Fifth, to distance oneself from individuals who associate with the clamor of worldly bustle;
sixth, to distance oneself from individuals who are indolent;
seventh, to distance oneself from individuals who are attached to saṃsāra.
Eighth, to distance oneself from individuals who oppose and contradict perfect enlightenment;
ninth, to distance oneself from individuals who are attached to domestic affairs;
tenth, to distance oneself from all afflictions.
"Good son! Although a bodhisattva remains far removed from such evil associates, he does not give rise to thoughts of harm or contempt toward them."
A bodhisattva should give rise to this thought:
"As the Buddha has said:
'If one associates with and becomes defiled by chaotic beings, one will immediately be destroyed by them.'"
"Therefore, I should remain far removed from such places of distraction. Noble son,
when a bodhisattva accomplishes these ten qualities, they remain far removed from evil associates.
"Furthermore, son of good family,
when a bodhisattva accomplishes ten dharmas, they attain the body of the dharma-nature (dharmatā-kāya). What are these ten?
First, attaining the body of equality;
second, attaining the pure body;
third, attaining the inexhaustible body.
Fourth, attaining the accumulated body;
fifth, attaining the dharma-body;
sixth, attaining the profoundly deep, unfathomable, and incalculable body.
Seventh, they attain an inconceivable body;
eighth, they attain a tranquil body;
ninth, they attain a body equal to space.
Tenth, they attain the body of wisdom.
Son of good family,
when bodhisattvas accomplish these ten kinds of dharmas, they attain the Dharma-nature body of the Tathāgata.
The Bodhisattva Nivaraṇaviṣkambhin said:
“World-Honored One!
At what stage do the bodhisattvas attain realization of the Tathāgata’s body of dharmatā?”
The Buddha said:
"Good son! A bodhisattva of the first stage attains the body of equality."
Why is this? Because they have forever departed from all inequality and have awakened to and entered the equal dharma-nature of all bodhisattvas;
thus, the bodhisattva of the second stage attains a purified body through the purity of their ethical discipline (*śīla*).
Bodhisattvas on the third stage attain an inexhaustible body, because they have forever abandoned all anger and harm;
Bodhisattvas on the fourth stage attain a well-accumulated body, because they accumulate the Buddha-dharma;
Bodhisattvas on the fifth stage realize the Dharma-body, because they are able to penetrate all phenomena.
Bodhisattvas of the sixth stage attain an immeasurable, profound, and unfathomable body because they have accumulated immeasurable, profound, and unfathomable dharmas;
Bodhisattvas of the seventh stage attain an inconceivable body because they have accumulated inconceivable Buddha-dharmas and are able to accumulate skillful means (*upāyakauśalya*);
Bodhisattvas of the eighth stage attain a tranquil body because they are far removed from all conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*) and afflictions (*kleśa*).
Bodhisattvas of the ninth stage attain a body equal to space, because they fill it with boundless bodies;
Bodhisattvas of the tenth stage realize the wisdom-body, because they have accumulated all-encompassing wisdom.
The Bodhisattva Zhigai said:
“World-Honored One!
What is the difference between the Dharma-body of the Tathāgata and the Dharma-body of a bodhisattva?”
The Buddha said:
"Good son! The two kinds of dharma-body are without distinction in their nature, yet they differ in terms of their meritorious power and majesty."
The Bodhisattva Nivaranaviskambhin addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
how can there be distinctions when the nature is without distinction?”
The Buddha said:
"Good son! There is no difference between the dharma-nature of a Buddha and that of a bodhisattva."
"Why is this? Because these two kinds of bodies are of the same nature; there is only a distinction in the power of their merits.
The Bodhisattva Zhigai addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
How should one understand the distinction between the merit and majestic power of a Buddha and that of a bodhisattva?
The Buddha said:
“Good son! I shall now explain this meaning for you at length through a parable. Good son!”
It is like mani-jewels: some have been polished and others have not. Although they are both jewels, those that have been polished are fully endowed with radiance and are cherished by people;
those that have not yet been polished do not possess their full radiance.
"Good son! Although the jewel of the Tathāgata and the jewel of the bodhisattva are identical in their essential nature, there are nevertheless differences between them. Why is this so?"
Because the jewel of the Tathāgata is already purified and free from all defilements,
the jewel of the dharma-nature within the bodies of bodhisattvas has not yet been able to universally illuminate all worlds.
Why is this? Because there remains something further, and because there still exists defilement, it is like a mani-jewel that has not yet been polished.
Therefore, such is the distinction between the Dharma-body of the Tathāgata and the Dharma-body of a bodhisattva.

"Good son! It is like the moon during the waxing phase, from the first day until the fifteenth day; its radiance shines forth and it gradually becomes full. Although it is the same moon, its radiance is not equal [at different times]. Likewise, although the Dharma-body of a Bodhisattva and the Dharma-body of a Tathāgata share the same nature and characteristics, their merits and majestic powers differ in such a way."
"Furthermore, son of good family,
when a bodhisattva accomplishes ten dharmas, he attains a body as firm and solid as a vajra. What are these ten?
First, they cannot be thwarted or destroyed by greed, hatred, delusion, and the like;
second, they cannot be thwarted or destroyed by anger, resentment, envy, conceit, arrogance, or inverted views;
third, they cannot be thwarted or destroyed by the eight worldly dharmas.
Fourth, they cannot be thwarted by the suffering and afflictions of the evil realms;
fifth, they cannot be thwarted by any form of suffering whatsoever;
sixth, they cannot be thwarted by birth, old age, sickness, and death.
Seventh, he cannot be thwarted by the various treatises of non-Buddhists;
eighth, he cannot be thwarted by Māra and his hosts;
ninth, he cannot be thwarted by śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas.
Tenth, they cannot be thwarted or destroyed by the objects of desire.
Son of good family,
when bodhisattvas accomplish these ten dharmas, they attain a body as firm and solid as a vajra.
"Furthermore, noble son,
when a bodhisattva accomplishes ten qualities, he becomes a great caravan leader. What are these ten?
First, attaining an even-minded intention;
second, being worthy of receiving offerings;
third, being able to bring about renunciation.
Fourth, they are able to serve as a basis;
fifth, they are able to provide benefit;
sixth, they are well able to accumulate the provisions for the path.
Seventh, one obtains excellent wealth and treasures;
eighth, the mind knows no satiety;
ninth, one constantly acts as a guide for others.
Tenth, skillfully following along toward the city of omniscience.
"Good son! How does a bodhisattva attain an even-minded intention, and so forth, up to how does he attain skillful conformity in proceeding toward the great city of the nature of omniscience?"
"Good son! Just as a merchant leader is beloved by various kings and princes,
so too is the bodhisattva!"
He acts as a caravan leader of the Dharma, becoming beloved by all Tathāgatas, śrāvakas, and others. Good son!
Just as a caravan leader ought to receive the offerings of village brahmins, kṣatriyas, and so forth.
The Bodhisattva is likewise!
As a merchant leader of the Dharma, he should receive offerings from those in training (śaikṣa), those beyond training (aśaikṣa), and others such as devas and nāgas. Good son!
For example, it is like a caravan leader who, traveling through a wilderness plagued by famine, guides the merchants to safety and well-being without ever succumbing to weariness.
The Bodhisattva is likewise!
Acting as a caravan leader of the Dharma, traversing the wilderness of birth and death, you are able to cause sentient beings to escape oppression and all attain peace and happiness.
O son of good family!
Just as a caravan leader can serve as a great refuge for all suffering beings, enabling them to escape the wilderness of famine,
so too is the Bodhisattva!
Acting as a caravan leader of the Dharma, he was able to deliver the outsiders Caṅkī, Śāṇakavāsin, and Upatiṣya from saṃsāra, preserving their very lives.
“Good son! Just as a caravan leader is able to bring benefit to kings, ministers, and all the people,
so too is the bodhisattva!”
He acts as a caravan leader for the Dharma, able to bring benefit to all sentient beings who are attached to the cycle of birth and death. Good son!

It is like a caravan leader who leads many merchants toward various regions; passing through a wilderness plagued by famine, he is skillfully able to amass vast provisions, cross over the perilous difficulties, reach a great city, and attain peace and happiness.
The Bodhisattva is likewise!

Acting as a caravan leader for the Dharma, he is skillfully able to accumulate the provisions of merit and wisdom, guiding sentient beings across the wilderness of birth and death until they reach the city of the all-knowledge of all Buddhas.

Good son! It is like a caravan leader who nurtures a multitude of people, desiring to travel to another region to gather precious treasures—namely, gold, silver, mani-jewels, pearls, lapis lazuli, conch shells, jade, coral, and other such gems.
The Bodhisattva is likewise!

Acting as a caravan leader for the Dharma, he nurtures sentient beings, desiring to travel to the great city of all-encompassing wisdom, and is well able to accumulate the precious jewels of the Buddha-dharma.
"Good son! Just as a merchant leader never tires of seeking all manner of wealth,
so too is the bodhisattva!"
As a caravan leader of the Dharma, he seeks all treasures of the true Dharma without ever becoming satiated. Good son!

It is like a caravan leader who stands as the foremost among all merchants; because he has accumulated wealth and is able to lead, because he is most honored and supreme, and because he is able to cause all the merchants to trust and accept his words.
The Bodhisattva is likewise!

He is a caravan leader of the Dharma because he is the most honored and supreme among all sentient beings, because he is able to act as their leader, and because his accumulation of merit is never in vain.
"Good son! Just as a caravan leader, through skillful means, can traverse dangerous paths and reach that great city,
so too is the bodhisattva!"
They lead all sentient beings beyond birth and death to the city of wisdom.
Noble son, this is called the bodhisattva’s attainment of equal intention, and so forth, up to skillfully reaching the great city of omniscient wisdom.
"Furthermore, son of good family,
when a bodhisattva accomplishes ten dharmas, he is skillful regarding the path. What are these ten?
First, the ability to know the path of equality;
second, the ability to know the path of inequality;
third, the ability to know the path of peace and security.
Fourth, they are able to know the path of skillful means;
fifth, they are able to know the path where water and grass are found;
sixth, they are able to know the paths of all directions.
Seventh, one is able to know the path of signs;
eighth, one is able to know the right path;
ninth, one is able to know the deviant path.
Tenth, they are able to know the path of renunciation.
Son of good family,
when a bodhisattva accomplishes these ten kinds of dharmas, they are skillful regarding the path.
"Furthermore, son of good family,
when a bodhisattva accomplishes ten dharmas, he attains the non-perverted path. What are these ten?
First, if there are sentient beings who should be disciplined by means of the Great Vehicle, he disciplines them by teaching the path of the bodhisattva, and does not teach the path of the śrāvaka;
