second, if there are sentient beings who should be disciplined by means of the Śrāvaka Vehicle, he disciplines them by teaching the path of the śrāvaka, and does not teach the path of the bodhisattva;
third, if there are sentient beings who should be disciplined by means of omniscience, he disciplines them by teaching the path of omniscience, and does not teach the path of the pratyekabuddha.
Fourth, if there are sentient beings who should be disciplined by means of the Pratyekabuddha Vehicle, he teaches them the path of the Pratyekabuddhas, and does not teach the path of omniscience;

fifth, if there are sentient beings who cling to a self and to phenomena, he teaches them selflessness and the doctrine of emptiness, and does not speak of a self, a sentient being, a life-principle, a nourisher, or a person (pudgala);
sixth, if there are sentient beings who cling to the two extremes, he teaches them the path that transcends the two extremes, and does not speak of relying upon the two extremes.
Seventh, if there are sentient beings whose minds are distracted, he teaches them śamatha and vipaśyanā, and does not teach the path of distraction;

eighth, if there are sentient beings who cling to conceptual proliferation (prapañca), he teaches them suchness (tathatā), and does not teach the conceptual proliferation in which foolish people indulge;
ninth, if there are sentient beings who are attached to birth and death (saṃsāra), he teaches them nirvāṇa, and does not teach saṃsāra.

Tenth, if there are sentient beings who are attached to false paths, one speaks to them of the path that is free from fetters and thorns, rather than speaking of the path of universal afflictions and thorns.
"Noble son! When a bodhisattva accomplishes these ten dharmas, they are able to accomplish the non-perverted path.
Furthermore, noble son!"
When a bodhisattva accomplishes ten dharmas, they are able to skillfully practice the mind of samāhita.
What are these ten? First, skillfully practicing the application of mindfulness to the body;
Second, skillfully practicing the foundation of mindfulness of feelings;
third, skillfully practicing the foundation of mindfulness of the mind;
fourth, skillfully practicing the foundation of mindfulness of phenomena.
Fifth, skillful practice regarding the foundation of mindfulness of objects;
sixth, skillful practice regarding the foundation of mindfulness of forest hermitages (araṇya);
seventh, skillful practice regarding the foundation of mindfulness of villages, countries, royal capitals, and settlements.
Eighth, the application of mindfulness in skillfully practicing for gain, honor, and fame;
ninth, the application of mindfulness in skillfully practicing the training rules established by the Tathāgata;
tenth, the application of mindfulness in skillfully practicing regarding the afflictions and secondary afflictions that constitute defilement.
"How does a bodhisattva practice the mindfulness of the body?
Son of good family!

A bodhisattva uses right prajñā to discern those dharmas associated with the body, thereby being able to abandon unwholesome dharmas. He contemplates this body from head to foot as being without self or what belongs to a self."
This nature does not endure for long; it must ultimately perish and disintegrate.
Bound by sinews and veins, it is foul, filthy, and impure.
When the Bodhisattva contemplates in this manner, he finds no pleasure, desire, or attachment therein.
For this reason, regarding all loathsome phenomena within the body, only a bodhisattva possesses the sovereign power to relinquish them, whereas ordinary sentient beings do not.
This is called practicing the application of mindfulness to the body with skill.
"How does a bodhisattva practice the mindfulness of feelings?
Son of good family!
A bodhisattva reflects in this way:"
"All sensations whatsoever are entirely suffering; the foolish, through their perversion, claim them to be pleasure.
Those who possess all-knowledge know that pleasure is itself suffering; therefore, they practice with vigor to sever suffering, and cause other sentient beings likewise to train in this way."
"When a bodhisattva-mahāsattva contemplates feelings, he is ultimately neither stained by attachment nor does he feel aversion.
This is called the bodhisattva’s skillful practice of the mindfulness of feelings."
"What is the application of mindfulness to mental formations? Good son,
a bodhisattva reflects in this way:
"The mind is truly impermanent, yet one clings to it as permanent;
it is truly suffering, yet one clings to it as pleasure;
fundamentally there is no self, yet one clings to it as a self."
Originally impure, yet one clings to it as pure;
this mind is light and restless, never pausing for a moment.
Because it does not cease, it serves as the root of all defilements, destroying the paths of goodness, opening the gates to evil destinies, and causing the three poisons to grow.

It acts as the causal condition for the secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*) and so forth, serving as their sovereign and guide; furthermore, it accumulates pure and impure karma, swiftly revolving like a whirling firebrand, like a galloping horse, like a consuming fire, and like swelling water, perceiving all objects as vividly as a worldly painting.
When the bodhisattva observes the mind in this manner, he attains mastery.
Having attained mastery, he is likewise free from obstruction regarding all phenomena.
This is called the bodhisattva’s skillful practice of the application of mindfulness to the mind.
“What is the bodhisattva’s practice of the application of mindfulness to dharmas?
Son of good family!

The bodhisattva understands, as they truly are, all unwholesome dharmas—such as greed, hatred, and delusion—as well as the other dharmas that arise based upon them; and he is able to cultivate the antidotes to the afflictions, so that all evil dharmas are forever severed.”

Being able to fully understand all wholesome dharmas and dwelling therein, they make solemn vows and aspirations, and further enable all sentient beings to establish themselves in such practice and training.
This is called the bodhisattva’s skillful practice of the application of mindfulness to phenomena (*dharmasmṛtyupasthāna*).
"What, son of good family, is the bodhisattva’s practice of the application of mindfulness to the objective sphere (*viṣayasmṛtyupasthāna*)? Son of good family!"
The bodhisattva is neither defiled nor attached amidst agreeable or disagreeable forms, sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, and mental phenomena, nor does he give rise to a mind of anger.
The bodhisattva reflects thus:
"I should not give rise to craving or defilement toward all non-existent phenomena.
If I were to give rise to such defilement, it would be the nature of a fool, the nature of ignorance, the nature of non-comprehension, and the nature of unwholesomeness."
As the Blessed One said:
"If one is defiled by craving, one becomes dull and obtuse, unable to discern wholesome and unwholesome dharmas; by reason of this, one falls into the evil destinies."
The Bodhisattva reflects thus:
"I ought not to give rise to anger toward phenomena that are empty.
If I were to give rise to anger, I would be unable to practice patience."
"This entanglement of anger is censured by the noble ones and reviled by those who lead the holy life.
When a bodhisattva observes such objects, he is neither bound by them nor possesses attachment toward them; furthermore, he teaches others to practice and train in this same way.
This is called the Bodhisattva’s mindfulness foundation of skillfully practicing the sphere of activity.
*The Sūtra Spoken by the Buddha on the Precious Rain*, Scroll Seven;
*The Sūtra Spoken by the Buddha on the Precious Rain*, Scroll Eight.
Translated by the Tang Dynasty Indian Tripitaka Master Dharmaruci:
"How does a bodhisattva practice the mindfulness foundation of the araṇya? Son of good family, the bodhisattva reflects as follows:"

"Abiding in the practice of non-contention and abiding in the practice of tranquility, if there are devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, or others possessing the supernormal power of knowing the minds of others who can know my mind and its mental factors, I should therefore attend to things in accordance with reality, distance myself from improper attention, and extensively cultivate the practice within the dharmas that accord with reality."
This is called the bodhisattva’s skillful practice of the foundation of mindfulness regarding the araṇya.
"What is the bodhisattva’s skillful practice of the foundation of mindfulness regarding villages, towns, countries, and royal capitals?
"Good son! If there are places that are contrary to the Dharma, a bodhisattva must abandon them.

These include wine shops, brothels, royal households, gambling dens, the company of the intoxicated, places of public amusement, and venues for singing and dancing. Such are not places where those who have left the household life should frequent; they should all be kept at a distance."
This is called the bodhisattva’s skillful practice of the mindfulness of dwelling among human beings.
What is the bodhisattva’s skillful practice of the mindfulness of gain, service, honor, and praise?
Good son! A bodhisattva is able to give rise to such a thought amidst gains and offerings:

"For the sake of acting as a field of merit for all donors and for the sake of distributing gifts, I shall never become attached or develop craving; nor shall I, for my own sake, grasp at 'I' or 'mine'."
"Whatever things I receive, I shall share them with all sentient beings and dedicate them to those who suffer.
For this reason, regarding the gains and offerings he receives, the bodhisattva never relies upon them to give rise to a mind of pride or arrogance, but reflects thus:

"The nature of these acquired fame, gain, and other such things is empty and quiescent; they are utterly unattainable. They are phenomena that must ultimately perish and decay, and are therefore not to be trusted!"
"Who among the wise would give rise to attachment toward impermanent phenomena, and further give rise to arrogance, negligence, and haughty pride?
This is called the bodhisattva’s skillful practice of the mindfulness of gain and so forth.
"How does a bodhisattva practice the application of mindfulness regarding the training rules established by the Tathāgata?
Son of good family,
a bodhisattva reflects as follows:"
"The Buddhas of the past practiced these points of training; having cultivated them, they attained manifest perfect enlightenment and entered parinirvāṇa.
The Buddhas of the future will practice in this way; they shall attain manifest perfect enlightenment and enter parinirvāṇa.
The Buddhas of the present, having already cultivated them, now attain manifest perfect enlightenment and enter parinirvāṇa."
"A Bodhisattva Mahāsattva is able, regarding such points of training, to give rise to faith, reverence, and vigor, and to practice in reliance upon them."
This is called the bodhisattva’s skillful practice of the foundation of mindfulness regarding the training rules established by the Tathāgata.
What is the bodhisattva’s skillful practice of the foundation of mindfulness regarding the defilements of all afflictions and secondary afflictions?
"Noble son! A bodhisattva skillfully maintains mindfulness toward the defiled phenomena of the afflictions and secondary afflictions, considering: 'From what cause do they arise?
By what condition are they produced?'"
Thus, having completely relinquished such dependent origination and such dependently arisen phenomena,
this is called the bodhisattva’s skillful practice of the application of mindfulness regarding afflictions and secondary afflictions.
“Good son! When a bodhisattva accomplishes these ten kinds of dharmas, they constantly realize the state of samāhita-citta. Furthermore, good son!”
When a bodhisattva accomplishes ten dharmas, they accept rag-robes (pāṃśukūla). What are these ten?
First, their vow is firm and steadfast.
Second, being humble and self-effacing;
third, being free from weariness or rejection;
fourth, being without attachment.
Fifth, being free from faults and afflictions; sixth, seeing merits;
seventh, not praising oneself;
Eighth, not disparaging others;
ninth, being fully endowed with ethical discipline;
tenth, being closely approached by the devas.
“Good son! How is it that a bodhisattva’s vow is firm and steadfast, such that even the devas draw near to them? Good son!”

When a bodhisattva attains faith and is endowed with the perfect mental disposition, they give rise to profound faith toward all Buddhas; even for the sake of protecting their life, they do not violate their vows, nor do they waver from them.
Because their vows are firm and steadfast, they attain a humble mind.
Because their minds are humble, they become free from pride.
They collect all discarded rags that others have cast away, washing, mending, and stitching them without ever growing weary or abandoning the task.
For this reason, there is no attachment.

Although it is said that these robes are coarse and tattered, worn out, and have become soiled, and though they harbor many fleas and lice, one does not regard these as afflictions, but rather perceives their merits.

The refuse-rag robe is worn by sages, praised by the Tathāgata, and declared auspicious by the Buddha; it distances one from stinginess and greed, accords with the noble lineages, and through these causes and conditions, one attains freedom from self-praise and refrains from disparaging others, thereby achieving the perfection of the precepts.

Because they are fully endowed with the precepts, the devas descend to associate with them; they are constantly praised by all Buddhas and instructed by the great Bodhisattvas; furthermore, they are protected by humans and non-humans alike; they are held in the highest esteem and respected by Kṣatriyas and Brāhmaṇas in villages and cities; and they are always lauded by their fellow practitioners of the Brahma-faring life.
“Good son! When bodhisattvas accomplish these ten kinds of dharmas, they accept rag-robes.
The Bodhisattva Cessation-of-Coverings addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Since the minds of all bodhisattvas are vast and expansive, for what cause and condition do they engage in inferior practices?
The Buddha said:
“Good son! Only those bodhisattvas who possess great power are able to perform such inferior practices;
those without power cannot do so.”

Why is this? It is because the Bodhisattva of Great Power, in order to protect the world, is able to counteract afflictions before they arise; it is not the practice of those who are weak or inferior!
"Good son! What do you think? Are the Tathāgata’s practice and realization vast and great, or are they inferior?"
The Bodhisattva Nivaranaviskambhin addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
I am currently unable to respond to this.”
Why is this? Because the Tathāgata has nothing realized and no practice or understanding; since he does not perceive any phenomena, he is immeasurable.
How could I now possibly discern the superiority or inferiority of the Tathāgata’s conduct?
The Buddha said: “Good son, what do you think?”

Within the four continents, the Tathāgata manifests such inferior conduct before all sentient beings—devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, and so forth—and further praises the virtues of *dhūta* (ascetic purification) for the sake of such beings.
The Bodhisattva Nivaranaviskambhin addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
It is for the sake of subduing those who have newly set out in the Mahāyāna and to counteract the unarisen afflictions of all sentient beings that the Tathāgata manifests inferior ascetic practices.”
The Buddha said: "Good son! So it is, so it is!"
In the same way, bodhisattvas of great power, for the sake of taming sentient beings, wear rag-robes without any sense of inferiority.
"Good son! This is called the bodhisattva’s acceptance of rag robes. Furthermore, good son!"
Bodhisattvas who accomplish ten dharmas make use of the three robes. What are these ten?
The first is contentment.
Second, having few desires;
third, being free from longing;
fourth, having no accumulation.
Fifth, freedom from loss;
sixth, freedom from accumulation, loss, and affliction;
seventh, freedom from sorrow and distress.
Eighth, freedom from sorrow and lamentation;
ninth, absence of grasping;
tenth, through diligent cultivation, the exhaustion of all taints (*āsravas*).
"Good son! A bodhisattva knows contentment with inferior clothing;
because of this contentment, he is able to have few desires."
Because of having few desires, there is nothing sought after;
because there is nothing sought after, there has never been any accumulation;
because there is no accumulation, there is no loss.
Because there is no loss, there is no suffering or affliction;
because there is no suffering or affliction, there is no lamentation;
because there is no lamentation, there is also nothing that is experienced.
Because they have nothing to grasp, they are able to diligently practice until all outflows (*āsrava*) are exhausted. Good son,
this is called a bodhisattva accomplishing ten dharmas to obtain the use of the three robes.
"Furthermore, good son, if a bodhisattva accomplishes ten kinds of dharmas, they will not follow the practices of others. What are these ten?
First, not following the course of craving;
second, not following the course of anger;
third, not following the course of delusion.
Fourth, not following conduct that causes harm;
fifth, not following conduct characterized by stinginess and envy;
sixth, not following conduct of pride and conceit.
Seventh, not following the practice of seeking to have one's reputation and conduct known by others;
eighth, not following the practice of honoring gain and offerings;
ninth, not following the practice of showing reverence to the celestial Māras.
Tenth, they do not follow the conduct of arrogance.
Son of good family,
when a bodhisattva accomplishes these ten kinds of dharmas, he is therefore said to be one who does not follow others.
"Furthermore, noble son,
when a bodhisattva accomplishes ten dharmas, it is called 'begging for alms.
First, he practices begging for alms in order to gather and sustain all sentient beings."
Second, one practices alms-gathering for the sake of following the proper sequence;
third, one practices alms-gathering for the sake of avoiding weariness;
fourth, one practices alms-gathering for the sake of contentment.
Fifth, he goes on almsround for the sake of distribution;
sixth, he goes on almsround for the sake of non-indulgence;
seventh, he goes on almsround for the sake of knowing moderation.
Eighth, he practices alms-gathering for the sake of bringing wholesome qualities to manifestation;
ninth, he practices alms-gathering for the sake of perfecting the roots of goodness;
tenth, he practices alms-gathering for the sake of abandoning the notion of self-grasping.
“Good son! How does a bodhisattva gather and sustain sentient beings, even to the point of abandoning the notion of self-grasping? Good son!”

When a bodhisattva sees all sentient beings undergoing various sufferings and afflictions—even if they have accomplished even a slight root of virtue, yet that root of virtue is but temporary and not enduring—he practices alms-seeking for the sake of gathering in and benefiting such sentient beings.

When a bodhisattva enters a city or a village, he dwells in right mindfulness, maintains perfect deportment, keeps his sense faculties tranquil, remains neither haughty nor arrogant, and does not allow himself to become heedless.

Because they have attained this sequence, they never abandon those impoverished households to enter wealthy and noble families—namely, those of the Brahmins, the Kṣatriyas, or the great houses of householders.

When begging for alms in sequence, one proceeds from one household to the next until the task is completed, never deviating from this order. However, one must exclude those places where it is improper to beg for food—namely, the houses of fierce dogs, the houses of those who have recently given birth to a calf, and the houses of those of wicked character. Furthermore, one should avoid any place where men, women, boys, or girls might give rise to afflictions, as well as places of public reproach or the dwellings of various non-Buddhist sects; such locations should all be bypassed.

When a bodhisattva goes on his almsround in due order, he does not give rise to weariness or aversion, nor does he become fatigued; he harbors neither hatred nor attachment toward those sentient beings.
Through this lack of fatigue and weariness, he gives rise to contentment, accepting whatever is given—whether good or bad—in accordance with what is appropriate.

Once they have received food and returned to their dwelling, they should set aside their *pātra* bowls and robes, and before an image of the Tathāgata, or before a *caitya*, or before a *stūpa*, they should offer worship, show reverence, honor, and praise.
Divide the food obtained into four portions:
one portion to give to fellow practitioners of the holy life, one portion to give to the poor, one portion to give to sentient beings in the miserable realms, and one portion to eat oneself.

Although the bodhisattva eats, he is without greed for the food, without defilement, and without attachment; he accepts food solely for the sake of sustaining life, neither allowing the body to become emaciated nor allowing it to become heavy.
Why is this? If the body is excessively emaciated, one will be unable to cultivate wholesome qualities;
if the body is excessively heavy, it will increase sleepiness.
Once the Bodhisattva has eaten, he is able to cause the growth of wholesome qualities to manifest.
Through diligent cultivation, he is free from indolence and laziness, thereby attaining the full perfection of the provisions for enlightenment.
Because they are well able to mature the factors conducive to enlightenment (bodhipakṣadharma), they remain far removed from the grasping at a self.
Having attained the realization of non-self (anātman), they are able to relinquish their own bodies and flesh as gifts to sentient beings.
“Good son! When a bodhisattva accomplishes these ten kinds of dharmas, he is able to practice alms-gathering. Furthermore, good son!”
When Bodhisattvas accomplish ten dharmas, they attain [the state of] sitting in a single session. What are these ten?
First, when sitting at the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa), all Māras are struck with terror, yet he alone remains unmoved.
Second, having realized supramundane meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), he alone remains unmoved while all Māras are struck with terror;
third, having attained supramundane wisdom (*prajñā*), he alone remains unmoved while all Māras are struck with terror;
fourth, having attained supramundane knowledge (*jñāna*), he alone remains unmoved while all Māras are struck with terror.
Fifth, having realized its emptiness, he alone remains unmoved while all māras are struck with terror;
sixth, having realized the suchness of all phenomena, he alone remains unmoved while all māras are struck with terror;
seventh, having realized the path of perfect enlightenment, he alone remains unmoved while all māras are struck with terror.
Eighth, having realized the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), all māras are terrified, yet he alone remains unmoved;
ninth, having realized suchness (*tathatā*), all māras are terrified, yet he alone remains unmoved;
tenth, having attained omniscience (*sarvajñatā*), all māras are terrified, yet he alone remains unmoved.
As for what is called "sitting once," it refers to the seat of omniscience, which is also named the Dharma-seat.
Son of good family!
When a bodhisattva accomplishes these ten kinds of dharmas, they are able to attain sitting once.
"Furthermore, son of good family,
when a bodhisattva accomplishes ten dharmas, he attains the practice of eating a single meal. What are these ten?
First, one does not indulge in gluttonous eating;

second, one is without attachment to food, meaning that once food has been received, one should not further accept various flavors such as clarified butter, oil, or rock honey, whether at the proper time or otherwise;
third, if one sees another person receiving clarified butter and the like, one does not give rise to anger or vexation.
Fourth, when others receive ghee and such, one does not give rise to envy;
fifth, when a bodhisattva practices the practice of eating only once a day, if they encounter a serious illness, they should accept ghee and such;
sixth, when a bodhisattva practices the practice of eating only once a day, if there is a threat to life, they should eat ghee and such, and thus accept it.

Seventh, when a bodhisattva practices the practice of eating one meal a day, if there is an obstacle to the cultivation of wholesome dharmas such that they ought to consume ghee and other substances, they accept them;

eighth, when a bodhisattva practices the practice of eating one meal a day, if there are any of the three aforementioned obstacles and they have already consumed ghee and other substances, they feel no regret;
ninth, when a bodhisattva practices the practice of eating one meal a day, if there are the three obstacles such that they ought to consume ghee and other substances, they harbor no doubt.

Tenth, when a bodhisattva practices eating a single meal a day, if there should be three kinds of difficulties that require the consumption of ghee or other such substances, they should regard them as medicine.
Son of good family!
Because a bodhisattva accomplishes these ten dharmas, they attain the practice of eating a single meal a day.
"Furthermore, son of good family,
when a bodhisattva accomplishes ten dharmas, he attains the state of an araṇya-dweller. What are these ten?
First, long-abiding in the holy life;
second, attaining skillfulness in the Vinaya;
third, the perfection of the sense faculties.
Fourth, being fully endowed with extensive learning;
fifth, being skillful in expounding the essential points of the Dharma;
sixth, being free from the grasping of "mine-ness."
Seventh, being like a wild animal;
eighth, dwelling at a distance from others;
ninth, abiding in tranquility.
Tenth, he is without weariness or detachment and free from hindrances and obscurations. "Good son,
how does a bodhisattva dwell long in the holy life, even to the point of not becoming weary of or detached from the araṇya?"

"Good son! When a bodhisattva leaves home to enter the homeless life, they purify the three karmas within the Vinaya, fulfill the precepts (śīla), possess great skillfulness by nature, and delight in practicing dignified deportment."

Regarding the rules for seniority and juniority taught by the Buddha, they are able to understand and realize them spontaneously without depending on others, attain skillfulness in the teachings and their meanings, and further discern the points of observance and transgression.
Seeing those who uphold the precepts, they are able to give rise to reverence;
seeing those who violate the precepts, they are able to abandon them.
Furthermore, over a long period of time, they repeatedly repent their transgressions, feeling remorse for the evil deeds they have committed, never concealing them until the end.

Furthermore, they are able to discern that the offenses committed are of superior, middling, or inferior degrees, and they are also able to discern the long or short duration of time required for the ripening results (*vipākaphala*) of the evil karma created to manifest.

Because the Bodhisattva practices with purity, he attains the perfection of the sense faculties—his faculty of sight is undiminished, his faculty of hearing is unimpaired, and his physical limbs are complete—and only then is he fit to dwell in that forest hermitage (āraṇya).
It is solitary and still, free from people and disturbances;
alms are easily obtained, being neither too far nor too near;
there are many trees, and the flowers, fruits, branches, and leaves are all in full and flourishing bloom.
Pure and beautiful water is available without labor;
the caves and dwellings are peaceful and secure, free from wild beasts;
the mountain paths are secluded and quiet, making travel and residence easy—such places as these are fit for reliance.
Having relied upon such a place, the bodhisattva constantly practices day and night during the three periods according to what was previously recited and heard;
the sound of the recitation is neither coarse nor subtle;
and they skillfully restrain the sense faculties so that they do not undergo transformation.
All objects of enjoyment are entirely pure;
one thoroughly understands the distinct characteristics of all phenomena;
one abandons mental torpor and contemplates the principles of the teachings.
His mind remains unmoving and does not engage with external objects.
"If a king, a prince, a kṣatriya, a brāhmaṇa, or others should come to the bodhisattva's dwelling, the bodhisattva, having seen them, greets them respectfully and says:
'Welcome, Great King!'"
"Please take your seat upon what has been prepared!
When the king sits, the bodhisattva also sits;
when the king does not sit, the bodhisattva also stands.
Observing that the king’s faculties are agitated, the Bodhisattva should immediately praise him, saying:

"Great King, you are truly able to benefit others; within your kingdom dwell many śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas who maintain the precepts, possess merit, are learned, and are wise. There are no thieves nor officials who would oppress or deceive the people."
Furthermore, observing that the faculties of the king and his retinue are tranquil, peaceful, and well-subdued, the Bodhisattva should at that time expound upon various dharmas for them.
If the king does not delight in hearing various dharmas, the Bodhisattva should then preach the dharma of wearying detachment (*nirveda*) in accordance with his disposition.
If the king does not wish to hear the dharma of wearying detachment, he should instead be taught the profound and vast dharma of the Tathāgata, as well as its great majestic power.
In this manner, for other Brahmins and Kṣatriyas who come from human villages and settlements, he likewise teaches the Dharma as is appropriate.
"Because the Bodhisattva is possessed of great learning, he is able to preach the Dharma such that all who hear it have their hearts filled with joy and conceive pure faith toward the Bodhisattva."
By being able to preach the Dharma and cultivate wholesome qualities, one counteracts and eliminates the afflictions;
furthermore, by the power of extensive learning (*bahuśruta*), one attains freedom from the grasping at a self (*ātma-grāha*).

Moreover, because one is further able to distance oneself from the fear of self-grasping, one is neither startled nor terrified in forest hermitages (*āraṇya*) and attains fearlessness (*vaiśāradya*).
When a bodhisattva dwells in an araṇya, they observe directly that there is nothing to which they may cling or be attached; this is not like wild beasts who lack such observation.
When a bodhisattva dwells in an araṇya, they have no fear and no afflictions; this is not like wild beasts who are constantly afraid of being harmed.

When a bodhisattva dwells in an araṇya, they distance themselves from human habitation—not because their minds are distracted by men, women, boys, or girls in the village, nor for the sake of protecting their lives like wild beasts—but rather for the sake of upholding the true Dharma and for the sake of non-attachment.

Because the bodhisattva dwells in seclusion, they attain manifest tranquility; seeing that forest hermitages possess great merit, and further seeing them as peaceful, free from weariness, and free from obscuration, they cultivate all dharmas while dwelling in the forest hermitage.
This is called the bodhisattva’s long-term abiding in the holy life, up to and including being neither weary nor concealing it.
Son of good family!
When a bodhisattva accomplishes these ten kinds of dharmas, they attain dwelling in an araṇya.
"Furthermore, son of good family,
when a bodhisattva accomplishes ten qualities, he is able to sit beneath a tree. What are these ten?
First, one must not sit under a tree that is too close to a village;
second, one must not sit under a tree that is too far from a village;
third, one must not sit under a tree in a dense thicket of thorns.
Fourth, one must not sit under a tree near a thicket of creeping vines or in a place frequented by monkeys;
fifth, one must not sit under a tree with withered leaves;
sixth, one must not sit under a tree where monkeys dwell.
Seventh, one must not sit under a tree that is frequented by many birds;
eighth, one must not sit under a tree where predatory beasts dwell;
ninth, one must not sit under a tree situated near a road.
Tenth, one must not sit under a tree in a place frequented by coarse and wicked people.
A bodhisattva should sit under a tree in a location free from obstacles and difficulties, so that the body attains pliancy and the mind remains constantly joyful.
"Noble son! When a bodhisattva accomplishes these ten dharmas, they attain the practice of sitting at the foot of a tree.
Furthermore, noble son!"
If a bodhisattva accomplishes ten dharmas, they are able to sit in the open air. What are these ten?
First, during spring, summer, autumn, and winter, one should not rely on sitting in places near walls.
Second, one should not rely on sitting beneath forest trees;
third, one must not rely on sitting in places overgrown with straw, chaff, or grass;
fourth, one must not rely on sitting in mountain clefts or rocky hollows.
Fifth, one must not sit in a hollow by a riverbank;
sixth, one must not sit while shielding oneself from the cold with an object;
seventh, one must not sit while shielding oneself from the wind with an object.
Eighth, one must not sit with an object shielding oneself from the rain;
ninth, one must not sit with an object shielding oneself from the heat;
tenth, one must not sit with an object supporting oneself against the dew.
If a bodhisattva is sitting in the open air and encounters various illnesses or lacks physical strength, they should enter a monastery and form this thought:

"The Tathāgata, wishing to counteract and eliminate the afflictions (*kleśa*), has extensively taught the merits of the ascetic practices (*dhūta-guṇa*) in various places. Although I am now within a monastery, my mind shall not find pleasure therein nor become attached; I shall diligently cultivate the True Dharma to counteract and eliminate the afflictions."
He reflects thus: "I dwell in this monastery solely for the sake of receiving the offerings of various donors, not for my own nourishment;
therefore, regarding my own person, I maintain the perception of it as being in the open air."
“Good son! When a bodhisattva accomplishes these ten kinds of dharmas, they attain the practice of sitting in the open air. Furthermore, good son!”
When Bodhisattvas accomplish ten dharmas, they attain the practice of dwelling in cemeteries (śmāśānika). What are these ten?
First, Bodhisattvas develop a profound sense of weary detachment toward pleasant dwellings.
Second, all bodhisattvas always maintain the perception of death at all times;
third, all bodhisattvas are constantly able to maintain the perception of what remains;
fourth, all bodhisattvas constantly contemplate the parts of the body and maintain the perception of it being bloody.
Fifth, all bodhisattvas constantly contemplate the parts of the body, giving rise to the perception of blueness;
sixth, all bodhisattvas constantly contemplate the parts of the body, giving rise to the perception of pus;
seventh, all bodhisattvas constantly contemplate the body, giving rise to the perception of bloatedness.
Eighth, all bodhisattvas constantly contemplate the body, giving rise to the perception of it as parched and withered;
ninth, all bodhisattvas constantly contemplate the body, giving rise to the perception of its dissolution and dispersal;
tenth, all bodhisattvas constantly contemplate the body, giving rise to the perception of it as a skeleton.

“Good son! When a bodhisattva sits in a cemetery, for the sake of benefiting and having compassion for all sentient beings, he dwells in a mind of loving-kindness; furthermore, for the sake of maintaining pure precepts and perfecting proper conduct, he does not give rise to the thought of eating meat.”
Why is this? Son of good family!

Cemeteries are everywhere inhabited by non-human beings; if they see a bodhisattva eating meat, they will conceive impure faith and give rise to afflictive thoughts. For this reason, a bodhisattva should not eat meat.

"Noble son! When a bodhisattva dwelling among burial mounds enters a monastery, he should first pay homage to the stūpas of the Tathāgata; next, he should pay homage to the elder bhikṣus; and finally, he should inquire after the health of the junior bhikṣus. He must not sit upon the beds, mats, or other furnishings belonging to the Saṃgha, but should remain standing with reverence."
Why is this? Son of good family!

Because a bodhisattva wishes to conform to the world and protect sentient beings, he does not sit upon the beds, mats, or other items belonging to the Saṃgha. A bodhisattva dwelling among tombs conforms to the noble ones; if he were to contravene worldly custom, he would not be acting as a noble one.

If a bhikṣu offers his own seat and invites a bodhisattva to sit upon it, the Śmaśānika Bodhisattva should carefully examine that bhikṣu’s intention to ensure there will be no subsequent regret and that the rest of the saṅgha will not give rise to anger or resentment; only then, maintaining a sense of inferiority like that of a candāla youth, should he sit upon this seat.
"Noble son! When a bodhisattva accomplishes these ten kinds of dharmas, they attain the practice of dwelling in cemeteries.
Furthermore, noble son!"
If a bodhisattva accomplishes ten dharmas, they are able to attain constant sitting (*prahāṇa*). What are the ten?
First, one sits constantly so as not to afflict the body.
Second, one sits constantly so as not to disturb the mind;
third, one sits constantly so as not to succumb to drowsiness;
fourth, one sits constantly so as not to become weary or disheartened.
Fifth, one sits constantly for the sake of fulfilling the provisions for awakening;
sixth, one sits constantly for the sake of one-pointedness of mind;
seventh, one sits constantly for the sake of realizing the path that stands before one.
Eighth, one sits constantly for the sake of proceeding to the bodhimanda;
ninth, one sits constantly for the sake of benefiting all sentient beings;
tenth, one sits constantly out of the desire to eternally sever all afflictions.
"Noble son! When a bodhisattva accomplishes these ten dharmas, they are able to achieve constant sitting.
Furthermore, noble son!"
If a bodhisattva accomplishes ten dharmas, they attain the practice of sitting wherever a seat is spread. What are these ten?
First, they have no attachment or craving for their bedding and seats.
Second, one never personally prepares bedding or seating;
third, one does not send others to prepare bedding or seating;
fourth, one does not manifest signs to cause others to prepare bedding or seating.
Fifth, one should sit immediately upon whatever grass or leaves are available there;
sixth, one should abandon and not sit in places where there are many venomous snakes, mosquitoes, gadflies, or holes;

seventh, when a Bodhisattva wishes to lie down, he should lie on his right side with his feet stacked, covering his body with his Dharma robes, maintaining right mindfulness and right awareness while forming a clear perception.
Eighth, he lies on his right side and does not indulge in sleep;
ninth, he does so solely for the sake of nourishing the great elements and, ultimately, for the sake of sustaining life;
tenth, at all times and in all circumstances, the Bodhisattva causes wholesome qualities to manifest before him.
"Noble son! When a bodhisattva accomplishes these ten dharmas, they attain the practice of sitting wherever a seat is spread.
Furthermore, noble son!"
When a bodhisattva accomplishes ten dharmas, they become one who practices yoga. What are these ten?
First, being able to constantly practice the meditation on impurity;
Second, being able to constantly cultivate loving-kindness and compassion;
third, being able to constantly cultivate dependent origination;
fourth, constantly cultivating skillfulness regarding all faults and afflictions.
Fifth, they are able to constantly cultivate emptiness;
sixth, they are able to constantly cultivate signlessness;
seventh, they are able to constantly cultivate yoga.
Eighth, they are able to constantly and diligently practice;
ninth, they attain freedom from regret regarding their transgressions;
tenth, they are able to fulfill the precepts.
“Good son! How is it that a bodhisattva is able to cultivate the meditation on impurity? Good son!
The bodhisattva dwells alone in quiet seclusion, with body upright and relaxed, sitting cross-legged;
he observes directly before him, his mind filled with profound wearying detachment;
abiding in right mindfulness, his mind does not wander toward external objects, and he reflects thus:

"Whatever food and drink exists among human beings—whether pure or impure, excellent or inferior, flavorful or flavorless—once it has been consumed and touched by the body's fire, all becomes impure, putrid, and loathsome; yet worldly fools do not conform to this reality, but instead indulge in and become stained by attachment to them."

We noble ones, relying on the Dharma of the Vinaya, are able to observe our own bodies with right wisdom; we neither give rise to defiled attachment nor indulge in craving, yet still our minds do not give rise to revulsion.
"For this reason, a bodhisattva is able to cultivate the meditation on impurity.
How does a bodhisattva cultivate loving-kindness and compassion? Good son!"
That is to say, when bodhisattvas dwell alone in a secluded and quiet place, sitting in meditative retreat with their bodies upright and relaxed in the full lotus posture;
they observe directly before them with a mind of profound renunciation,
abide in right mindfulness without the mind wandering toward external objects, and reflect as follows:
"Many sentient beings frequently give rise to anger and malice, performing unwholesome deeds.
Furthermore, they constantly associate with unwholesome persons and, without cause, conceive thoughts of enmity toward me, performing such actions either in the past, the future, or the present."
"My intention is to cause all those sentient beings to sever every instance of anger and malice they have aroused, and to cause them to sit at the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa).
Such matters are not merely words; they are truly the profound aspiration of a bodhisattva.
Contemplating in accordance with this is called a bodhisattva’s ability to cultivate loving-kindness and compassion.
How does a bodhisattva cultivate dependent origination?
It means that when a bodhisattva gives rise to thoughts of craving or anger, they reflect as follows:

"From me arise states such as greed and hatred; since the 'I' that gives rise to them is produced from conditions, the greed, hatred, and the objects of greed and so forth that are produced must likewise arise from conditions."
"What wise person would give rise to attachment to a self within these falsely imagined phenomena produced by multiple conditions?
This is called a bodhisattva being able to cultivate dependent origination.
"How does a bodhisattva become skillful in regard to all faults and afflictions?"
This means that bodhisattvas constantly practice for the sake of severing their own faults and afflictions.
If others' mental continuums possess faults and afflictions, and they are capable of being taught, the bodhisattva causes them to sever them;
if they are not capable of being taught, the bodhisattva should simply abandon them and depart.
What are the faults?

They consist in being by nature disrespectful toward the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha; toward the precepts, the noble ones, and those who lead the holy life; and toward the world’s elders and juniors, both high and low.
This is a fault: relying on one's own person, one constantly gives rise to pride and treats others with contempt.

One becomes attached to the various objects present before them, turns their back on nirvāṇa, and gives rise to the view of a self, the view of a sentient being, the view of a life-principle, the view of a person, the view of annihilation, and the view of emptiness; they cling to the nature of permanence and impermanence.

They do not serve any of the noble ones, but instead associate with fools; they distance themselves from those who uphold the precepts and honor those who violate them; they abandon virtuous beings and draw near to those who are unvirtuous.
They slander the profound collection of sūtras and constantly harbor fear and dread toward this gateway of the treasury.
They are indolent and lazy, holding themselves in contempt;
by nature they lack eloquence, and their majestic radiance is inferior.
They repent for that which should not be repented of,
yet are unable to repent of that which should be repented of.
They are constantly bound by the fetters of the hindrances and entanglements, pursued by delusions, deceptions, and flattery, and shrouded by dullness and drowsiness.

By nature they always delight in and respect gain and offerings; they are greedily attached to their lineage and crave their kinsmen; they take pleasure in countries and assemblies, abandoning the Dharma they have received and upheld;
by nature they delight in approaching worldly incantations, while constantly feeling weary of and detached from the supramundane True Dharma.
They habitually practice what is unwholesome and do not cultivate various virtues.
They praise the faults of those who have gone forth, and they praise women, men, boys, girls, and all those of other sects.
They do not delight in dwelling in forest hermitages;
they do not know moderation in eating;
and they do not delight in associating with their venerable elders.
When reciting and practicing, they set their own limits;
regarding matters outside their sphere of practice, they do not perceive faults or evils.
By nature, they lack reverence for even subtle *śīla*, and their minds feel no alarm or dread toward minor transgressions.
Seeing those who are ignorant, with dull and obscured faculties, they praise them as being tranquil;
seeing those who possess wisdom, with clear and sharp faculties, they dismiss them as being restless and agitated.
They act with arrogance and hold perverted attachments;
by nature they delight in coarse speech and cling to agreeable or disagreeable forms as they encounter them.
When they see one who gives rise to anger, they do not produce a mind of loving-kindness.
Seeing those who suffer, they do not give rise to compassion;
seeing those who are ill, they have no mind of weary detachment;
seeing those who die, they feel no alarm or fear.
They do not seek liberation from the place of burning;

they do not examine the body, they do not examine ethical discipline, and they do not examine the nature of phenomena regarding what has been done, what is to be done, and what is currently being done.

One should not engage in conceptualization where it is inappropriate to do so; one should not give rise to deliberation where it is inappropriate to do so; one should not harbor aspirations where they are inappropriate.
One perceives that which is not liberation as liberation;
one perceives that which is not the path as the path.
To claim one has attained what has not been attained;
to fail to do what ought to be done;
to be addicted to unwholesome dharmas and to abandon the categories of the wholesome.
They disparage the Mahāyāna and praise the Hīnayāna;
they revile those individuals who have deep faith in the Mahāyāna and praise those individuals who have deep faith in the Hīnayāna.
They constantly engage in contentious debate and perpetually give rise to strife and litigation;
by nature they harbor coarseness and ferocity, delighting in harsh speech;
they are arrogant and loquacious, severe, cutting, violent, and cruel.
Greedy and deceitful, their nature is full of falsehood;
their speech lacks coherence, and they delight in frivolous proliferation.
These are their faults and afflictions.
"Once a bodhisattva has attained skill in these faults and afflictions, they diligently cultivate emptiness, desiring to abandon all conceptual proliferations (*prapañca*).

Although the bodhisattva thus diligently cultivates emptiness, their mind may still scatter and find delight in dwelling upon this or that object. As the bodhisattva searches everywhere for those various objects, they find that their intrinsic nature is empty and cannot be apprehended."

Since the nature of the apprehended object is empty, the nature of the apprehending mind is likewise non-existent; having realized that the observed mind and its objects are empty, one understands that the essence of the observing wisdom is truly non-existent.
When a bodhisattva contemplates emptiness, they cultivate signlessness.
Although the bodhisattva diligently cultivates signlessness, various signs nevertheless continue to appear before them.
Furthermore, the bodhisattva contemplates that the essential nature of all present phenomena is empty.

Since such phenomena are thus unapprehendable, he observes that the characteristics of the internal body are likewise unapprehendable, and even the application of mindfulness to the body is unapprehendable.
The mind does not cling to external signs, and even the essential nature of the foundations of mindfulness cannot be apprehended.
The bodhisattva, having relinquished such signs, is constantly able to arouse the aspiration for cultivation.

When a bodhisattva cultivates various samādhis, they abide uninterruptedly within their objective spheres; that is to say, one-pointedness of mind is śamatha, while observing things as they truly are is vipaśyanā.
When a bodhisattva cultivates samāhita, the mind becomes free from regret and further experiences joy.
Why is this? Because their ethical discipline is pure.
Because the precepts of the bodhisattvas are pure, they attain yoga.
Those who are fully endowed with the precepts increase yoga and cultivate yoga;
therefore, they are called "those who have attained yoga."
“Good son! A bodhisattva who accomplishes these ten kinds of dharmas is able to practice yoga.
Furthermore, good son!”
If a bodhisattva accomplishes ten kinds of dharmas, they are able to uphold the Sūtra Piṭaka. What are these ten?
First, they listen to and receive the teachings for the sake of guarding the true Dharma, not for the sake of material wealth.
Second, they listen and receive [the teachings] for the sake of guarding and upholding them, not for the sake of gain and offerings;
third, they listen and receive them for the sake of ensuring that the lineage of the Triple Gem is not severed, not seeking worship or honor;
fourth, they listen and receive them for the sake of correctly gathering and guiding those sentient beings who have set out upon the Mahāyāna, not for the sake of fame or praise.
Fifth, they listen and receive [the teachings] for the sake of benefiting all sentient beings who are without support or refuge;
sixth, they listen and receive them for the sake of bringing peace and happiness to sentient beings who are afflicted by suffering;
seventh, they listen and receive them so that those sentient beings who lack the eye of wisdom may obtain the eye of wisdom.
Eighth, because they listen to and receive [the teachings] in order to expound the path of the Śrāvaka vehicle for those sentient beings who have set out upon the Śrāvaka vehicle;
ninth, because they listen to and receive [the teachings] in order to expound the path of the Mahāyāna for those sentient beings who have set out upon the Mahāyāna;
tenth, because they listen to and receive [the teachings] for the sake of realizing unsurpassed wisdom themselves, and not for the sake of seeking inferior vehicles.
"Noble son! If a bodhisattva accomplishes these ten kinds of dharmas, they are able to uphold the Sūtra Piṭaka.
Furthermore, noble son!"
If a bodhisattva accomplishes ten kinds of dharmas, they are able to uphold the Vinaya Piṭaka. What are these ten?
First, they are able to thoroughly understand the Vinaya;
Second, they are able to understand the meaning of the Vinaya;
third, they are able to understand the profound principles of the Vinaya;
fourth, they are able to understand the subtleties of the Vinaya.
Fifth, being able to discern what should be done and what should not be done;
sixth, being able to discern transgressions of essential nature (*svabhāva-āpatti*);
seventh, being able to discern transgressions of formal designation (*prajñapti-āpatti*).
Eighth, he is able to thoroughly understand the origins of the training in the *prātimokṣa*;
ninth, he is able to thoroughly understand the *vinaya* of the śrāvakas;
tenth, he is able to thoroughly understand the *vinaya* of the bodhisattvas.
"Noble son! When a bodhisattva accomplishes these ten kinds of dharmas, they are able to uphold the Vinaya-piṭaka.
Furthermore, noble son!"

When bodhisattvas accomplish ten dharmas, they are able to skillfully observe the rules of conduct within their spheres of activity and become fully endowed with dignified decorum (*īryāpatha*). What are these ten?
First, they skillfully train in all the precepts (*śikṣāpada*) of the śrāvakas;
Second, they have well trained in all the training rules of the pratyekabuddhas;
third, they have well trained in all the training rules of the bodhisattvas;
fourth, having attained proficiency in all these training rules, they are able to maintain excellent conduct and their practice is complete.
Fifth, having fully perfected their conduct and observances, they are able to abandon all that is unbecoming of a śramaṇa;
sixth, by virtue of these causes and conditions, the bodhisattva does not frequent improper places or engage at improper times;
seventh, having fully perfected the dignified deportment and observances of a śramaṇa, neither śramaṇas nor brahmins are able to unjustly revile or disparage them.
Eighth, by means of this, the bodhisattva is also able to cause others to skillfully train in all such rules of training;
ninth, the bodhisattva’s conduct and standards are perfected, having attained dignity and tranquility, and being fully endowed with dignified deportment;
tenth, having accomplished such deportment, they are free from hypocrisy.
"Noble son! When bodhisattvas accomplish these ten dharmas, they are able to skillfully regulate their conduct within the spheres of activity and are fully endowed with dignified deportment.
The Sūtra of the Precious Rain, Scroll Eight.
The Sutra of the Precious Rain Spoken by the Buddha, Scroll Nine. Translated by the Tang Dynasty Indian Tripiṭaka Master Dharmaruci.

"Furthermore, noble son, when a bodhisattva accomplishes ten dharmas, they become free from stinginess and envy. What are these ten? First, they give away their own body; second, they give away their wealth and possessions; third, they give away their roots of goodness; fourth, they give away their Dharma-teachings; fifth, they give away their fearlessness; sixth, they give away their limbs and joints; seventh, they give away their head and eyes; eighth, they give away their heart and blood; ninth, they give away their marrow and bones; and tenth, they give away their life-force. Noble son, when a bodhisattva accomplishes these ten dharmas, they become free from stinginess and envy."
What are the ten? First, one becomes a donor oneself;
second, one is able to exhort others to practice giving.
Third, being able to praise giving;
fourth, congratulating and comforting others for their giving;
fifth, praising other donors so that they may attain joy.
Sixth, when seeing others being given gifts, one never gives rise to the thought: "Give only to me and not to others; such things should belong to me alone.
Seventh, the Bodhisattva generates the resolve to bring benefit to all sentient beings, meaning he is able to provide them with the necessities for sustaining life.
Eighth, the Bodhisattva generates the resolve to bring happiness to all sentient beings, meaning he brings about all forms of happiness, both mundane and supramundane.
Ninth, I shall diligently cultivate practice for the sake of benefiting all sentient beings;
tenth, I should give rise to a mind that relinquishes stinginess and envy.
"Noble son! When bodhisattvas accomplish these ten kinds of dharmas, they are able to forever leave behind stinginess and envy.
Furthermore, noble son!"
When a bodhisattva accomplishes ten dharmas, they are able to attain a mind of equanimity toward all sentient beings. What are these ten?
First, attaining skillful means of equanimity toward all sentient beings;
Second, attaining a mind free from obstruction toward all sentient beings;
third, attaining a mind free from affliction or harm toward all sentient beings;
fourth, practicing generosity.
Fifth, the cultivation of ethical discipline;
sixth, the cultivation of patience;
seventh, the cultivation of right effort;
Eighth, the cultivation of meditative concentration;
ninth, the cultivation of wisdom for the sake of benefiting all sentient beings;
tenth, the accumulation of the causes of omniscience.
“The bodhisattva’s accumulation never relies upon two types of mind, for it is accumulated equally and universally for the sake of all sentient beings.

If a bodhisattva can accumulate in this manner, they will swiftly realize the nature of phenomena (dharmatā), be able to emerge from all the heat and affliction of birth and death, and also enable others to transcend birth and death.”
The Bodhisattva is impartial toward all sentient beings; his mind harbors neither craving nor attachment, nor does it harbor hatred or envy. Good son!

It is like a householder who has six sons, all of whom are handsome and pleasing to their father’s heart; the householder, out of compassion, nurtures them with an impartial mind, free from partiality.
However, those sons were young, foolish, and lacked skill; suddenly, a fire broke out in the elder’s house, at which time the sons were each in different places.
“Good son! What do you think? At that time, did the elder have the thought, ‘I am causing my sons to exit one after another’?
Cessation-of-Coverings Bodhisattva replied:
"No, World-Honored One! Why is this?
"Because that householder’s mind was impartial, he allowed his sons to emerge one after another as they were ready.
The Buddha said, "So it is, so it is!"
The Bodhisattva is likewise!
All sentient beings dwell within the burning house of birth and death; they are deluded and ignorant, lacking wisdom and skillful means.
Such sentient beings reside separately within each of the six realms of existence.
By means of skillful means, the bodhisattva causes all beings to attain liberation and further establishes them in the realm of tranquility.
Son of good family!
When a bodhisattva accomplishes these ten kinds of dharmas, they attain a mind of equanimity toward all sentient beings.
"Furthermore, noble son,
when a bodhisattva accomplishes ten dharmas, they attain skillful means for making offerings to all Tathāgatas. What are these ten?
First, making offerings through the Dharma is to make offerings to all Tathāgatas, not through material wealth;
second, practicing according to the teachings is to make offerings to all Tathāgatas, not through material wealth;
third, acting for the benefit and happiness of all sentient beings is to make offerings to all Tathāgatas, not through material wealth.
Fourth, for the sake of gathering all sentient beings, one makes an offering to all Tathāgatas that is not an offering of material wealth;
fifth, because whatever actions one performs are all for the benefit of sentient beings, one makes an offering to all Tathāgatas that is not an offering of material wealth;
sixth, by not abandoning one's vows, one makes an offering to all Tathāgatas that is not an offering of material wealth.
Seventh, not abandoning the bodhisattva’s activities is itself making offerings to all Tathāgatas; it is not an offering of material wealth.
Eighth, because of reflecting according to reality, this is itself making offerings to all Tathāgatas; it is not an offering of material wealth.
Ninth, because the mind is free from weariness, this is itself making offerings to all Tathāgatas; it is not an offering of material wealth.
Tenth, because of not abandoning the bodhicitta, one thereby makes an offering to all Tathāgatas; this is not an offering of material wealth.
What is meant by "Dharma-offering"?
"Good son! Since the Dharma-body is itself all Tathāgatas, once one has made the offering of Dharma, one has thereby made an offering to all Tathāgatas.
What is meant by 'practicing according to what is taught'?"
This means that by practicing as taught, one becomes a Tathāgata.
How does this bring benefit and happiness to all sentient beings?
It means that the appearance of a Tathāgata is for the sake of bringing benefit and happiness to all sentient beings.
What is meant by "gathering in all sentient beings"?
It refers to the fact that the Tathāgata appears in the world to gather in all sentient beings.
What is meant by "benefiting all sentient beings"?
Because all the deeds one performs are for the sake of benefiting all sentient beings,
how could one abandon one's vow?
For if one abandons the vow, one will be unable to benefit all sentient beings.
What is meant by not abandoning the bodhisattva’s activities?
If one were to turn away from the bodhisattva’s activities, one would be unable to make offerings to all Tathāgatas.
What is reflection in accordance with reality?
It is that which is not improper reflection, for it enables one to make offerings to all Tathāgatas.
What is mental indefatigability?
This means that if the mind becomes weary, one will be unable to make offerings to all Tathāgatas.
How can one not abandon the bodhicitta?
For by abandoning the bodhicitta, one will be unable to make offerings to all Tathāgatas.
Why is this? Good son!

Because it is for the sake of benefiting sentient beings that bodhisattvas shall attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi; if there were no sentient beings, bodhisattvas would not manifest equal enlightenment.
Therefore, by means of the offering of the Dharma, one immediately makes an offering to all Tathāgatas, rather than through material offerings. Noble son,
when a bodhisattva accomplishes these ten kinds of dharmas, they attain skillfulness in serving and making offerings to all Tathāgatas.
"Furthermore, son of good family,
when a bodhisattva accomplishes ten kinds of dharmas, he is able to subdue his pride. What are these ten?
First, when a bodhisattva leaves home to renounce the world, all his relatives abandon him as if he were a corpse; by this cause and condition, he is able to subdue his pride.
Second, I have altered my physical appearance, donned robes of dyed color, and my outward form differs from that of the laity; by this cause and condition, he is able to subdue his pride.
Third, I have shaved off my hair and beard, hold an alms bowl in hand, and wander from house to house begging for food; by this cause and condition, he is able to subdue his pride.
Fourth, when wandering from house to house for alms like the son of a *caṇḍāla*, one gives rise to a sense of inferiority; for this reason, one is able to subdue the pride of self-conceit.
Fifth, because one begs food from others, one’s life depends on others; one should regard one’s own body as a beggar, and by this means, one is able to subdue the pride of self-conceit.

Sixth, although the food one receives may be treated with contempt by others, one remains without weariness or fatigue in the act of begging; by this means, one is able to subdue the pride of self-conceit.
Seventh, by making offerings to the venerable Ācāryas and regarding them as fields of merit, one is thereby able to subdue pride;
eighth, by maintaining my conduct according to the rules of dignified deportment so that my fellow practitioners of the holy life may all see it and rejoice, one is thereby able to subdue pride;
ninth, by aspiring to attain the Buddha-dharma which I have not yet attained, one is thereby able to subdue pride.
Tenth, I am able to constantly give rise to patience toward those sentient beings who are angry and harmful; by this means, I am able to subdue my pride.
"Noble son! When a bodhisattva accomplishes these ten kinds of dharmas, they are able to subdue the pride of 'I' and 'mine.
Furthermore, noble son!"
If a bodhisattva accomplishes ten kinds of dharmas, they are able to attain pure faith. What are these ten?
First, because they are fully endowed with the causes and conditions of roots of goodness planted in previous lives, they give rise to merit and virtue.
Second, attaining right view without relying on the instruction of a teacher;
third, abandoning deceitful and crooked conduct to achieve the fulfillment of aspiration;
fourth, being free from the nature of perversity to attain a straightforward mind.
Fifth, by virtue of having sharp faculties, one attains the perfection of wisdom;
sixth, because the pure mind flows in uninterrupted succession, one is able to abandon the hindrance of sleep;
seventh, one abandons evil associates and relies upon virtuous friends.
Eighth, seeking the wholesome Dharma without giving rise to pride;
ninth, expounding the true Dharma without inverted grasping;
tenth, being able to know the vast majesty and virtue of the Tathāgata through expansive faith.
“Good son! When bodhisattvas accomplish these ten kinds of dharmas, they attain pure faith.
The Bodhisattva Citta-nivaraṇa-viṣkambhin addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
I wish to hear even a small portion of the meaning regarding the vast majestic power of the Tathāgata.
The Buddha said:
“Good son! You should listen attentively and reflect upon it well!
I shall now proclaim for you a small portion of the meaning of the Tathāgata’s vast and majestic power!”
Śamathakara addressed the Buddha, saying:
“Excellent, World-Honored One!
We wish and desire to hear it.”
“Good son! The Tathāgata has accomplished great compassion that is impartial, universally for the sake of all sentient beings.
The great compassion the Tathāgata arouses toward a single sentient being is no different from that which he arouses toward all sentient beings.”
Although the Tathāgata’s great compassion pervades the realm of sentient beings and the entirety of space, the limit of that great compassion is truly unattainable.
Son of good family!
The Tathāgata has accomplished great compassion that is not shared with any śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, or bodhisattvas.
When the Tathāgata gives rise to great compassion for a single sentient being, it is no different from his doing so for all sentient beings.
Son of good family!

The Tathāgata has accomplished inexhaustible teaching of the Dharma; throughout immeasurable kalpas and immeasurable asaṃkhyeya aeons, he can instantaneously expound for all sentient beings through various names and distinct principles, yet the Dharma taught by the Buddha remains inexhaustible.
"Good son! The Tathāgata has accomplished immeasurable inquiries and challenges, being able to answer and explain them. Good son!"

Suppose all sentient beings, even including those merely counted among the category of sentient beings, were to question the Buddha simultaneously, each with distinct sets of names, phrases, and syllables; the Tathāgata would be able to answer and explain them all in a single kṣaṇa, a lava, or a muhūrta, without ever reaching exhaustion.
"Good son! The Tathāgata has accomplished the sphere of activity of meditative concentration and attained non-obstruction. Good son!"

Suppose all sentient beings were to abide in the stage of the bodhisattvas of the ten bhūmis, and suppose these bodhisattvas were all simultaneously to enter immeasurable hundreds of thousands of samādhis; even if they remained in those various meditative absorptions for immeasurable hundreds of thousands of kalpas, each entering different concentrations, they would truly be unable to know the limit or reach of the Buddha’s samādhi and the scope of his sphere of activity.

"Good son! The Tathāgata has accomplished immeasurable form-bodies (*rūpakāya*). If there are sentient beings who should be taught and transformed by means of the Tathāgata’s form-body, the Tathāgata is able, in a single kṣaṇa, or a single lava, or a single muhūrta, to manifest the various marks of the Tathāgata’s form-body to each of those sentient beings."

If there are sentient beings who ought to see the physical forms of various distinct classes of sentient beings, the Tathāgata is able, in a single kṣaṇa, a lava, or a muhūrta, to manifest before each of those beings the physical forms of those various distinct classes of sentient beings.

“Good son! The objects perceived by the Tathāgata’s eye are of immeasurable kinds. Those sentient beings whom the divine eyes of others see, but whose fleshly eyes do not see—sentient beings of such types fill worlds that exceed all calculation and thought. The World-Honored One perceives all those sentient beings exactly as they are, as if looking at an *āmala* fruit in the palm of his hand.”

"Good son! The objects apprehended by the Tathāgata’s ear are of immeasurable kinds. As previously described, immeasurable and boundless worlds are filled with sentient beings; yet, if all those sentient beings in those worlds were to produce sounds simultaneously for the duration of a single kṣaṇa, a lava, or a muhūrta, their voices would differ in their melodic modulations, their inflections, and the magnitude of their speech."
The Tathāgata hears those sounds, each distinct from the others, and is able to comprehend them all.
Good son! The Tathāgata has accomplished noble wisdom that is inexhaustible and immeasurable, just like empty space.
"Good son! All sentient beings within the entire realm of sentient beings each conceive their own plans and engage in individual reflections, performing various kinds of karma.

In a single kṣaṇa, a single lava, or a single muhūrta, the Tathāgata is able to fully know that these sentient beings have conceived such plans, reflected thus, performed such karma, and will obtain such results."
The Tathāgata, by means of unimpeded wisdom, is fully able to know the karmic fruits of those sentient beings throughout the three periods of time. Why is this?
Because the Tathāgata constantly abides in samādhi.
Why is this? Because the Tathāgata’s mindfulness is without lapse, his faculties are not distracted, and his mind does not wander. Why is this?
"Good son! Because the Tathāgata abides in tranquility—because he is profoundly tranquil and utterly tranquil—and because he is able to sever all afflictions. Good son!"
If those sentient beings possess various afflictions, their minds become distracted and they are unable to attain those samādhis.

The Tathāgata, being free from the dust and defilement of such afflictions, gives rise to untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-jñāna*), realizes the nature of equality and mastery over all phenomena, and thoroughly penetrates the spheres of activity of all samādhis and samāpattis.

"Good son! All four modes of deportment of the Tathāgata are each and every one abiding in samādhi; even until the Tathāgata enters parinirvāṇa, he remains in samādhi for that entire duration—how much more so during shorter periods, when he would not be in meditative concentration!"
"Good son! The Tathāgata has accumulated the provisions for enlightenment over immeasurable kalpas; by virtue of this, the Tathāgata dwells eternally in samādhi. Good son!"
“The Tathāgata is immeasurable, inconceivable, and beyond calculation!
Ceasing-Coverings Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying, “No,
World-Honored One.”
“World-Honored One!
It is because the Tathāgata has realized it by accumulating the provisions over three asaṃkhyeya kalpas.
The Buddha said:
“Good son! I have accumulated the provisions for countless eons to realize the inconceivable realm of the Tathāgata; it was not realized merely through those three asaṃkhyeya kalpas.”

However, it is only after a bodhisattva has realized the equality of the nature of all phenomena that they enter those three incalculable eons (*asaṃkhyeya-kalpa*), not from the very first generation of the mind of awakening.
The Bodhisattva Citta-nivāraṇa-viṣkambhin said:
“If sentient beings are able to hear of the Tathāgata’s great majestic power, they can give rise to pure faith, joy, and delight.”
World-Honored One!
You should know that those sentient beings are indeed possessors of merit, performers of various good deeds, and those who have severed karmic obstacles.

If they give rise to faith and understanding, they will draw near to Bodhi; how much more so if, having heard it, they receive, uphold, read, recite, master it thoroughly, and explain it extensively for others!
“World-Honored One!
Such sentient beings will, before long, be capable of accomplishing the majestic power of a Tathāgata.
The Buddha said:
"So it is, so it is! Son of good family!
These sentient beings shall be taken into the care of immeasurable Buddhas; they shall serve immeasurable Buddhas and plant various roots of goodness."
If a son of good family or a daughter of good family hears of the vast majesty and virtue of the Tathāgata, they should never give rise to hesitation or doubt.

Being able to contemplate the Tathāgata’s majesty with joyful resolve and pure, superior understanding, they should don new, clean garments and make offerings according to the Dharma. If they can, for seven days and seven nights, focus their thoughts in contemplation without distraction, then at the end of those seven days and seven nights, they will behold the Tathāgata that very night.
“If one’s practiced dharmas are not fully perfected, such a person will have an undistracted mind at the time of death and shall behold the Tathāgata appearing before them.
The Bodhisattva Zhigai addressed the Buddha, saying,
“World-Honored One!”
"When sentient beings hear it said that the Tathāgata possesses such great majestic power, do they give rise to lack of faith?
The Buddha said, "There are."

"Noble son! If there are sentient beings who, upon hearing an account of the Tathāgata’s great majestic power, harbor fierce and violent intentions, respond with coarseness, malice, and cruelty, and give rise to a harmful mind, perceiving the Dharma-preacher as an evil friend."
By reason of these causes and conditions, after the dissolution of the body, they will be reborn in the hells.
Son of good family!
If sentient beings, upon hearing of the vast majesty and power of the Tathāgata, give rise to pure faith in their hearts, and conceive of the Dharma-preacher as a spiritual friend and as a guide.

"Good son! You should know with certainty that these sentient beings, in whatever place they have been born, have in the past heard of the vast majesty and virtue of the Tathāgata; or else these sentient beings have reflected thus:
'I must have heard this Dharma-gate in the assemblies of Buddhas in former times,' and by virtue of this, they have conceived pure faith upon hearing of the Tathāgata’s vast majesty and virtue."
"As the Blessed One has said:
'Those who now hear of the Tathāgata’s vast majesty and give rise to pure faith do so because they have heard it in the past.

At that time, the Blessed One manifested the mark of his tongue, covering his face; he then covered his body, the lion throne, and the assembly of bodhisattvas and śrāvakas, as well as Śakra, Brahmā, the World Protectors, and even the entire great assembly.
At that time, the World-Honored One withdrew his tongue-phenomenon and addressed the great assembly, saying: "Good sons!
Such a tongue-phenomenon arises because the Tathāgata has attained non-false speech."
"You all should give rise to profound pure faith; this will bring benefit, peace, and happiness throughout the long night.
When this Dharma was spoken, eighty-four thousand bodhisattvas attained the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti);
immeasurable hundreds of thousands of sentient beings were freed from dust and removed from defilement, attaining the purity of the Dharma-eye (dharma-cakṣur-viśuddhi).
Furthermore, immeasurable sentient beings who had not previously resolved to attain enlightenment all now gave rise to that resolve.
At that time, the Bhagavān addressed the Bodhisattva Vighuṣṭaśabda, saying: "Good son!
When bodhisattvas accomplish ten kinds of dharmas, they attain skillfulness regarding the conventional world. What are these ten?

First, they provisionally designate form within the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), yet in the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) form cannot be apprehended, nor is there any attachment to it; they provisionally designate feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness within the conventional world, yet in the ultimate truth, even up to consciousness, none can be apprehended, nor is there any attachment to them.

Second, although the earth element is conventionally designated, in the ultimate sense the earth element is unfindable and there is no attachment to it; likewise, although the water, fire, wind, space, and consciousness elements are conventionally designated, in the ultimate sense even the consciousness element is unfindable and there is no attachment to it.

Third, although the eye base is conventionally designated, in the ultimate sense the eye base is unfindable and there is no attachment to it; likewise, although the ear base up to the mind base are conventionally designated, in the ultimate sense even the mind base is unfindable and there is no attachment to it.
Fourth, although a self is conventionally designated, in the ultimate sense a self is unfindable and there is no attachment to it.
Fifth, although sentient beings are conventionally designated in the worldly sense, in the ultimate sense sentient beings are unfindable, and there is no attachment to them;

sixth, although a life-principle, a nourisher, a mind-born, a person (pudgala), and a young brahmin (māṇavaka) are conventionally designated in the worldly sense, in the ultimate sense they are all unfindable, and there is no attachment to them;
seventh, although a world is conventionally designated in the worldly sense, in the ultimate sense a world is unfindable, and there is no attachment to it.
Eighth, although worldly phenomena are conventionally designated within the mundane, in the ultimate sense worldly phenomena are unattainable, and there is no attachment to them;
ninth, although the Buddha-dharma is conventionally designated within the mundane, in the ultimate sense the Buddha-dharma is unattainable, and there is no attachment to it;

tenth, although enlightenment is conventionally designated within the mundane, in the ultimate sense both the enlightenment realized and the one who awakens are unattainable, and there is no attachment to them.
