"Good son! All verbal expressions established through conceptualization are called the conventional (saṃvṛti).
Although the conventional cannot be found within the ultimate (paramārtha), apart from the conventional, there is no ultimate."
"Good son! If a bodhisattva attains skillfulness regarding the conventional, but not regarding the ultimate truth, for this reason they are said to possess 'skillfulness in the conventional.'"
"Noble son! When a bodhisattva accomplishes these ten kinds of dharmas, they attain mundane skillfulness.
Furthermore, noble son!"
When Bodhisattvas accomplish ten dharmas, they attain skillfulness in the ultimate meaning (*paramārtha*). What are these ten?
First, they realize the nature of non-arising phenomena (*anutpattika-dharmatā*).
Second, the realization of the nature of phenomena that is non-extinguished;
third, the realization of the nature of phenomena that is indestructible;
fourth, the realization of the nature of phenomena that neither enters nor emerges.
Fifth, they realize the nature of phenomena that transcends the sphere of linguistic expression;
sixth, they realize the nature of phenomena that is beyond words;
seventh, they realize the nature of phenomena that is free from conceptual proliferation.
Eighth, the realization of the ineffable nature of phenomena;
ninth, the realization of the quiescent nature of phenomena;
tenth, the realization of the noble nature of phenomena.
Why is this? Son of good family!

Because in the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), there is no arising, no ceasing, and no destruction; there is no entering and no exiting; it transcends the path of speech and cannot be grasped by words; it is not realized through conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*); it is ineffable, profoundly tranquil, and is that which is personally realized within by the noble ones (*ārya*).
"Good son! Whether Tathāgatas appear in the world or do not appear, the ultimate principle remains eternally present and indestructible.

For this reason, a bodhisattva shaves off his hair and beard, dons the kāṣāya robe, gives rise to right faith in his heart, leaves home for the homeless life, and this is called 'leaving home' (pravrajyā)."

Having gone forth, he practiced with diligent effort, as if his head were wrapped in silk that was being consumed by fire; without pausing to extinguish the fire, he sought exclusively the ultimate truth.
If the ultimate truth did not exist, the holy life would be in vain, and the appearance of the Buddhas in the world would likewise be without purpose or benefit. Noble son!
Because the ultimate truth exists, bodhisattvas are able to attain skillfulness in this dharma.
"Noble son! When a bodhisattva accomplishes these ten kinds of dharmas, they attain skillfulness in the ultimate meaning.
Furthermore, noble son!"
When a bodhisattva accomplishes ten dharmas, they attain skillfulness regarding dependent origination. What are these ten?
First, they are able to know emptiness.
Second, they are able to know the nature of non-existence;
third, they are able to know the nature of lack of solidity;
fourth, they are able to know the nature of being like a shadow.
Fifth, they are able to know the nature of being like a reflection;
sixth, they are able to know the nature of being like an echo;
seventh, they are able to know the nature of being like an illusion.
Eighth, they are able to know the nature of non-abiding;
ninth, they are able to know the nature of movement;
tenth, they are able to know the nature of dependent origination.
“The Bodhisattva reflects thus:

‘All phenomena are empty in this way, non-existent in this way, insubstantial in this way; they are like a reflection, like an image, like an echo, like a magical illusion; they are without abiding, they are fluctuating, and they arise through conditions.’”
He further reflected:
"In these phenomena, one can thoroughly understand their arising and thoroughly understand their cessation.
The Bodhisattva then again pondered:
"For what cause do all phenomena arise?
For what cause do they cease?
With ignorance as a condition, they are able to give rise to all phenomena."
Ignorance is the foremost; ignorance is the basis.
Depending upon ignorance, volitional formations arise;
depending upon volitional formations, consciousness arises.
Dependent upon consciousness having arisen, name-and-form comes into being;
dependent upon name-and-form, the six sense bases come into being;
dependent upon the six sense bases, the various contacts come into being.
Once various contacts have arisen, feeling is designated;
because there is feeling, craving is designated;
and because the fool is oppressed by craving, grasping is designated.
Grasping means the act of taking up; because grasping arises, there is the continuity of becoming;
depending upon becoming, birth is obtained; and depending upon birth, aging occurs.
Because there is old age, the *pudgala* all possess death;
because there is death, one is able to give rise to sorrow, lamentation, suffering, and affliction; through the accumulation of these phenomena, a great mass of suffering is formed.
"Therefore, a wise person should diligently strive to destroy ignorance and uproot it; because ignorance is extinguished, all phenomena are extinguished. "Good son!"
Just as when the life-faculty ceases, all other faculties cease,
so too, because ignorance ceases, there is nothing upon which to rely;
and because there is no reliance, afflictions do not arise.
Because the causes of birth and death are extinguished, the fruits of the various realms of existence are extinguished; by this means, the bodhisattva is able to realize nirvāṇa.
Son of good family!
When a bodhisattva accomplishes these ten kinds of dharmas, they attain skillfulness regarding dependent origination.
"Furthermore, son of good family,
by accomplishing ten kinds of dharmas, a bodhisattva is able to know himself. What are these ten?
"First, the bodhisattva examines his own lineage:
Is he of the Brahmin caste, the Kṣatriya caste, or from a householder family?"
Among the various castes—whether wealthy, noble, poor, or low-born—in which caste is he born?
Although a bodhisattva may be born into any of these wealthy or noble lineages, he never relies upon this to give rise to arrogance.
If one is born into a poor or lowly lineage, one reflects:
"Because I performed various kinds of mixed karma in the past, this has caused me to be born into this lineage."
"By these causes and conditions, one becomes weary of and detached from all states of existence;
through this weariness and detachment, one seeks to go forth into homelessness. Second, having gone forth, one should reflect thus:
'For what purpose and benefit have I sought to go forth? "
He reflected thus: "I have now gone forth from home desiring to deliver myself and cause others to attain deliverance;
to achieve liberation for myself and cause others to achieve liberation."
"Therefore, a bodhisattva should always remain far removed from indolence and laziness.
"Third, a bodhisattva should reflect:
'Now that I have left the household life, I must eliminate all obstructive karmas and unwholesome dharmas.'"
Why is this? If one has already been able to eliminate various transgressions, one should give rise to joy and gladness within one's own mind;
if they have not yet been eliminated, one should diligently practice in order to bring about their elimination.
"Fourth, a bodhisattva should observe in this way:
'Since I have gone forth from home, all wholesome dharmas will increase. Why is this?'"
"If wholesome dharmas have already increased, the mind gives rise to joy;
if they have not yet increased, one should practice with earnest diligence so that they may increase.
Fifth, a bodhisattva should further observe in this way:
"If I can increase wholesome dharmas and eliminate sinful obstructions, I shall rely upon such a venerable one!

For this reason, a bodhisattva should regard their preceptor (upādhyāya)—whether they uphold the precepts or violate them, have little learning or much learning, or possess fame or lack fame—with the thought that they are a guide, just like the World-Honored One, giving rise to pure faith and feeling joy and delight.
"Sixth, a bodhisattva should always respect, revere, and make offerings to the ācārya, reflecting thus:
'By relying upon the ācārya, may I now attain fulfillment regarding those factors conducive to enlightenment that are not yet fulfilled;
may I attain the severance of those afflictions that have not yet been severed.'"
A bodhisattva serves an ācārya with the same regard as for an upādhyāya.
If there are wholesome dharmas, he accepts them accordingly;
if there are unwholesome dharmas, he understands them and does not practice them.
"From this, joy and delight arise in his mind.
Seventh, a bodhisattva should give rise to this reflection:
'Who is my teacher?'"
He further thought: "The Omniscient One is my teacher. Who is the Omniscient One?"
It means that through understanding all phenomena and out of compassion for the world,
one is able to give rise to great compassion,
becoming a great field of merit and a supreme guide for all the world, including its gods, humans, and asuras.
"He is my teacher.
Through this, the bodhisattva experiences joy and delight, attaining great benefit.
He then reflects further:
"The Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, are my teachers.
I shall practice the Noble Path and the precepts taught by the Buddha, and shall not commit any transgression against them until the end of my life."
"I should thus revere all Buddhas, honor and make offerings to them, and always follow their teachings with my mind. Eighth, the Bodhisattva reflects:
"From whom shall I beg to obtain food?"
The Bodhisattva further reflected:
"I should beg for food from the brahmins, kṣatriyas, and others in those cities and villages.
I shall cause these sentient beings, by means of this gift of food, to obtain great rewards, great benefit, and great majesty; therefore, I go to beg for food."
"9. Furthermore, the Bodhisattva reflects thus:
'What kind of perception should the brahmins, kṣatriyas, and others in the cities and villages have toward me when they give me food?'"
The Bodhisattva further thought:
"They should regard me as a śramaṇa, as a bhikṣu, and as a field of merit, and then give me food."
"I should reflect: 'Whatever merits belong to these śramaṇas and fields of merit, I shall cultivate them all.
Tenth, the bodhisattva reflects: "I am now departing from the beginningless cycle of birth and death."
"What is renunciation?
The Bodhisattva reflected:
"To leave the household life and become a bhikṣu according to the Dharma—this is the foremost renunciation."
I have now accomplished the virtues of a śramaṇa; this is the second departure.
Because I am constantly diligent, free from indolence, and have realized the nature of phenomena (dharmatā), I am able to depart from beginningless saṃsāra; this is the third departure.
I shall manifest complete enlightenment in unsurpassed, perfect, and full awakening (anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi); this is the fourth departure.
"By performing such observations, the bodhisattva is able to know for themselves:
'O son of good family!
When a bodhisattva accomplishes these ten kinds of dharmas, they attain self-knowledge.'"
"Furthermore, noble son,
when a bodhisattva accomplishes ten qualities, he is able to know the world. What are these ten?
First, one is able to humble oneself before those who are arrogant;
second, one is able to abandon pride before those who are conceited;
third, one is able to be upright and sincere before those who are crooked and deceitful.
Fourth, one is able to speak truthfully toward those who are deceitful;
fifth, one is able to speak with loving words toward those who speak harshly;
sixth, one is able to speak with gentle words toward those who are stubborn.
Seventh, one is always able to practice patience toward those who are violent and wicked;
eighth, one is able to cultivate loving-kindness toward those who are angry;
ninth, one is able to cultivate compassion toward those who are suffering and distressed.
Tenth, among those who are stingy, they are able to practice generosity.
Son of good family!
When bodhisattvas accomplish these ten kinds of dharmas, they are able to know the world.
"Furthermore, son of good family,
when bodhisattvas accomplish ten dharmas, they are born in pure buddha-fields. What are these ten?
First, they achieve the precepts—without deficiency, without admixture, without blemish, and with pure precepts;
second, they attain a mind of equanimity toward all sentient beings;
third, they are able to accomplish vast roots of goodness.
Fourth, regarding gain, fame, honor, and praise, their minds are always detached, free from any defilement or attachment;
fifth, they attain pure faith, with no doubt or uncertainty in their hearts;
sixth, they constantly cultivate diligence, remaining free from a mind of indolence.
Seventh, they are able to enter tranquil meditative concentration, free from a distracted mind;
eighth, they are able to attain extensive learning without possessing evil wisdom;
ninth, they achieve sharp intelligence rather than a dull faculty.
"Tenth, they possess the nature of compassion and mercy, and have no mind of harm.
The Bodhisattva Zhigai addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
"Regarding these ten dharmas, must they be fully possessed for one to be born [in that realm], or can one be born even if some are lacking?
The Buddha said, "Good son!..."

If there is a bodhisattva who accomplishes one dharma—being without deficiency, without even the slightest transgression, and being pure and bright—that bodhisattva will then fully accomplish ten dharmas.
"Noble son! When bodhisattvas accomplish these ten kinds of dharmas, they are born in pure buddha-fields.
Furthermore, noble son!"
If a bodhisattva accomplishes ten dharmas, they will attain a state where the womb is free from the defilement of dust and grime. What are these ten?
First, creating images of the Tathāgata;...
Second, repairing and restoring the ruined *caityas* of all Buddhas;
third, making offerings by anointing the Buddha *caityas* with various exquisite incenses;
fourth, making offerings by washing the images of the Tathāgata with various fragrant waters.
Fifth, to sweep, sprinkle, and smear the ground within the stūpas of the Buddha as an act of worship;
sixth, to personally serve and provide for one’s parents;
seventh, to personally provide offerings to one’s ācāryas and upādhyāyas.
Eighth, he is personally able to make offerings to those who practice the holy life (*brahmacarya*), yet the bodhisattva’s mind remains free from expectation;

ninth, the bodhisattva vows to dedicate his roots of virtue (*kuśalamūla*) to sentient beings, [praying] that by means of these roots of virtue, they may be born without being defiled by the impurities of the womb;
tenth, the bodhisattva’s dedication is characterized by an intention that is earnest, fierce, and profound.
"Noble son! When a bodhisattva accomplishes these ten dharmas, they attain a state where they are undefiled by the impurities of the womb.
Furthermore, noble son!"
When Bodhisattvas accomplish ten dharmas, they attain the renunciation of home and family. What are these ten?
First, they attain the state of non-appropriation.
Second, dwelling without confusion;
third, attaining weariness toward and turning away from sense objects;
fourth, being free from attachment to sense objects.
Fifth, not giving rise to the faults of attachment toward sense objects;
sixth, revering and respecting all the training rules established by the Buddha, being able to practice them well with courageous diligence;
seventh, regarding food, drink, clothing, requisites, and medicine—whatever items one receives—one’s mind is always content.
Eighth, they are well able to relinquish all accumulation regarding the alms-bowl, the saffron robes, and other requisites;
ninth, their minds are constantly fearful toward sense objects, giving rise to weary detachment;
tenth, they constantly and diligently practice, being able to abide in manifest tranquility.
"Noble son! When a bodhisattva accomplishes these ten kinds of dharmas, they attain the renunciation of the home life.
Furthermore, noble son!"
If a bodhisattva accomplishes ten dharmas, they are able to attain pure livelihood. What are these ten?
First, being able to skillfully abandon hypocrisy, flattery, and crookedness for the sake of gain and offerings;
Second, they are well able to abandon manifesting signs for the sake of gain and offerings;
third, they are well able to abandon empty talk and incitement for the sake of gain and offerings;
fourth, they are well able to abandon evil seeking of gain and offerings.
Fifth, they are well able to relinquish gains that are contrary to the Dharma;
sixth, they are well able to relinquish impure gains;
seventh, they do not become addicted to gains.
Eighth, one attains freedom from attachment to gain and offerings;
ninth, one attains a nature free from feverish affliction;
tenth, one is well able to be content with gain and offerings that accord with the Dharma.
“Good son! How does one skillfully abandon the hypocrisy and crookedness practiced for the sake of gain and offerings?
It means that this bodhisattva, for no reason of gain and offerings, does not practice hypocrisy through the actions of body, speech, or mind.”
"What is meant by 'the body being free from hypocrisy'?
It means that when this bodhisattva sees a donor or an assistant to the donor, he does not manifest affected deportment.
What is meant by 'not manifesting affected deportment'?"
That is to say, when this bodhisattva lifts his foot, he does not feign a slow gait;

when he sets his foot down, he does not look forward for the distance of one fathom while manifesting an appearance of contemplation, nor does he feign looking straight ahead without regard for anything.
“What is speech that is not deceitful?
It means that this bodhisattva, for the sake of gain and offerings, does not speak with slow, deliberate, or subtle words, nor with gentle, affectionate, or compliant speech.”
"What is meant by the mind being free from hypocrisy?

When a donor or an assistant to the donor invites him, the Bodhisattva does not, for the sake of gain and offerings, speak of having few desires while his mind is actually full of greed and he harbors inner distress; this is called the Bodhisattva’s freedom from hypocrisy, flattery, and crookedness for the sake of gain."
"What is meant by 'skillfully abandoning the manifestation of signs for the sake of gain'?

If a bodhisattva sees a donor or an assistant donor, he never manifests a sign by saying, 'I need robes, a bowl, or medicine for the treatment of illness. Even though that donor or assistant donor does not grant them, the bodhisattva never begs from them. This is called a bodhisattva skillfully abandoning the manifestation of signs for the sake of gain."
"How does a bodhisattva skillfully abandon the empty talk and incitement for the sake of gain and offerings?
When a bodhisattva sees a donor or an assistant to a donor, they never falsely say:
'A certain donor gave me such-and-such an object, and I have repaid that kindness with such-and-such an object.'"
Furthermore, he says:
"Such-and-such a person, because I observe the precepts, possess great learning, and have few desires, has brought various items to give to me.
Out of a heart of compassion and pity for them, I have accepted them."
This is called a bodhisattva being well able to abandon empty talk and incitement for the sake of gain and offerings.
*The Buddha-spoken Sūtra of the Precious Rain*, Scroll Nine;
*The Buddha-spoken Sūtra of the Precious Rain*, Scroll Ten.
Translated by the Tang Dynasty Indian Tripiṭaka Master Dharmaruci:
"How does a bodhisattva skillfully abandon evil seeking for gain and offerings? Good son!
A bodhisattva does not commit evil with body or mind for the sake of gain and offerings."
Those who commit evil through bodily conduct do so by rushing to and fro for the sake of gain and profit, thereby violating the *śīla*.

Those who commit evil through mental conduct, out of a longing for gain and profit, give rise to a mind intent on harming others when they see the gains obtained by others or their fellow practitioners of the holy life (*brahmacārin*).
This is called a bodhisattva’s relinquishing of evil pursuits for gain and offerings.
How does a bodhisattva relinquish unrighteous gain and offerings?

It means that this bodhisattva does not practice deceit to obtain gain and offerings; he does not employ fraud with measures or scales, nor does he ever violate the trust placed in him by others. He does not practice deceit.
This is called the bodhisattva’s relinquishing of unrighteous gain.
How does a bodhisattva relinquish impure gain?

It means that regarding the gains obtained by this bodhisattva—whether they be objects belonging to a stūpa, the Dharma, or the Saṅgha—if others have neither given them nor authorized their use, he will certainly not accept those items even if he obtains them.
This is called the bodhisattva’s relinquishing of impure offerings and gain.
How does a bodhisattva not become attached to offerings and gain?
It means that when this bodhisattva receives offerings and gain, they do not take them as their own property, do not claim to be wealthy, and do not accumulate them.

From time to time he gives to śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, and others; he gives to his parents, those who assist him on his left and right, and his friends and kinsmen; and from time to time he uses it for himself.
Even when using things for their own enjoyment, they remain free from attachment.

When a bodhisattva does not obtain offerings or gain, their mind does not give rise to suffering or distress; even if a donor or an assistant to the donor fails to bestow gifts, the bodhisattva does not harbor ill will toward them.

If one obtains righteous offerings and proceeds according to the order of the Saṃgha, all Tathāgatas will grant their approval, the Bodhisattvas will have no cause for reproach, the devas will offer praise, and fellow practitioners of the Brahma-faring life will harbor no criticism; regarding such benefits, one should always be content.
“Good son! If a bodhisattva accomplishes these ten kinds of dharmas, they are able to attain pure livelihood. Furthermore, good son!”
When bodhisattvas accomplish ten dharmas, they attain a mind free from weariness. What are these ten?
First, for the sake of all sentient beings, they dwell for a long time within saṃsāra without weariness.
Second, for the sake of all sentient beings, one does not grow weary of the suffering of birth and death;
third, one does not grow weary within the act of benefiting sentient beings;
fourth, one never grows weary of constantly performing all deeds for the sake of sentient beings.
Fifth, they are able to cause sentient beings to perform virtuous deeds without weariness;
sixth, they proclaim the path and Dharma for individuals of the Śrāvaka vehicle without weariness;
seventh, they do not manifest a lack of faith in the Śrāvaka vehicle before individuals of the Śrāvaka vehicle.
Eighth, they embrace the factors conducive to enlightenment without weariness;
ninth, they fulfill the provisions for enlightenment without weariness;
tenth, they do not seek the actual realization of the realm of nirvāṇa, nor do they have the intention to proceed toward nirvāṇa.
It is because, by means of this, the bodhisattva is able to accord with great enlightenment, to advance toward great enlightenment, and to draw near to great enlightenment. Good son!
When Bodhisattvas accomplish these ten kinds of dharmas, they attain a mind free from weariness.
"Furthermore, son of good family!
When Bodhisattvas accomplish ten kinds of dharmas, they are able to carry out all the instructions of the Tathāgatas."
What are the ten? First, practicing heedfulness by abandoning all forms of negligence;
second, attaining wholesome restraint of the body by refraining from evil physical conduct.
Third, attaining the excellent restraint of speech, because one does not commit evil with speech;
fourth, attaining the excellent restraint of mind, because one does not commit evil with the mind;
fifth, fearing future worlds, being able to completely abandon all unwholesome dharmas.
Sixth, they are able to expound correct principles and remain free from all that is irrational;
seventh, they are able to skillfully preach the Dharma and censure what is contrary to the Dharma;
eighth, they are able to abandon karma that invites reproach and practice in accordance with pure karma.
Ninth, they do not speak of faults or defects within the teachings of the Tathāgata, and are able to completely abandon and leave behind the poisons of all afflictions;
tenth, they are able to accord with and protect the nature of the Tathāgata’s Dharma, warding off all evil and unwholesome dharmas.
"Noble son! When bodhisattvas accomplish these ten kinds of dharmas, they are able to carry out all the instructions of the Tathāgatas.
Furthermore, noble son!"
When a bodhisattva accomplishes ten dharmas, they attain a smiling countenance and are forever free from frowning. What are these ten?
First, they attain clarity and purity of the sense faculties.
Second, they attain the complete purity of all faculties;
third, they attain the non-deficiency of all faculties;
fourth, they attain the freedom from defilement of all faculties.
Fifth, they attain the purity of the sense faculties;
sixth, they attain permanent freedom from harm;
seventh, they attain permanent freedom from latent tendencies.
Eighth, they attain permanent liberation from entanglements and bonds;
ninth, they attain permanent liberation from fetters and resentments;
tenth, they attain permanent liberation from anger and rage.
“Good son! When a bodhisattva accomplishes these ten kinds of dharmas, they attain a smiling countenance and are forever free from frowning.
The Bodhisattva Citta-vighna-vinivartana addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
As I understand the meaning and intent of what the Buddha has taught, it is because their faculties are pure that bodhisattvas attain a smiling countenance;
furthermore, because they have forever abandoned all afflictions, they attain freedom from frowning.”
The Buddha said: "Good son! So it is, so it is, just as you have said!"
"Furthermore, noble son,
when a bodhisattva accomplishes ten dharmas, they are able to attain great learning. What are these ten?
First, one understands as it truly is that the fire of greed blazes with such arising and ceasing;
second, one understands as it truly is that the fire of hatred blazes with such intensification;
third, one understands as it truly is that the fire of delusion grows with such confusion.
Fourth, they understand as it truly is that all conditioned phenomena are impermanent;
fifth, they understand as it truly is that all such formations are suffering;
sixth, they understand as it truly is that this world is entirely empty.
Seventh, they understand as it truly is that all such conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are without self;
eighth, they understand as it truly is that such attachments are all termed conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*);
ninth, they understand as it truly is that all phenomena arise from causes and conditions.
Tenth, one understands as it truly is that nirvana is peace.
This meaning is not merely a matter of words; it must be understood as it truly is through the wisdoms accomplished by hearing, reflection, and cultivation.
Having understood this, with firm compassion, they arouse diligence for the sake of all sentient beings. Noble son,
when a bodhisattva accomplishes these ten dharmas, they are able to attain great learning.
"Furthermore, son of good family,
when bodhisattvas accomplish ten kinds of dharmas, they embrace the true Dharma. What are these ten?

First, at a later time, in a later period, during the final five hundred years when the True Dharma is about to perish, the era having declined, sentient beings will be unable to practice and will abide in unrighteous paths; the lamp of wisdom will have been extinguished, and there will be no one capable of teaching it.

At this time, if there are those who can uphold, recite, and perform various services with reverence and offerings toward the vast sūtras—which provide great benefit, possess great majestic power, and give birth to all wholesome dharmas like a mother to sentient beings—[they shall attain these fruits].
Second, to successively proclaim and reveal it to others;
third, to give rise to pure faith, rejoice with exultation, and provide support for those individuals who study such vast sūtras.
Fourth, hearing the true Dharma without any expectation of gain;
fifth, conceiving the thought of this Dharma teacher as a guide;
sixth, being able to conceive the thought of the true Dharma as nectar.
Seventh, they are able to conceive of the true Dharma as an elixir of immortality.
Eighth, they conceive of the true Dharma as an excellent medicine.
Ninth, they seek the true Dharma with single-minded devotion, disregarding even their own bodies and lives.
Tenth, they seek the true Dharma with the thought of engaging in its practice.
Son of good family,
when bodhisattvas accomplish these ten kinds of dharmas, they are able to embrace and uphold the true Dharma.
"Furthermore, good son, there are ten kinds of dharmas which,
when accomplished by a bodhisattva, make him a prince of the Dharma. What are these ten?
First, being adorned with all the primary marks;
second, the body attaining the secondary signs;
third, the faculties being complete and entirely perfected.
Fourth, they practice in accordance with the spheres of activity of all Tathāgatas;
fifth, they attain in accordance with the noble paths realized by all Tathāgatas;
sixth, they awaken in accordance with the enlightenment of all Tathāgatas.
Seventh, they are able to eliminate the sufferings and afflictions of the world;
eighth, they skillfully train in all that is practiced by the noble ones;
ninth, they attain the thorough cultivation of the holy life (brahmacarya).
Tenth, they are able to dwell in the city of omniscience, which is the place where all Tathāgatas abide. Noble son,
when a bodhisattva accomplishes these ten kinds of dharmas, they become a prince of the Dharma.
"Furthermore, son of good family,
when a bodhisattva accomplishes ten dharmas, he becomes one who is honored and served by Śakra, Brahmā, and the World-Protectors (Lokapālas). What are these ten?
First, they are able to remain non-retrogressive regarding bodhi;
second, they cannot be moved by any māras;
third, they do not suffer any decline or loss within the Buddha-dharma.
Fourth, to accord with and be able to enter into all true characteristics;
fifth, to accord with and thoroughly penetrate that all phenomena are entirely equal;
sixth, to be able to have faith and understanding within all Buddha-dharmas without depending on external conditions.
Seventh, attaining the wisdom of excellent realization;
eighth, accomplishing all the uncommon dharmas of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas;
ninth, being able to transcend all those worlds.
Tenth is the realization of the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
Son of good family,
when a bodhisattva accomplishes these ten dharmas, they receive the honor and service of Śakra, Brahmā, and the World-Protectors (*lokapāla*).
"Furthermore, son of good family,
when a bodhisattva accomplishes ten qualities, he is able to know the inclinations and latent tendencies of sentient beings. What are these ten?
First, to know, as they truly are, the mental dispositions of desire in all sentient beings;
second, to know, as they truly are, the mental dispositions of hatred in all sentient beings;
third, to know, as they truly are, the mental dispositions of delusion in all sentient beings.
Fourth, knowing as they truly are the superior dispositions of all sentient beings;
fifth, knowing as they truly are the middling dispositions of all sentient beings;
sixth, knowing as they truly are the inferior dispositions of all sentient beings.
Seventh, he knows, as they truly are, the various virtuous inclinations of all sentient beings;
eighth, he knows, as they truly are, the firm inclinations of all sentient beings;
ninth, he knows, as they truly are, the latent tendencies that constantly arise in all sentient beings.
Tenth, he knows, as they truly are, the violent latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) of all sentient beings.
Son of good family,
when a bodhisattva accomplishes these ten qualities, he is able to know the inclinations and latent tendencies of sentient beings.
"Furthermore, noble son,
when a bodhisattva accomplishes ten kinds of dharmas, they are able to attain skillfulness in maturing sentient beings. What are these ten?
First, if there are sentient beings who should be liberated by means of the physical form of a Tathāgata, he manifests the physical form of a Tathāgata;
second, if there are those who should be liberated by means of the physical form of a Bodhisattva, he manifests the physical form of a Bodhisattva;
third, if there are those who should be liberated by means of the physical form of a Pratyekabuddha, he manifests the physical form of a Pratyekabuddha.
Fourth, for those who are to be saved by the form of a śrāvaka, he manifests the form of a śrāvaka;
fifth, for those who are to be saved by the form of Śakra, he manifests the form of Śakra;
sixth, for those who are to be saved by the form of a Māra king, he manifests the form of a Māra king.
Seventh, for those who are to be delivered by the physical appearance of a Brahmā, he manifests the physical appearance of a Brahmā;
eighth, for those who are to be delivered by the physical appearance of a Brāhmaṇa, he manifests the physical appearance of a Brāhmaṇa;
ninth, for those who are to be delivered by the physical appearance of a Kṣatriya, he manifests the physical appearance of a Kṣatriya.
Tenth, for those who are to be liberated by appearing in the form of a householder, he manifests the form of a householder.
Good son! If there are sentient beings who can be tamed through such skillful means of appearance, the Bodhisattva manifests various forms of appearance as skillful means to tame them.
"Noble son! When a bodhisattva accomplishes these ten dharmas, they are able to attain skillfulness in maturing sentient beings.
Furthermore, noble son!"
When a bodhisattva accomplishes ten qualities, they attain dwelling in accordance with reality. What are these ten?
First, a straightforward mind;
Second, a supple mind; third, a mind free from crookedness;
fourth, a mind free from malice.
Fifth, a stainless mind; sixth, a pure mind;
seventh, a mind free from hardness;
Eighth, they are free from harsh speech;
ninth, they are able to always practice patience;
tenth, they are fully endowed with compliance.
"Noble son! When a bodhisattva accomplishes these ten kinds of dharmas, they attain dwelling in accordance [with reality].
Furthermore, noble son!"
When bodhisattvas accomplish ten dharmas, they attain dwelling in peace and happiness. What are these ten?
First, they are able to attain the fulfillment of right view and complete purity.
Second, the attainment of the perfection of precepts;
third, the purity of one's conduct;
fourth, the attainment of a sphere of activity that accords with what should be practiced.
Fifth, being free from defiled attachment;
sixth, accomplishing compassion;
seventh, being able to constantly maintain anxious concern.
Eighth, they are able to attain those of the same class;
ninth, they are able to give rise to the One Vehicle;
tenth, they do not serve other teachers.
"Noble son! When a bodhisattva accomplishes these ten kinds of dharmas, they attain dwelling in peace and happiness.
Furthermore, noble son!"
When a bodhisattva accomplishes ten dharmas, they attain skillfulness in the means of integration (*saṃgrahavastu*). What are these ten?
First, for the sake of integrating sentient beings, they cultivate the giving of benefit.
Second, for the sake of gathering sentient beings, one practices the giving of peace and happiness;
third, for the sake of gathering sentient beings, one practices inexhaustible giving;
fourth, for the sake of gathering sentient beings, one provides beneficial speech.
Fifth, for the sake of gathering sentient beings, one cultivates the meaning of discourse;
sixth, for the sake of gathering sentient beings, one cultivates the discourse of the Dharma;
seventh, for the sake of gathering sentient beings, one demonstrates the principles of discourse.
Eighth, for the sake of gathering sentient beings, one benefits them with what is wholesome;
ninth, for the sake of gathering sentient beings, one benefits them by sharing food, drink, and so forth;
tenth, for the sake of gathering sentient beings, one benefits them by sharing the necessities of life, such as the requisites for survival.
"Good son! That which benefits through the Dharma is what is called the gift of Dharma;
that which bestows peace and happiness is what is called the gift of material wealth."
Inexhaustible giving refers to constantly proclaiming the path and showing it to others;
speech that benefits refers to speaking of roots of goodness;
speech that conveys meaning refers to speaking of reality.
"Teaching the Dharma" refers to the teachings expounded in accordance with the Tathāgata’s instructions;
"explaining the principle" refers to not subverting the true meaning;
and "skillfully benefiting" refers to causing sentient beings to eliminate what is unwholesome and establish them in the state of goodness.
Regarding "benefiting others by sharing food, drink, and so forth," this refers to sharing the enjoyment of various items such as food, drink, and clothing.

Regarding "benefiting others by sharing the requisites for sustaining life," this refers to sharing the enjoyment of such things as gold, silver, mani-jewels, pearls, jade, lapis lazuli, conch shells, coral, elephants, horses, and carriages.
"Noble son! When bodhisattvas accomplish these ten kinds of dharmas, they attain skill in the means of integration (*saṃgrahavastu*). Furthermore, noble son!"
If a bodhisattva accomplishes ten kinds of dharmas, they are able to attain physical grace and dignity. What are these ten?
First, being able to attain serene deportment;
2. One is able to attain a demeanor free from hypocrisy and deceit;
3. one is able to attain a pure demeanor;
4. one is able to cause those who see it to feel love and joy.
Fifth, it causes all evils to cease and the minds of those who see it to become tranquil;
sixth, it causes those who see it to never feel satiated;
seventh, it causes the minds of those who see it to be joyful and delighted.
8. It enables those who see it to have minds free from obstruction;
9. It enables those who see it to fulfill their aspirations;
10. It enables those who see it to give rise to pure faith in their hearts.
"Noble son! When bodhisattvas accomplish these ten kinds of dharmas, they are able to attain physical excellence and dignity. Furthermore, noble son!"
When a bodhisattva accomplishes ten kinds of dharmas, they serve as a basis for reliance. What are these ten?
First, being able to protect others, because all sentient beings fear the afflictions.
Second, it is able to bring about deliverance, because the wilderness of birth and death is full of hunger and thirst;
third, it is well able to provide rescue and relief, meaning it causes sentient beings to emerge from the ocean of birth and death;
fourth, it is able to act as a kinsman, because sentient beings are for the most part destitute and solitary.
Fifth, they act as great physicians, for they are able to counteract and eliminate the disease of afflictions;
sixth, they are able to serve as a source of reliance, for all sentient beings lack anyone to depend upon;
seventh, they are able to serve as a refuge, for all sentient beings lack a place of reliance.
Eighth, they are able to act as a refuge, because sentient beings have no one to rely upon;
ninth, they are able to act as a lamp of wisdom, because sentient beings dwell in ignorance;
tenth, they are able to act as a destination, because sentient beings have nowhere to turn.
"Noble son! When a bodhisattva accomplishes these ten kinds of dharmas, they attain that which serves as a basis.
Furthermore, noble son!"
If a bodhisattva accomplishes ten kinds of dharmas, they are like a great medicinal tree. What are these ten?
O son of good family!
Like a great medicinal tree, it enables all sentient beings to enjoy its benefits:
first, by enjoying its roots; second, by enjoying its trunk.
Third, they enjoy its branches;
fourth, they enjoy its leaves;
fifth, they enjoy its flowers.
Sixth, the enjoyment of its fruit;
seventh, the enjoyment of its color when seeing it;
eighth, the enjoyment of its fragrance when smelling it.
Ninth, one experiences its flavor when tasting it;
tenth, one experiences its touch when massaging it. Good son!

In this way, from the first generation of the mind of awakening until the attainment of Buddhahood, a bodhisattva is able to bestow upon all those various sentient beings the diverse medicinal dharmas for the diseases of their afflictions, enabling them to partake of them—whether by partaking of the bodhisattva’s perfection of generosity, or the bodhisattva’s perfection of ethical discipline, or the bodhisattva’s perfection of patience, or the bodhisattva’s perfection of diligence, or the bodhisattva’s perfection of meditative concentration, or the bodhisattva’s perfection of wisdom; or by seeing the bodhisattva’s body and thereby gaining benefit, or hearing the bodhisattva’s name and thereby gaining benefit, or tasting the bodhisattva’s virtues and thereby gaining benefit, or again, by making offerings to the bodhisattva and thereby gaining benefit.
“Noble son! When a bodhisattva accomplishes these ten dharmas, they are like a great medicinal tree.
Furthermore, noble son!”
When bodhisattvas accomplish ten kinds of dharmas, they are able to diligently cultivate merit. What are these ten?
First, within the Three Jewels, they make offerings according to their capacity.
Second, to be able to provide medicine to all sentient beings who are afflicted by illness;
third, to be able to provide food and drink to all sentient beings oppressed by hunger and thirst;
fourth, to be able to provide clothing to all sentient beings who are tormented by cold, heat, and the like.
Fifth, one should always respect, revere, and make offerings to one's ācāryas and upādhyāyas with a devoted mind;
sixth, one should inquire after the well-being of fellow practitioners of the holy life (brahmacārin), join the palms in prostration, and respectfully make offerings to them;
seventh, one should establish monasteries, groves, and gardens.
Eighth, from time to time, he is able to practice generosity by bestowing his wealth, grain, and all that is stored in his treasuries;
ninth, he treats his slaves and laborers with equal compassion and nurtures them;
tenth, from time to time, he is able to honor and make offerings to those who maintain pure precepts, as well as to śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, and others.
"Noble son! When a bodhisattva accomplishes these ten kinds of dharmas, they are able to diligently cultivate merit.
Furthermore, noble son!"
When Bodhisattvas accomplish ten dharmas, they attain skill in transformations. What are these ten?
First, while their physical form remains unmoving within a single buddha-field, they are able to hear the profound meaning from the presence of all Tathāgatas throughout immeasurable buddha-fields.
Second, while remaining unmoving in physical form within a single buddha-field, one is able to hear the true Dharma from the presence of all Tathāgatas in immeasurable buddha-fields;
third, while remaining unmoving in physical form within a single buddha-field, one is able to reverently make offerings to all Tathāgatas in immeasurable buddha-fields;

fourth, while remaining unmoving in physical form within a single buddha-field, one is able to cultivate and accumulate the provisions for enlightenment until they are perfected throughout immeasurable buddha-lands.

Fifth, while remaining unmoved in physical form within a single buddha-field, they are able to see various bodhisattvas manifesting perfect enlightenment in immeasurable buddha-fields, and they pay them respect, make offerings, honor, and praise them;
sixth, while remaining unmoved in physical form within a single buddha-field, they are able to manifest their arrival at the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa) in immeasurable buddha-fields;
seventh, while remaining unmoved in physical form within a single buddha-field, they are able to manifest their own perfect enlightenment in immeasurable buddha-fields, allowing all others to see it.
Eighth, while remaining unmoved in physical form within a single buddha-field, one is able to turn the wheel of the true Dharma throughout immeasurable buddha-fields;
ninth, while remaining unmoved in physical form within a single buddha-field, one is able to manifest parinirvāṇa throughout immeasurable buddha-fields;

tenth, while remaining unmoved in physical form within a single buddha-field, one is able to manifest various transformations to subdue those sentient beings who require training—from the first generation of the mind of enlightenment until the attainment of Buddhahood—throughout that entire duration across immeasurable buddha-fields.
Although the bodhisattva manifests such transformations, he does not discriminate, thinking, "I am able to transform";
nor does he discriminate regarding the objects transformed, thinking, "Such things as these have been created by me."
The Bodhisattva Nivaraṇaviṣkambhin addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
A bodhisattva is able to perform various kinds of transformations.”
"How is it that the one who performs the transformation and the object transformed attain non-discrimination?
The Buddha said, "Good son!
I shall now speak a parable for you; you should listen attentively. Noble son!

It is like the sun and moon, whose radiance illuminates the four continents and extensively benefits all sentient beings. Although the sun and moon benefit all sentient beings, they do not discriminate, thinking, "I am the one who illuminates," nor do they discriminate, thinking, "those sentient beings are the ones being illuminated."

Nevertheless, because the celestial sons Sūrya and Candra have accomplished this through the maturation (*vipāka*) of their past karma, they are able to perform such deeds for the benefit of sentient beings.

Noble son, it is the same for all bodhisattvas: although they manifest various transformations, these occur without effort (*anābhoga*), and they do not give rise to discrimination between the transformer and the transformed—thinking, "I am the transformer" or "sentient beings are the transformed."
Why is this? Such various manifestations are each and every one the result of the maturation of the Bodhisattva’s wholesome karma.

Because in the past they cultivated practice, made such vows, and performed such deeds, they have thereby attained freedom from conceptual discrimination regarding both the transformer and the transformed.
"Noble son! When a bodhisattva accomplishes these ten kinds of dharmas, they attain skill in emanation.
Furthermore, noble son!"
If a bodhisattva accomplishes ten dharmas, they will be able to swiftly manifest equal enlightenment in unsurpassed bodhi. What are these ten?
First, they attain the perfection of giving, because they have accomplished giving through its skillful accumulation.
Second, they attain the full precepts, achieving pure morality that is without deficiency or flaw and free from defilement, surpassing all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas;
third, they are fully endowed with patience;
fourth, they are fully endowed with right effort.
Fifth, being fully endowed with meditative concentration;
sixth, being fully endowed with wisdom;
seventh, being fully endowed with skillful means;
Eighth, they are endowed with supreme vows;
ninth, they are endowed with all powers;
tenth, they are endowed with right knowledge.
Because the bodhisattva is able to accomplish wisdom, they transcend all stages of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.

By being able to accomplish the uncommon wisdom (*āveṇika-jñāna*), they can further transcend the first bodhisattva stage up to the ninth stage, because the bodhisattva has attained the perfection of wisdom.
“Good son! Because bodhisattvas accomplish these ten kinds of dharmas, they are able to swiftly manifest equal enlightenment in unsurpassed bodhi.
When the World-Honored One spoke this Dharma-gate, this trichiliocosm shook in six ways.

Furthermore, all the mountains existing in this world—namely Sumeru, Mucilinda, Mahāmucilinda, Cakravāḍa, Mahācakravāḍa, and all the jewel-mountains—bowed their peaks and ridges toward Gayā Mountain in order to make offerings to the Buddha.
Furthermore, all the flowers, fruits, trees, and so forth in this world all bent low toward Gayāśīrṣa Mountain, making offerings to the Buddha and making offerings to the Dharma.

Furthermore, there were immeasurable hundreds of thousands of koṭis of nayutas of bodhisattvas who, with various garments and all kinds of ornaments piled up as high as Mount Sumeru, made offerings to the Buddha and the Dharma.

Furthermore, there were immeasurable hundreds of thousands of koṭis of Śakras, Brahmās, and Lokapālas who joined their palms toward the Buddha, paid homage with reverence, and scattered mandārava flowers and mahāmandārava flowers over the Buddha.

Furthermore, immeasurable hundreds of thousands of devaputras in the sky each held celestial robes, raised their hands and whirled them, producing hundreds of thousands of sounds, and scattered various heavenly flowers over the Buddha, saying these words:
"The Buddhas of the past have already appeared in the world and turned the wheel of the sublime Dharma."
World-Honored One, you have now once again appeared to turn the sublime wheel of Dharma.

If there are sentient beings who, in the past, made offerings to various Buddhas, cultivated meritorious deeds, and accumulated roots of goodness, such beings are only now able to hear this Dharma-gate; how much more so those who, having heard it, give rise to profound pure faith!

Furthermore, immeasurable hundreds of thousands of mahoragas, also for the sake of making offerings to this dharma-gate, let out a great sound like the roar of thunder, its resonance pervading everywhere.
Furthermore, he further manifested various clouds of incense, raining down all kinds of fragrant water.
This rain pervaded this trichiliocosm as well as the summit of Gayāśīrṣa Mountain, yet it did not disturb or afflict any sentient beings.
Furthermore, immeasurable hundreds of thousands of nāga maidens performed various kinds of music before the World-Honored One, offering praise and worship.

Additionally, immeasurable hundreds of thousands of gandharvas and kiṃnaras circumambulated the trichiliocosm and Mount Gayā to the right, producing exquisite sounds as they offered praise and worship.
Furthermore, immeasurable hundreds of thousands of koṭis of yakṣas rained down various lotus flowers as an offering.

Additionally, immeasurable hundreds of thousands of brahmins and kṣatriyas made offerings to the Buddha with flower garlands, burning incense, blended perfumes, unguents, powdered incense, robes, flower canopies, and various banners and streamers.
Furthermore, all the Buddhas residing within immeasurable worlds, in order to make offerings to Śākyamuni Buddha and to honor the Dharma, each emitted light from between their eyebrows.
Within that radiance appear various colors, various forms, and various lights—namely, blue, yellow, red, white, and crimson rock crystal.
The light rays he emitted circled this great trichiliocosm to the right, capable of shattering all obscurations of darkness.
The light then circled the peak of Mount Gayā and the body of the Tathāgata to the right, before entering through the crown of the World-Honored One’s head.
Furthermore, wherever they were fanned by these wondrous winds, those who touched them experienced peace and bliss.

When the World-Honored One was expounding this Dharma-gate, seventy-two nayutas of bodhisattvas within the assembly attained the forbearance of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*);
and immeasurable hundreds of thousands of koṭis of nayutas of sentient beings became free from dust and defilement, attaining the pure Dharma-eye.
Countless hundreds of thousands of koṭis of sentient beings who had not yet resolved their minds toward enlightenment now gave rise to the bodhicitta.

At that time, there was a goddess on Mount Gayā named Dīrghāyuḥ, who had long resided upon this mountain; leading her army and accompanied by her retinue, she came to where the Buddha was and rose from her seat within the assembly.
To make offerings to the Buddha, he went to his own palace to fetch the requisites for worship, returned to the Buddha’s presence, and having paid respectful homage, addressed the Buddha, saying:

“I know that throughout immeasurable lifetimes in the past, the World-Honored One has always dwelt upon this Mount Gayā; there, seventy-two thousand Buddhas all expounded for the World-Honored One the words and meanings of this Dharma-gate.”
"Now the World-Honored One is dwelling again on this mountain, and for our sake he has expounded all the words and phrases of this Dharma-gate.
The Buddha said, "O Goddess!"
"It is of great benefit for you now to have heard such a jewel of the Dharma!
At that time, there were also a multitude of devaputras who thought to themselves:
"This long-lived goddess has served the Tathāgata for so long and has heard this Dharma-gate."
"Why is it that they are unable to transform this female body?
At that time, the Bodhisattva Vidyutpradīpa, knowing what the sons of the gods were thinking in their minds, addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"

For what reason and by what causal conditions has this long-lived goddess, having made offerings to the Tathāgata for such a long time and having heard this Dharma-gate of great majestic power, still been unable to transform this female body?
The Buddha said,
“Good son! This goddess Dīrghāyuṣā dwells in the dharma-gate of inconceivable liberation for the sake of benefiting all sentient beings.”
"Good son! I know that in the past, this goddess was able to exhort and entreat countless Buddhas, Tathāgatas, to resolve upon bodhicitta and even until their parinirvāṇa."

This goddess possesses great majesty and power; she has made offerings to all the Buddhas throughout the Bhadrakalpa, and in this buddha-field, she shall manifest perfect enlightenment under the name of Jīvita Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha.
At that time, the Bhagavān addressed the goddess, saying: “Goddess!
You should manifest your own buddha-field.”
At that moment, the goddess immediately manifested the entry into the *sarvarūpakāyapraveśa-samādhi*.
Having entered this meditative absorption, this trichiliocosm became as level as the palm of a hand, composed entirely of vaidūrya jewels.

Having removed all the evil mountains, rocks, grasses, and trees, he manifested everywhere kalpavṛkṣa trees, flowing springs, and bathing pools; the pools were filled with water of eight virtues, and upon the surface of that water, various flowers spread in profusion.
Furthermore, it can eliminate the inferiority of those sentient beings, to the point that even the name "woman" is not heard.
Everywhere there appear various lotus flowers as large as chariot wheels, within which various bodhisattvas sit in the full-lotus posture.
He also manifests the body of a Bhagavān—namely, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Amitāyus—expounding the sublime Dharma for the sake of all bodhisattvas.
Surrounded before and behind by immeasurable hundreds of thousands of koṭis of nayutas of Śakras, Brahmās, Lokapālas, and great Bodhisattvas, he taught this Dharma-gate.
At that time, the goddess Dīrghāyuṣā rose from her meditative concentration, circumambulated the World-Honored One three times to the right, and vanished from the midst of the great assembly.
The Bodhisattva Vighuṣṭaśabda addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!”

If there are good men or good women who, upon hearing this Dharma-gate, are able to receive and uphold it, read it, recite it, reflect upon it, or explain it extensively for others—how much merit will such persons produce?
The Buddha said, "Good son!

Suppose there were someone who could practice giving to all sentient beings throughout the trichiliocosm, continuing such acts of giving without interruption for immeasurable hundreds of thousands of kalpas; [yet this would not equal the merit of one who hears this Dharma-door of the Great Vehicle with a single thought of faith]."

If a son of good family or a daughter of good family is able to transcribe this Dharma-gate, having carefully proofread it, and is able to bestow it upon others so that they may give rise to pure faith, the merit of this person surpasses the previous merit.
Why is this? Good son! Because that gift of material wealth is an inferior dharma, for it is subject to destruction.
The gift of Dharma is preeminent and possesses great majestic power. Why is this?
O son of good family!

Because sentient beings are stained by and attached to property and wealth, they transmigrate through birth and death for immeasurable periods; delighting in worldly dharmas, they are ultimately unable to receive the vast flavor of the Dharma.

"Good son! If there were one who could establish all sentient beings within the trichiliocosm in the ten paths of wholesome action, and another who could hear, read, recite, contemplate, practice, and explain to others this supreme Dharma-gate, the merit of this latter person would surpass the former's merit."
Why is this? Good son, it is because the ten paths of wholesome action arise from this Dharma-gate.
"Good son! If there were someone who taught and transformed all sentient beings in the trichiliocosm so that they all attained the fruits of śrāvaka and pratyekabuddha;

and if there were another who, upon hearing this Dharma-gate, received, upheld, read, recited, contemplated, practiced, and extensively explained it to others—the merit of this latter person would surpass the previous merit."
Why is this? Son of good family!

By relying on this Dharma-gate, one attains the fruits of all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas; furthermore, by relying on this Dharma-gate, one attains the fruits of all bodhisattvas and the supramundane Buddhas.
"Good son! If one is able to hear, receive, uphold, read, and recite this Dharma-gate, that person has already received, upheld, read, and recited all the sūtras."
Why is this? Because this Dharma-gate is the mother of all dharmas. Good son!
"It is not that one can realize the vast Dharma-nature without first attaining this Dharma-nature.

At that time, the great Śrāvakas, empowered by the Buddha’s majestic spiritual authority, rose from their seats, bared their right shoulders, knelt with their right knees on the ground, and with palms joined in reverence, addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
"Having heard this Dharma-gate, we shall certainly be able to emerge from the vast cycle of birth and death!
The Buddha said, "O Bhikṣus!..."
"So it is, so it is! It is just as you have said!
At that time, the Bhagavān addressed the great assembly, saying:
“Good son! If this Dharma-gate is taught in such places, you should know that those lands are sites of the bodhimaṇḍa and places where the wheel of Dharma is turned.”
Furthermore, one should contemplate that this ground is the site of a great caitya, and that all our Teachers dwell therein. Why is this?
Good son! Because the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) is itself great bodhi, because it is also the turning of the wheel of Dharma, and because the Dharma-body (dharmakāya) is itself all Tathāgatas.
If one makes offerings to the Dharma, it is equivalent to making offerings to all Tathāgatas.

Wherever the Dharma teacher resides, one should conceive of that place as a sacred site; toward the Dharma teacher, one should conceive of him as worthy of veneration, as a spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra), and as one who expounds the path of true liberation.
If you see a Dharma teacher, you should feel joy, pure faith, and delight; you should invite him to take his seat, respectfully make offerings to him, and praise him, saying, "Excellent!
O son of good family!
Even if I were to praise the merits of a Dharma-preacher until the end of an eon, I could not describe even a small fraction of those merits. Why is this?

If there were a son of good family or a daughter of good family who loves the Dharma and, at the place where a Dharma-preacher travels, were to sprinkle their own blood upon the path, they still could not repay even a small portion of the kindness and virtue of that Dharma-preacher.
Why is this? Because a Dharma teacher is able to uphold the Tathāgata’s eye of the Dharma, which is most rare and marvelous. Good son!

When any Dharma-preachers wish to expound this Dharma-gate—whether they are currently expounding it or have already expounded it—they should manifest fearlessness, not become despondent, show no signs of distress, and harbor no harmful intent; they should wear fresh, clean robes and give rise to pure faith.

When praising others, one should not be arrogant, nor give rise to conceit; one should not praise oneself or disparage others, and being free from expectations, one should always respectfully expound this Dharma.
At that time, Śakra Devānām Indra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

In whatever regions there may be a place where this Dharma-gate is being expounded, I shall lead my armies and retinue to that location for the purpose of hearing this Dharma-gate and to protect the teacher who preaches it.”
The Buddha said, “Kauśika, excellent, excellent!”
"You should now properly perform such deeds; you must protect the dharmatā of the Tathāgata.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Vighuṣṭaśabdagañja addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!..."
"What should this Dharma gate be named?
How should we receive and uphold it?
The Buddha said:

“Good son! This is called the ‘Dharma Gate of the Jewel Rain,’ and it is also called the ‘Accumulation of Jewel Merit,’ and also called the ‘Lamp of Wisdom,’ and also called the ‘Dharma Gate Asked by the Bodhisattva Sarvanīvaraṇaviṣkambhin.’”
"You should receive and uphold this!
When the Blessed One had finished speaking this sutra, he was filled with immeasurable joy.

All the Śrīs, as well as the bodhisattvas, all the śrāvakas, Śakra, Brahmā, the World Protectors, Maheśvara, the gods of the Pure Abodes, and countless hundreds of thousands of devaputras—along with the devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, and mahoragas—hearing what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
The Sūtra of the Precious Rain Spoken by the Buddha, Scroll Ten.
